                 CHAPTER 1

INTRODUCTION, OVERVIEW, AND BASIC INFORMATION




                     -1-
 1                 PACIFIC GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY
 2                 ELECTRICAL UNDERGROUNDING PLAN
 3                             CHAPTER 1
 4           INTRODUCTION, OVERVIEW, AND BASIC INFORMATION

 5   A. Introduction
 6           Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) presents our 10-Year Electrical
 7       Undergrounding Plan (EUP) to the Office of Energy Infrastructure Safety
 8       (Energy Safety). Our EUP describes our framework to select overhead circuit
 9       segments to be undergrounded in Tier 2 or Tier 3 High Fire Threat Districts
10       (HFTD) or Fire Rebuild areas. The remainder of this chapter is organized as
11       follows:
12       •   Section B provides an Executive Summary;
13       •   Section C summarizes the background regarding PG&E’s wildfire mitigation
14           programs and the EUP;
15       •   Section D provides an overview of risk reduction, program benefits, and
16           customer affordability;
17       •   Section E includes basic information required by Section 2.2 of the EUP
18           Guidelines;1
19       •   Section F provides a summary of EUP requirements and identifies the
20           location of responsive information throughout the EUP; and
21       •   Section G lists supporting attachments.

22   B. Executive Summary
23           PG&E’s EUP is designed to deliver meaningful, long-term benefits for our
24       customers, communities, and the broader public by improving safety, reliability,
25       affordability, and resilience in the face of growing wildfire risk. Undergrounding
26       virtually eliminates wildfire risk and keeps our communities safe in the locations
27       where it is most needed, providing a targeted and durable solution for the
28       highest-risk areas. Our EUP provides significant, quantifiable, and meaningful
29       benefits including:




     1   Office of Energy Infrastructure Safety, 10-Year Electrical Undergrounding Plan
         Guidelines (Feb. 20, 2025) (EUP Guidelines).

                                                 -2-
 1       •   Greater safety for customers and communities: Wildfire risk continues to
 2           increase as weather events become more frequent and severe, reinforcing
 3           the need for long-term investments that deliver lasting risk reduction. The
 4           EUP will protect communities by undergrounding 5,000 miles of electric
 5           distribution lines in the highest-risk areas, permanently reducing wildfire risk
 6           by approximately 98 percent where undergrounding has taken place and
 7           lowering total Wildfire and Outage Program Risk by approximately
 8           $117 billion over the life of the assets.2
 9       •   Fewer outages and improved reliability: Customers benefit from a safer,
10           more reliable electric system as undergrounding can eliminate the need for
11           Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) and Enhanced Powerline Safety
12           Settings (EPSS) on underground lines and has been shown to reduce
13           outages by approximately 90 percent where undergrounding has been
14           completed.
15       •   Lower costs and improved affordability: The EUP will help reduce
16           undergrounding costs over time by leveraging economies of scale and
17           innovation through long-term planning and program development, including
18           new installation methods and more efficient sourcing and contracting. The
19           EUP prioritizes the most cost-effective solutions by comparing
20           undergrounding with other system hardening mitigations so customers
21           benefit from the most efficient investments. Since 2018, we have reduced
22           the cost of undergrounding per mile by approximately 25 percent through
23           innovation and efficiencies. The EUP will facilitate further cost reductions for
24           our critical undergrounding work.
25       •   Undergrounding benefits exceed customer costs: The EUP represents
26           capital expenditures of approximately $11.4 billion3 to install


     2   $117 billion is the present value of the combined measure of Ignition Risk and Outage
         Program Risk over the 55-year underground asset life. This measure applies a risk
         scaling factor and is based on unmitigated wildfire risk, which assumes operational
         mitigations such as EPSS and PSPS are not in place. Consistent with Energy Safety’s
         requirements, PG&E will report compliance metrics throughout the plan using the
         unscaled, mitigated baseline described in Chapter 1 Section D, Chapter 2 Section C,
         and Chapter 7, Core Capability 6 (Establishing and Updating the Baseline).
     3   $11.4 billion is the present value of the estimated capital expenditure costs for 5,000
         underground miles from 2028 to 2037. This is equivalent to approximately $16.6 billion
         in escalated capital expenditures.

                                                 -3-
 1            5,000 underground miles, delivering total, permanent risk reduction benefits
 2            of approximately $117 billion. These benefits are approximately ten times
 3            the capital cost of undergrounding the proposed miles.
 4       •    Reduced ongoing operating costs and infrastructure investments:
 5            Customers will also benefit from reduced operations and maintenance costs
 6            for underground assets by approximately $1.5 million per mile (or $6.0 billion
 7            total),4 as underground facilities are less exposed to vegetation, weather,
 8            and many other sources of infrastructure damage that drive maintenance
 9            and replacement costs for overhead facilities.
10       •    Lower wildfire-related losses and costs for our communities: The EUP
11            reduces the economic impacts of wildfire by reducing:
12            −       Systemwide, permanent wildfire risk by approximately $105 billion;5
13            −       Average annual utility infrastructure losses by approximately
14                    $83 million;6
15            −       Average annual losses from utility-reportable wildfires by approximately
16                    21 percent for residential and commercial customers;7 and
17            −       Homeowners’ insurance premiums, which are estimated to be reduced
18                    by insurers as a result of reducing wildfire risk through undergrounding.8
19            Our EUP is based on extensive analyses to target and select
20       undergrounding projects in areas of highest wildfire risk. We describe our
21       framework for prioritizing undergrounding projects based on wildfire risk
22       reduction, public safety, cost efficiency, and reliability benefits. We also include
23       timelines for completing prioritized undergrounding projects along with unit cost
24       targets and mileage completion forecasts for each year of the EUP. We
25       compare the substantial benefits of undergrounding to other system hardening



     4   Avoided costs are presented based on expected O&M savings over the 55-year asset
         life for each overhead mile removed.
     5   $105 billion of wildfire risk reduction is the present value of the monetized, scaled risk
         over the 55-year asset life, leveraging unmitigated wildfire risk. For reference, the
         unscaled wildfire risk value, with operational mitigations in place, is calculated as
         approximately $4.5 billion.
     6   Attach. B, WP005 (Marsh, Third Party Impact Analysis of PG&E’s 10-Year
         Undergrounding Plan, September 2026, p. 10).
     7   Id., p. 3.
     8   Id., p. 12.

                                                   -4-
 1       mitigations over the life of the EUP. We also include our plan for utility and
 2       contractor workforce development, an evaluation of project costs and projected
 3       economic benefits, and plans to reduce undergrounding costs and continue our
 4       sustainable supply chain.
 5            The remainder of this summary provides additional detail regarding the
 6       significant, quantifiable, and meaningful benefits of the EUP, as well as the
 7       analytical approach that we used to develop the EUP.

 8       1. Achieving Substantial Risk Reduction
 9                PG&E’s EUP is designed to achieve the legislative objective9 of
10            substantially and permanently reducing wildfire risk and improving electrical
11            reliability by replacing the highest-risk overhead distribution lines with
12            underground infrastructure. The proposed portfolio will install approximately
13            5,000 miles of underground distribution facilities, replacing approximately
14            4,000 miles of overhead distribution lines located in Tier 2 and Tier 3 High
15            Fire Threat Districts and Fire Rebuild areas. Over the 55-year life of the
16            underground assets, the EUP is expected to reduce total Wildfire and
17            Outage Program Risk by approximately $117 billion,10 including

14           undergrounding necessary to deliver substantial system-level wildfire and

16           program over the ten-year planning horizon. In developing the portfolio,

 8         PG&E’s EUP achieves these benefits through a data-driven framework
 9     that identifies and prioritizes locations with the greatest wildfire and reliability
10     risk. Using the Wildfire Distribution Risk Model, Outage Program Risk Model,
11     benefit-cost analyses, and project-level screening criteria, PG&E has
12     developed a portfolio that focuses investment where undergrounding provides
13     the greatest overall benefit. This framework ensures that PG&E is
14     undergrounding the right facilities in the right locations to deliver substantial
15     and measurable risk reduction for customers and communities.

16   2. Framework and Models for Selecting the Right Work in the Right
17      Places
18          PG&E’s Project Acceptance Framework provides a structured,
19      risk-based process to systematically identify, evaluate, and prioritize
20      undergrounding projects for the EUP. Through this framework, we derived a
21      targeted portfolio of approximately 5,000 miles of underground distribution
22      lines. The Project Acceptance Framework applies four sequential screens
23      to the full population of circuit segments in PG&E’s service territory,
24      progressively narrowing the population to those located in high-fire-risk or
25      Wildfire Rebuild Areas that meet defined risk thresholds, and demonstrate
26      meaningful wildfire risk reduction, public safety, reliability, and
27      cost-efficiency benefits. Through standardized benefit-cost comparisons,
28      project-specific scoping, and refinement of alternative mitigations, we will
29      advance the highest-value projects through the framework and prioritize a
30      final, executable portfolio sized to achieve the Plan Mitigation Objective.
31      The framework also establishes transparent methods for staying up-to-date
32      by incorporating data changes over time, subdividing projects when needed
33      for efficiency and implementation, and sequencing work to maximize
34      portfolio-level risk reduction. The Project Acceptance Framework ensures

                                            -9-
 1           that we are undergrounding the right lines in the right places to deliver
 2           substantial benefits for the investment.
 3                To implement the framework and meet the analytical requirements, we
 4           use a suite of risk models to establish, measure, and monitor the substantial
 5           risk reduction achieved through the EUP.
 6                Our integrated, risk-informed modeling framework quantitatively
 7           evaluates wildfire risk and electric reliability impacts across the electric
 8           distribution system. The framework combines the Wildfire Distribution Risk
 9           Model (WDRM), which estimates ignition likelihood and potential wildfire
10           consequences at the circuit-segment level; the Outage Program Risk Model
11           (OPRM), which quantifies customer reliability impacts associated with EPSS
12           and PSPS; and the Wildfire Benefit-Cost Analysis (WBCA), which evaluates
13           lifecycle costs and benefits of system hardening mitigations. Together,
14           these models support consistent, bottom-up portfolio and system-level
15           decision-making, enabling PG&E to identify high-risk locations, evaluate
16           tradeoffs between different mitigation strategies, and account for climate
17           change and uncertainty. Through our modeling, we demonstrate substantial
18           wildfire risk reduction and reliability improvements from these cost-effective
19           investments in the communities we are privileged to serve.

20   C. Background
21                California Senate Bill (SB) 884, which was enacted in 2022, requires the
22           California Public Utilities Commission (Commission) to establish a ten-year
23           utility distribution infrastructure undergrounding program for the dual
24           purpose of reducing wildfire risk and reliance on outage programs to
25           mitigate wildfire risk. SB 884 divides responsibility for implementing the
26           program between Energy Safety and the Commission. If a large electrical
27           corporation wishes to participate in the program, they must submit a
28           distribution infrastructure undergrounding plan to Energy Safety. Once
29           submitted, Energy Safety is responsible for review and approval of the
30           utility’s plan in compliance with SB 884 requirements for project selection
31           and risk reduction (Phase 1).16 The Commission is then responsible
32           for approval of the utility’s application for cost recovery for SB 884 projects


     16 Pub. Util. Code, § 8388.5(c)(1).

                                               -10-
 1           (Phase 2).17 In Resolution SPD-37, the Commission adopted updated
 2           Phase 2 Guidelines and directed the Investor Owned Utilities (IOUs) to
 3           submit proposals addressing certain cost recovery issues that remained
 4           unresolved, including Benefit Cost Ratio (BCR)18 methodology, audit
 5           methodology, and additional cost recovery conditions.19
 6               Since passing SB 884, both Governor Newsom and the California
 7           Legislature have continued to emphasize the risks posed to the state by
 8           wildfires and the heightened need to reduce those risks and improve
 9           resilience. In September 2025, Governor Newsom signed California SB 254
10           to improve wildfire resilience, lower electricity costs, and accelerate clean
11           energy development. The Legislature found and declared the following
12           urgent climate-driven risks in SB 254:
13               (a) Climate change is driving an increase in the frequency and severity
14               of extreme weather events, … including … a significant increase in the
15               incidence and severity of catastrophic wildfires. These extreme weather
16               events impose profound risks to public health, natural resources,
17               infrastructure, and California’s economy.
18               (b) Wildfires [in California] have grown significantly more intense and
19               destructive in recent years….
20               (c) [C]limate change has dramatically increased the number of acres in
21               California considered High Fire Risk Areas [HFRA].
22               (d) Wildfire risk is destabilizing the . . . insurance market, increasing the
23               number of California homeowners who are unable to obtain
24               insurance….20

25               The California Earthquake Authority echoed these climate-driven risks
26           and economic impacts in its April 2026 SB 254 report:

23   D. Risk Reduction and Other Benefits
24           Undergrounding the highest risk circuit segments in PG&E’s service territory
25       is the best solution to address wildfire risk, which is increasing in both frequency
26       and severity. Undergrounding primary electric distribution lines permanently
27       reduces wildfire risk by approximately 98 percent in that location.23 The
28       benefits of undergrounding, including permanent wildfire risk reduction, reliability
29       improvement, and operational cost avoidance (e.g., less vegetation
30       management), make it the best long-term investment for customers and
31       communities in many high wildfire risk areas.

 1       1. Substantial Wildfire Risk Reduction
 2                In SB 884, the Legislature identified wildfire risk reduction as a central
 3            objective of the EUP and requires a utility to demonstrate that its plan will
 4            substantially reduce wildfire risk and substantially improve electrical
 5            reliability. Specifically, Energy Safety may approve an EUP only if the utility
 6            demonstrates that the plan will substantially increase electrical reliability by
 7            reducing the use of PSPS, EPSS, de-energization events, and other outage
 8            programs, while also substantially reducing wildfire risk.24
 9                Since 2018, PG&E's wildfire mitigation strategy has combined
10            permanent system hardening measures, including undergrounding, with
11            operational mitigations such as PSPS and EPSS to reduce wildfire risk
12            during periods of elevated fire danger. While operational mitigations provide
13            important layers of protection, they complement but not replace long-term
14            infrastructure investments. As undergrounding projects are completed, the
15            need for PSPS decreases because underground infrastructure is
16            substantially less susceptible to the ignition mechanisms that affect
17            overhead electric facilities.
18                The Commission has repeatedly emphasized that PSPS should be
19            treated as a mitigation measure of last resort rather than a permanent
20            wildfire mitigation strategy and has directed utilities to reduce reliance on
21            PSPS as infrastructure improvements are deployed.25 PG&E agrees with
22            this policy direction and believes that permanent system hardening
23            measures, including undergrounding, should be prioritized over continued

        settings, deenergization events, and any other outage programs, and substantially
        reduce the risk of wildfire. (emphasis added). Section 8388.5(c)(2) requires the utility to
        include in the EUP: a means of prioritizing Undergrounding Projects based on “wildfire

 1           reliance on operational mitigations. The Commission further recognized in
 2           PG&E's 2023 General Rate Case that increased undergrounding is
 3           expected to reduce reliance on both PSPS and EPSS and provide
 4           meaningful benefits to customers and communities by avoiding power
 5           outages associated with those programs.26
 6               Consistent with Energy Safety guidance, PG&E evaluates
 7           undergrounding projects relative to a baseline that includes existing
 8           operational mitigations such as PSPS and EPSS. This mitigated baseline
 9           calculates the incremental benefit of undergrounding relative to current
10           system operations. However, using PSPS and EPSS as a permanent
11           baseline assumption effectively assumes that those outage programs will
12           remain in place indefinitely. Such an assumption understates the long-term
13           value of undergrounding because it compares a permanent infrastructure
14           investment against temporary operational mitigations that the Commission
15           has directed utilities to reduce over time. Further, using this mitigated
16           baseline to select projects discounts the actual wildfire risk reduction value
17           of undergrounding (which permanently reduces wildfire risk) as these
18           temporary operational mitigations should not be relied on in perpetuity.
19               Accordingly, in addition to the Energy Safety-required analysis, PG&E
20           presents an alternative analysis using a scaled, unmitigated baseline that
21           excludes the impacts of PSPS and EPSS. This analysis is necessary to
22           demonstrate the full magnitude of the permanent wildfire risk reduction and
23           reliability benefits that undergrounding provides and more accurately reflects
24           the objectives of SB 884 to demonstrate that the EUP will substantially
25           reduce wildfire risk and improve reliability.
26               Table 1-2 compares the results under both approaches. Using Energy
27           Safety's required unscaled mitigated baseline with PSPS and EPSS in
28           place, the proposed EUP produces approximately $15.1 billion in total

10   3. Mitigating the Impacts of Climate Change
11              Climate change is making California’s wildfire conditions more frequent,
12          severe, and destructive, and is expanding high-fire-risk areas. In the face of
13          these growing wildfire risks, proactive investments in mitigation,
14          infrastructure resilience and community preparedness are necessary to




                                               -16-
 1           reduce future wildfire impacts.28 The proposed undergrounding
 2           investments materially reduce annual losses attributable to climate change
 3           from approximately 7 percent to less than 1 percent by 2037.29 The
 4           benefits of the proposed EUP are even more pronounced for severe wildfire
 5           scenarios—reducing climate-driven extreme losses30 by approximately
 6           $1.2 billion and most-extreme losses31 by approximately $869 million.32
 7           Thus, in addition to reducing current wildfire risk, these results demonstrate
 8           that undergrounding also strengthens system resilience against worsening
 9           future wildfire conditions.

11           (i.e., 1-in-100-year losses) in PG&E’s service territory due to forecast
12           climate change impacts from 2028 to 2037. As illustrated, there are
13           15 counties that can expect to see a significant increase in forecasted
14           extreme losses of more than $100 million.
15                Figure 1-3 illustrates the anticipated reduction in losses from extreme
16           wildfires (i.e., 1-in-100-year losses) by 2037 in PG&E’s service territory
17           resulting from the reduction of wildfire risk due to this EUP. Overall, we
18           forecast that 30 counties will see a decrease in extreme losses in areas
19           where PG&E expects to underground overhead lines.

 1               Given the impacts of climate change, the cost of inaction or less

 4       4. Reducing the Severity and Frequency of Utility-Caused Wildfires
 5               From 2014-2024, approximately 81 percent of the losses due to wildfires
 6           in PG&E’s service territory were attributed to electrical power infrastructure
 7           (distribution and transmission systems) even though electrical power
 8           infrastructure was the cause of only 9 percent of wildfires.33 Given the
 9           severity of recent fires, the growing threats from climate change and the
10           lasting damage that wildfires cause in our communities, it is imperative that
11           we do everything possible to reduce the likelihood that our infrastructure will
12           cause a wildfire.
13               The undergrounding work in our EUP, along with overhead hardening
14           and remote grid work and other wildfire mitigation activities presented in our
15           Wildfire Mitigation Plans, will allow us to significantly reduce wildfire risk,
16           reliability risk, and the associated economic losses in our service territory.
17           The EUP will help mitigate significant residential and commercial losses due
18           to utility-caused wildfire risk by approximately 21 percent. See Table 1-4
19           below for the summary of annual customer losses due to wildfire that would
20           be avoided due to the implementation of our EUP.34

                                                -20-
 1       5. Decreasing Losses to PG&E’s Distribution Infrastructure
 2                Climate impacts and infrastructure costs are closely linked because
 3            changing environmental conditions directly affect both the performance and
 4            lifespan of infrastructure assets, while also driving the need for new
 5            investments. As climate change increases the frequency and severity of
 6            weather-related hazards, it leads to faster equipment degradation, higher
 7            failure rates, and reduced asset lifespans, particularly for overhead electric
 8            assets exposed to the weather. These physical impacts translate into rising
 9            costs through more frequent repairs, increased operations and maintenance
10            expenses, and higher replacement needs for damaged assets. Ultimately
11            this drives significant long-term increases in infrastructure investment and
12            total system costs that must be borne by customers.35
13                PG&E currently faces an estimated average annual loss of $512 million
14            due to damage to our distribution infrastructure caused by wildfires.36 By
15            2037, this average annual loss is expected to increase to approximately
16            $584 million or an increase of 14 percent due to climate change.37 Due to
17            our proposed undergrounding work, we expect our average annual losses to
18            distribution infrastructure from wildfire damage to decrease by approximately
19            $83 million or 17 percent for the remaining lifetime of distribution assets in
20            the HFTD.38

21       6. Continuing the Successful Trajectory of the Undergrounding Program
22                PG&E's EUP builds on the strong foundation of the Undergrounding
23            Program established through prior General Rate Case (GRC) decisions and
24            reflects years of programmatic learning, innovation, and execution. The
25            Program has matured considerably since its inception — expanding from
26            rebuilding communities affected by wildfire, to proactively hardening facilities
27            across High Fire-Threat Districts (HFTD), and increasingly applying targeted

     35 Fant, et al., Science Direct, Vol. 195, Climate change impacts and costs to U.S.
        electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure (Mar. 15, 2020), available at:
        https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360544220300062?fr=RR-
        2&ref=pdf_download&rr=a06930fefc5f1321 (accessed June 4, 2026).
     36 Attach. B, WP005 (Marsh, Third Party Impact Analysis of PG&E’s 10-Year
        Undergrounding Plan, September 2026, p. 10).
     37 Id.
     38 Id.

                                                  -21-
 1           undergrounding where it delivers the greatest value, such as protecting
 2           critical egress routes and addressing elevated tree-strike risk.
 3               As the benefits of undergrounding became increasingly evident, PG&E
 4           accelerated this strategy and, in 2021, announced plans to significantly
 5           expand undergrounding in HFTDs as a cornerstone of its long-term wildfire
 6           mitigation strategy.
 7               The results to date demonstrate both the effectiveness and scalability of
 8           the Program. From 2021 to 2027, PG&E will install more than 1,900 miles
 9           of underground distribution miles and reduce approximately 14 percent of
10           Ignition Risk39 in the HFTD and HFRA. In that same time, we have reduced
11           the cost per mile by approximately 25 percent (over $1 million per mile
12           before escalation) through innovation and gaining efficiencies at scale.40
13           These achievements provide a strong foundation for the EUP and
14           demonstrate PG&E's ability to deliver substantial risk reduction while
15           continuing to improve program efficiency.

16       7. Incorporating Affordability into the EUP
17               We are proud of our Undergrounding Program, the work we have
18           completed, and the efficiencies we have achieved thus far. While
19           undergrounding is the best long-term solution to reduce wildfire risk and
20           significantly reduce outage risk, we also recognize that it should be
21           undertaken in the most appropriate, high-risk areas. Energy Safety has
22           highlighted the importance of cost effectiveness through the EUP
23           requirements for selecting the appropriate mitigation(s) for each circuit
24           segment. In addition, the CPUC, Safety Policy Division (SPD), and
25           Governor Newsom have all stressed the need to carefully balance risk
26           reduction and affordability.41 In its decision on PG&E’s 2023 GRC, the


     39 Value calculated based on the ignition risk reduced from system hardening

        this period.
     40 From 2018-2020, the average unit cost was $4.25 million per mile and from 2023-2025
        the average unit cost was approximately $3.25 million per mile.

                                               -22-
 1           CPUC similarly stated that it was “reasonable to find that ratepayers’ ability
 2           to pay for safety or risk reduction is not unlimited; as with all safety
 3           measures,” PG&E, the CPUC, and stakeholders “must consider the cost and
 4           impact on affordability.”42
 5               We agree that affordability is an essential consideration when evaluating
 6           risk reduction alternatives. In the highest risk locations, the benefits of
 7           undergrounding, including greater wildfire risk reduction, reliability
 8           improvement, and operational cost avoidance, ultimately make
 9           undergrounding the best investment for customers and communities. PG&E
10           remains focused on keeping our customers and communities safe and
11           providing reliable service at affordable rates, with undergrounding as a key
12           element in delivering that vision.
13               Our EUP considers affordability by analyzing the potential to use other
14           mitigations, including overhead hardening or remote grid as cost-effective
15           alternatives. PG&E only selects undergrounding where our data and
16           analyses support it as the appropriate mitigation for a particular location. As
17           a result, it is likely that our workplan will include hybrid mitigations—i.e.
18           mitigations including both undergrounding and overhead hardening—on
19           some circuit segments.
20               As we execute our EUP, we are committed to pursuing a range of
21           cost-containment strategies to reduce undergrounding costs. Our EUP will
22           drive further efficiency through achieving economies of scale and
23           encouraging additional technological and process innovations. PG&E has
24           identified and implemented operational efficiencies through new sourcing
25           approaches and updated construction standards, and implemented waste
26           reduction practices, innovations, and new installation methods. Greater
27           long-term certainty about program funding will allow us to negotiate more
28           favorable pricing with contractors, suppliers, and equipment manufacturers;
29           expand use of fixed-price and optimized contracts; bundle
30           geographically-related work; and build a more levelized, construction-ready
31           pipeline of projects. Further, a stable, multi-year view of projects will
32           improve PG&E’s ability to coordinate with communities, counties, and


     42 D.23-11-069, p. 799, Finding of Fact 98.

                                                  -23-
 1           customers—and to sequence work alongside planned community projects—
 2           improving the customer experience.
 3                In addition to reducing the upfront capital costs, PG&E is pursuing
 4           opportunities to create efficiencies and reduce costs over the life of the
 5           undergrounding assets. For example, undergrounding projects can deliver
 6           substantial savings by completing or eliminating the need for previously
 7           identified maintenance work as part of project construction; thereby avoiding
 8           duplicative work, reducing overall maintenance costs, and minimizing
 9           customer impacts. Between 2021 and 2025, undergrounding avoided
10           approximately $72 million in maintenance costs. PG&E expects to realize
11           similar savings with EUP undergrounding projects.
12                Further, undergrounding is expected to save approximately $1.5 million
13           per overhead mile removed, in long-term operations and maintenance costs
14           when compared to overhead hardening due to the reduced need for
15           maintenance activities such as vegetation management, outage response,
16           and patrols and inspections.43 PG&E is continuing to work to reduce the
17           cost of both the capital installation and lifetime operations and maintenance
18           costs to support affordability for our customers.

19       8. Improving System Reliability
20                Weather-related events such as snow, ice, high winds, flooding, and
21           lightning strikes account for most major power interruptions attributable to
22           electric distribution infrastructure nationwide, causing approximately
23           78 percent of major outages.44 This trend is likely to worsen as climate
24           change intensifies weather-related stresses on electric infrastructure in
25           addition to increasing the frequency and cost of outages. PG&E analyzed
26           the reliability performance on sections of circuits where undergrounding


     43 Chapter 5 Section C.3 of the EUP includes further information on the costs and benefits
        of undergrounding.
     44 Fant, et al., Science Direct, Vol. 195, Climate change impacts and costs to U.S.

        https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360544220300062?fr=RR-

 1           work was completed and found an approximate 90 percent reduction in
 2           sustained outages.45 While reliability benefits from non-EPSS and
 3           non-PSPS outages are not the focus of this EUP, they are expected to be a
 4           meaningful, additional benefit of undergrounding for our customers and
 5           should not be ignored.
 6               Finally, undergrounding is the most effective means to improve system
 7           reliability due to outages caused by PSPS and EPSS. These operational
 8           mitigations provide important, temporary layers of wildfire protection across
 9           PG&E’s system; however, PSPS and EPSS involve tradeoffs with electric
10           service reliability. In 2025, PG&E estimates that these measures resulted in
11           more than 280 million customer minutes interrupted. Where deployed,
12           undergrounding can reduce or eliminate distribution PSPS events and
13           eliminate EPSS-caused outages for those customers.

14       9. Protecting California Homeowners
15               Access to property insurance in California’s HFTD/HFRA locations has
16           deteriorated significantly in recent years, with insurers electing not to renew
17           policies, restricting new business policies, and some exiting the state
18           entirely.46 The costs to insure a home in California have increased by over
19           23 percent from 2017 to 2022,47 with many in the highest-risk areas being
20           forced into the Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan (FAIR Plan) and
21           paying more for coverage that is less comprehensive than standard
22           policies.48




     45 PG&E analyzed the reliability performance on sections of circuits where we performed

        overall improvements to service reliability. PG&E’s analysis included
        approximately 980 outages between 2021 and 2025 and showed an approximate
        90 percent reduction in faults that resulted in sustained outages after this
        undergrounding work was completed.

 1                 The increasing risk and losses attributable to wildfire are the primary
 2             drivers of increased costs and insurance policy cancellations. By
 3             significantly reducing the risk of wildfire associated with utility infrastructure
 4             through undergrounding, we are addressing a key driver of the insurance
 5             market instability in California. All else being equal, it is estimated that
 6             during the 10-year EUP period, the wildfire risk reduction achieved from
 7             undergrounding could facilitate a reduction in homeowner insurance
 8             premiums for commercially-available insurance plans in our service territory
 9             of 18 percent.49

 3   F. Undergrounding Plan Requirements
 4            PG&E’s EUP is designed to meet the EUP requirements in both SB 884 and
 5       the EUP Guidelines.
 6            Our EUP is coordinated with the Phase 1 Joint IOU Application pending
 7       before the CPUC50 and the forthcoming Phase 2 CPUC Application where we
 8       will seek cost recovery for the approved EUP. These filings are interdependent,
 9       particularly with respect to the BCR methodology that aligns with the CPUC’s
10       Risk-Based Decision-Making Framework (RDF) and associated data reporting
11       requirements. PG&E has endeavored to develop this EUP consistent with the
12       Commission’s regulatory guidance, including the cost recovery framework
13       established in CPUC Resolution SPD-37, the SPD 37 data reporting
14       requirements51 and the BCR methodology approved in Decisions 22-12-027
15       and 25-08-032.

 5   A. Introduction
 6           In this chapter, we address the requirements in Section 2.3 of the Electrical
 7       Undergrounding Plan (EUP) Guidelines to explain our Plan Mitigation Objective,
 8       targets and timeline, Plan Tracking Objectives, and risk calculations
 9           Section B lists the requirements from Senate Bill (SB) 884 and the EUP
10       Guidelines addressed in this chapter.
11           Section C provides our overarching demonstration of substantial risk
12       reduction. We explain how undergrounding reduces both Ignition Risk and
13       Reliability Risk, using Overall Utility Risk as an integrated, monetized metric.
14       We explain our identification of a Portfolio of approximately 4,000 overhead
15       miles (or 5,000 miles of undergrounding) that meets or exceeds the Plan
16       Mitigation Objective per mile target to reduce an average of $145,000 of Overall
17       Utility Risk per overhead mile per year,53 which is equivalent to $3 million of risk
18       reduction per mile over the 55-year life54 of the underground assets.
19           Section D explains the Plan Mitigation Objective, which is the measure that
20       will show that our execution of the EUP has substantially reduced Wildfire Risk
21       and increased reliability55 in the High Fire Threat Districts (HFTD) over the
22       ten-year period. The Plan Mitigation Objective is expressed as the monetized
23       value of the Overall Utility Risk reduced per primary overhead mile removed and
24       demonstrates that PG&E’s EUP will result in substantial risk reduction.
25           Section E describes the Plan Tracking Objectives, which are
26       forward-looking, quantifiable metrics used to monitor progress toward

        operational planning, PG&E uses scaled risk values.
     54 This is the present value of the Plan Mitigation Objective ($145,000 per mile of Overall

 5          Projects on Circuit Segments that include non-undergrounding Subprojects,
 6          such as Overhead System Hardening or other mitigations. We explain that only
 7          the risk reduction attributable to undergrounding is counted toward the Plan

 1       C. Demonstration of Substantial Risk Reduction (EUP Guidelines,
 2           Section 2.3)

              Pursuant to Section 8388.5(d)(2), the EUP can only be approved if it will (1)
          “substantially increase electrical reliability by reducing the use of public safety
          power shutoffs, enhanced powerline safety settings, deenergization events, and
          any other outage programs,” and (2) “substantially reduce the risk of wildfire.” To
          support this, the EUP must include the Plan Mitigation Objective, Plan Tracking
          Objectives, and other specific tracking objectives and targets as described below.


 3               Pursuant to Public Utilities Code Section 8388.5(d)(2), the EUP may be
 4           approved only if it will (1) “substantially increase electrical reliability by reducing
 5           the use of public safety power shutoffs, enhanced powerline safety settings,
 6           deenergization events, and any other outage programs,” and (2) “substantially
 7           reduce the risk of wildfire.” PG&E demonstrates that the EUP satisfies these
 8           requirements through the risk reduction achieved by the forecast EUP Portfolio,
 9           the Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives used to measure and
10           track that risk reduction, and supplemental analysis demonstrating the broader
11           long-term benefits of permanent underground infrastructure.

12           1. Risk Reduction Under the Energy Safety-Required Methodology
13                   Consistent with the EUP Guidelines, PG&E calculates Overall Utility
14               Risk56 on an unweighted and unscaled basis relative to a mitigated baseline
15               that reflects existing operational mitigations, including Public Safety Power


         56 The EUP Guidelines define Overall Utility Risk as “an unweighted and unscaled
            calculation.” EUP Guidelines, p. 31. For the purposes of operational planning, PG&E
            uses scaled risk values.

                                                    -45-
 1            Shutoffs (PSPS) and Enhanced Powerline Safety Settings (EPSS). Risk
 2            reduction is quantified as an integrated, monetized Overall Utility Risk
 3            reduced per primary overhead mile removed. PG&E’s EUP measures
 4            Overall Utility Risk reduction achieved through targeted undergrounding of
 5            the highest-risk Circuit Segments by quantifying the monetary value of the
 6            reductions in both Ignition Risk57 and Outage Program Risk.58 This
 7            measure provides the basis for establishing the Plan Mitigation Objective
 8            and Plan Tracking Objectives and for reporting progress under the EUP.
 9                Based on the Project Acceptance Framework59 and risk modeling,60
10            PG&E identified a forecast Portfolio of approximately 4,000 overhead miles
11            to be removed and deenergized. Replacing those overhead facilities is
12            expected to require approximately 5,000 underground miles, based on the
13            1.25 overhead-to-underground conversion factor used for EUP planning.
14            The two mileage values describe the same forecast portfolio: 4,000 miles
15            represents the primary overhead facilities removed, while 5,000 miles
16            represents the corresponding underground facilities installed. The forecast
17            Portfolio includes Circuit Segments that are eligible following Screen 2 and
18            have an undergrounding Benefit-Cost Ratio indicating that they are potential
19            candidates for inclusion in the EUP. Projects will continue to be evaluated,
20            refined, and selected through the remaining stages of the Project
21            Acceptance Framework.
22                Using the Energy Safety-required unscaled, mitigated methodology, the
23            forecast EUP Portfolio may reduce up to approximately $15.1 billion in
24            present-value Overall Utility Risk over the 55-year life of the underground
25            assets. This total includes approximately $4.5 billion in Ignition Risk
26            reduction and approximately $10.6 billion in Outage Program Risk




     57 Ignition Risk is the measure of impacts from wildfire at a given location. This metric is
        the product of two factors: (1) the likelihood a wildfire will occur, and (2) the potential
        consequences of a wildfire originating from this location.
     58 Outage Program Risk is the modeled risk associated with customer outages, including
        impacts from PSPS and EPSS, derived from outage risk modeling.
     59 See Chapter 3 for details.
     60 See Chapter 7 for details.

                                                  -46-
 1           reduction.61 These results demonstrate substantial reductions in both
 2           components of Overall Utility Risk under Energy Safety’s required
 3           methodology.
 4               Undergrounding provides a durable reduction in Ignition Risk by
 5           removing targeted overhead facilities and the associated ignition exposure.
 6           It also improves reliability by reducing the need to apply PSPS and EPSS to
 7           the undergrounded facilities. The magnitude and duration of these
 8           reductions demonstrate that the EUP will substantially reduce wildfire risk
 9           and substantially increase electrical reliability as required by Public Utilities
10           Code Section 8388.5(d)(2).

11       2. Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives
12               The Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives establish
13           the framework PG&E will use to measure, track, and report the risk
14           reduction achieved through implementation of the EUP.
15               Energy Safety defines the Plan Mitigation Objective as “the amount of
16           change in risk (wildfire and reliability) that is necessary to meet the
17           requirements of Public Utilities Code Section 8388.5(d)(2).”62 PG&E’s Plan
18           Mitigation Objective is: An annual average reduction of $145,000 in Overall
19           Utility Risk per primary overhead mile removed.
20               The Plan Mitigation Objective is based on the Energy Safety-required
21           unscaled, mitigated methodology described above. It reflects the combined
22           reduction in Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk attributable to EUP
23           undergrounding. The annual average reduction of $145,000 in Overall
24           Utility Risk is equivalent to approximately $3 million in present-value Overall
25           Utility Risk reduction per primary overhead mile removed over the 55-year
26           life of the underground assets. More detail about how the Plan Mitigation
27           Objective was developed can be found in Section D.1. below.
28               The Plan Tracking Objectives establish the annual, five-year, and
29           ten-year milestones PG&E will use to determine whether the EUP remains




     61 This value excludes the Risk Model Impact Factor described in Chapter 2 as described
        in Section 1.a. below.
     62 EUP Guidelines, Glossary, p. A-5.

                                                -47-
 1      on track to achieve the Plan Mitigation Objective. More detail about the Plan
 2      Tracking Objectives can be found in Section E below.
 3          The Plan Mitigation Objective defines the required risk reduction
 4      outcome on a per-mile basis, while the Plan Tracking Objectives provide the
 5      interim measures used to monitor progress toward that outcome. Together,
 6      the Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives provide an
 7      outcome-based framework for measuring the wildfire and reliability risk
 8      reduction delivered by the EUP.

 9   3. Supplemental Demonstration of the Long-Term Benefits of
10      Undergrounding
11          The Energy Safety-required unscaled, mitigated methodology provides
12      the basis for establishing and tracking the Plan Mitigation Objective and
13      Plan Tracking Objectives. However, as discussed in Chapter 1, this
14      methodology does not fully reflect the long-term value of replacing overhead
15      facilities with permanent underground infrastructure.
16          The mitigated baseline assumes that operational mitigations such as
17      PSPS and EPSS remain in place over the life of the underground assets.
18      Although PSPS and EPSS provide important layers of wildfire protection,
19      they result in customer outages and are intended to complement, rather
20      than replace, permanent infrastructure improvements. Comparing
21      undergrounding against a baseline that assumes these operational
22      mitigations remain in place indefinitely therefore understates the long-term
23      benefits of undergrounding and the value of reducing reliance on outage
24      programs.
25          The unscaled methodology also does not reflect risk aversion to
26      low-frequency, high-consequence wildfire events. PG&E therefore
27      supplements the required analysis with a scaled, unmitigated analysis that
28      removes the effects of PSPS and EPSS from the baseline and applies risk
29      scaling to reflect the consequences of catastrophic wildfire events. This
30      supplemental analysis does not replace the methodology used to establish
31      or track the Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives.
32      Instead, it provides additional context regarding the full magnitude of the
33      permanent wildfire and reliability benefits provided by undergrounding.



                                          -48-
 1                By replacing 4,000 overhead miles with 5,000 underground miles, under
 2            the supplemental scaled, unmitigated analysis, PG&E’s EUP will reduce
 3            approximately $117.4 billion in total Wildfire and Outage Risk over the
 4            55-year life of the underground assets,63 of which $104.9 billion is attributed
 5            to Wildfire Risk reduction64 and approximately $12.5 billion is attributed to
 6            Outage Program risk reduction.65 These results demonstrate the broader
 7            value of transitioning away from continued reliance on operational
 8            mitigations and investing in underground infrastructure that permanently
 9            removes targeted overhead ignition exposure and reduces the need for
10            PSPS and EPSS.
11                Taken together, the two analyses serve distinct but complementary
12            purposes. The Energy Safety-required unscaled, mitigated analysis
13            provides the compliance basis for establishing and tracking the Plan
14            Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives. The supplemental
15            scaled, unmitigated analysis more fully demonstrates the magnitude and
16            durability of the EUP’s long-term wildfire risk reduction and reliability
17            benefits. Under either analytical approach, the EUP is expected to deliver
18            substantial wildfire risk reduction and substantially improve electrical
19            reliability over the life of the underground assets.

20   D. Plan Mitigation Objective Requirements (EUP Guidelines Section 2.3.1)

           The Plan Mitigation Objective is the total amount of change in risk (wildfire and
      reliability) that is necessary to meet the requirement of Section 8388.5(d)(2). This
      change in risk must account for only the reduction due to Undergrounding Projects
      (see Core Capabilities Section 2.7.5) and be measured on a pro rata basis.
          The Large Electrical Corporation must set a Plan Mitigation Objective for the
      EUP and provide a supporting narrative and data in the EUP demonstrating how
      the EUP will achieve the Plan Mitigation Objective. In order to achieve the Plan

 1        1. PG&E’s Plan Mitigation Objective Addresses All Energy Safety
 2              Requirements
 3                 Below PG&E explains that its Plan Mitigation Objective meets the
 4              requirements of Section 2.3.1 of the EUP Guidelines.

 5              a. The Basis of the Plan Mitigation Objective (EUP Guidelines,
 6                 Section 2.3.1(a))
 7                     The Plan Mitigation Objective represents the total quantified
 8                 reduction in Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk achieved through
 9                 the implementation of the EUP. PG&E’s Plan Mitigation Objective is
10                 measured using the monetized Overall Utility Risk reduction per primary
11                 overhead mile removed, providing an outcome-based metric that directly
12                 links EUP execution to Ignition and Outage Program risk reduction. The
13                 metric demonstrates that PG&E will deliver substantial, measurable
14                 reduction in Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk through its
15                 execution of the EUP. The Plan Mitigation Objective ultimately provides
16                 a transparent, data‑driven basis for evaluating the EUP’s impact and

                                               -51-
 1   shows that the program materially advances statewide wildfire mitigation
 2   and reliability goals.
 3       PG&E’s implementation of the EUP is expected to reduce an
 4   average of $145,000 of Overall Utility Risk per mile of overhead
 5   conductor removed per year, based on unscaled risk values over
 6   PG&E’s 10-year EUP period. This is equivalent to approximately
 7   $3 million in present-value Overall Utility Risk reduction per primary
 8   overhead mile removed over the 55-year life of the undergrounding
 9   assets.
10       PG&E’s Plan Mitigation Objective was calculated using the Wildfire
11   Distribution Risk Model (WDRM) v4 and the Outage Program Risk
12   Model and was based on removal of approximately 4,000 miles of
13   primary overhead lines (equivalent to approximately 5,000 miles of
14   undergrounding), assuming the applicable entire Circuit Segments are
15   relocated underground.
16       PG&E established the Plan Mitigation Objective using the
17   approximately 4,000 overhead miles identified through the Project
18   Acceptance Framework because those miles represent the forecast set
19   of highest-risk Circuit Segments expected to be completed during the
20   ten-year EUP period. The forecast Portfolio reflects a balanced
21   consideration of risk reduction, affordability for customers, the pace at
22   which projects can advance in coordination with communities, workforce
23   availability, and constructability constraints.
24       PG&E expresses the Plan Mitigation Objective as a per-mile risk
25   reduction target rather than a fixed Portfolio-level risk reduction value
26   because it normalizes risk reduction across projects of varying size and
27   complexity, providing a consistent and transparent measure of
28   performance. The per-mile approach also allows the Plan Mitigation
29   Objective to remain applicable and comparable over time as Portfolio
30   composition evolves throughout the ten-year EUP period. Under this
31   approach, the Plan Mitigation Objective is calculated by dividing the total
32   projected Overall Utility Risk reduction associated with the forecast EUP
33   Portfolio by the corresponding overhead miles removed, resulting in a



                                   -52-
 1                target of $145,000 of Overall Utility Risk reduction per overhead mile
 2                removed per year.

 3                1) Plan Mitigation Objective Assumptions
 4                         The Plan Mitigation Objective applies climate-related risk
 5                     escalation and inflation adjustments to the underlying risk values66
 6                     to reflect the year in which the mitigation work is planned to occur.
 7                     For example, if a project is scheduled to be undergrounded in 2031,
 8                     the associated Wildfire and Outage Program Risk values are
 9                     adjusted from their 2028 baseline to 2031 levels by accounting for
10                     projected climate change impacts and inflation.
11                         The Plan Mitigation Objective only includes Circuit Segments
12                     that meet at least one of the Project Level Thresholds (i.e., high-risk
13                     eligible Circuit Segments) and are therefore eligible for
14                     consideration as high-risk projects. This includes, where applicable,
15                     Circuit Segments in Fire Rebuild Areas. For Fire Rebuild Projects,
16                     only risk reduction associated with Pre-Wildfire distribution
17                     infrastructure contributes to the Plan Mitigation Objective.67 Circuit
18                     Segments entirely outside HFTD/HFRA are excluded from the Plan
19                     Mitigation Objective.
20                         PG&E excludes Circuit Segments less than one mile long in the
21                     HFTD because the normalized costs and risk reduction metrics for
22                     such segments do not support meaningful per-mile comparisons
23                     and undergrounding them in isolation may present feasibility
24                     challenges.
25                         PG&E apportions monetized Ignition Risk to each Circuit
26                     Segment based on its relative share of risk as represented by its
27                     WDRM v4 risk score. Future updates to the WDRM may alter the
28                     distribution of risk across the system, while updates to Enterprise



     66 These values are consistent with the climate and escalation assumptions used in the
        Wildfire Benefit Cost Analysis (WBCA). See Chapter 7, Section G.4 (Core Capability 4)
        for details of the assumptions.
     67 The risk profile for the pre-wildfire distribution infrastructure for Fire Rebuild Projects
        where the fire occurred before January 1, 2023 would not be available for baseline
        comparisons. See discussion of previously-scoped projects in Chapter 3, Section D.5.

 1                   Bow Tie Model may alter the total quantity and monetized value of
 2                   risk on PG&E’s system.68
 3                        Because the Plan Mitigation Objective must remain fixed for the
 4                   duration of the 10-year EUP despite ongoing model evolution as
 5                   new data, methodologies, and regulatory requirements emerge,
 6                   PG&E must account for the inherent variability, uncertainty, and
 7                   model shifts that will occur over the life of the program.
 8                        Accordingly, PG&E expresses the Plan Mitigation Objective as a
 9                   per-mile risk reduction target and incorporates a Risk Model Impact
10                   Factor of 20 percent into the calculation.69
11                        The Risk Model Impact Factor reflects uncertainty arising from
12                   future changes between Ignition and Outage risk model versions.
13                   The Risk Model Impact Factor is comprised of two elements:
14                   •    Risk Model Change Factor for Ignition Risk: an estimated
15                        factor of 20 percent, representing the observed variance in
16                        Ignition Risk between WDRM v3 (previous version of the
17                        Wildfire Risk model) and WDRM v4 (current version of the
18                        Wildfire Risk model).
19                   •    Risk Model Change Factor for Outage Risk: an estimated
20                        factor of 18 percent which represents the observed variance in
21                        outage risk between the Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) 1.0
22                        and ICE 2.0 value of service.
23                        As described in the subsections below, PG&E combined these
24                   two change factors to derive a consolidated Risk Model Impact
25                   Factor, rounded to 20 percent, to represent the expected uncertainty
26                   between current and future risk model versions. PG&E applies this
27                   factor as a 20 percent reduction to the projected Ignition and Outage
28                   Risk reductions calculated using the risk models available at the
29                   time of filing. This adjustment factor ensures the Plan Mitigation
30                   Objective remains applicable following future model revisions and


     68 PG&E will update the WDRM and reliability risk models based on the schedule outlined
        in Chapter 8, Section C.
     69 PG&E developed the Risk Model Impact Factor methodology to quantify the uncertainty
        associated with future risk model changes.

                                              -54-
 1                    continues to reflect a durable and transparent measure of risk
 2                    reduction.
 3                        The adjusted risk reduction values for each EUP Circuit
 4                    Segment are then aggregated and normalized by the associated
 5                    mileage to calculate the Plan Mitigation Objective.

 6                2) Risk Model Change Factor for Ignition Risk
 7                        PG&E’s Risk Model Change Factor for Ignition Risk is derived
 8                    by first calculating the Portfolio-Level Ignition Risk per mile,70 also
 9                    known as risk density, once using WDRM v3 and a second time
10                    using WDRM v4, to calculate the variance between the two results.
11                    The following outlines the calculation steps, detailing both the
12                    standard formula and the specific data used to calculate the
13                    variance that is then incorporated into the overall Risk Model
14                    Change Factor in our Plan Mitigation Objective.
15                    1) WDRM v3: A WDRM v3 risk per mile value is calculated by
16                        dividing the percentage of Portfolio-Level WDRM v3 risk by the
17                        corresponding HFTD/High Fire Risk Area (HFRA) overhead
18                        primary miles. The starting population consists of 11,713 miles
19                        of overhead primary line associated with Circuit Segments
20                        containing one or more Confirmed Projects. To ensure a
21                        like-for-like comparison between WDRM v3 and WDRM v4,
22                        PG&E excludes approximately 683 miles where Circuit
23                        Segments cannot be reliably mapped between model versions,
24                        resulting in 11,029 comparable miles used in both
25                        calculations.71 Using the same mileage denominator under
26                        each model ensures that the calculated variance reflects
27                        changes in risk model outputs rather than changes in the
28                        underlying asset population.

        Confirmed Projects.

        name exists in a subsequent version, actual segmentation and geometry may differ
        substantially, impacting comparability.

 3   d. Overview of the EUP Implementation Approach and How the
 4      Approach Achieves the Plan Mitigation Objective (EUP Guidelines,
 5      Section 2.3.1(d))
 6          PG&E’s EUP implementation adheres to the Project Acceptance
 7      Framework of the EUP Guidelines, which is a four-screen, stepwise
 8      process that filters all Circuit Segments to identify, evaluate, and
 9      prioritize Undergrounding Projects that maximize Wildfire Risk reduction,
10      reliability, and public safety while remaining cost-efficient. Circuit
11      Segments progress from eligibility (Screen 1) to benefit-cost comparison
12      (Screen 2), to detailed scoping and risk analysis (Screen 3), and finally
13      to Portfolio-level prioritization and selection (Screen 4), with updates
14      re-applied as conditions change.
15          In Screen 1, PG&E identifies eligible Circuit Segments (Tier 2 or 3
16      HFTD or Fire Rebuild Areas) and applies risk thresholds to determine
17      which are eligible to proceed.
18          In Screen 2, PG&E first prioritizes Ignition Risk reduction by sorting
19      Eligible Circuit Segments from Screen 1 in order from highest to lowest
20      Wildfire Risk (i.e., from 1 through N or 1-N). We then evaluate these
21      Eligible Circuit Segments using a BCR Alternative Mitigation
22      Comparison. We use risk models and Alternative Mitigation analysis,
23      namely the WDRM v4, Outage Program Risk Model and Wildfire Benefit
24      Cost Analysis (WBCA) tool, to compare the potential Ignition Risk and
25      Outage Risk of undergrounding to Alternative Mitigations.
26          In Screen 3, PG&E undertakes a more detailed assessment of the
27      Undergrounding Projects by considering the mitigation comparison
28      analysis from Screen 2, incorporating local risk factors at each Project
29      location, and evaluating the appropriate mitigation approach within the
30      Circuit Segment. This assessment allows PG&E to determine where
31      undergrounding is appropriate within the Circuit Segment and where
32      hybrid mitigations, including non-undergrounding mitigations, may be
33      used to address localized risk and feasibility considerations while



                                      -59-
 1                ensuring undergrounding is targeted to the locations where it provides
 2                the greatest risk reduction and reliability benefit.
 3                     In Screen 4, PG&E sorts Confirmed Projects primarily by Overall
 4                Utility Risk per mile to consider both Ignition Risk and Outage Risk when
 5                prioritizing Undergrounding Projects.74 (See Chapter 3 for further
 6                details about the screen process including details of the additional
 7                prioritization factors considered within the EUP Project Acceptance
 8                Framework.)
 9                     PG&E will use the Project Acceptance Framework described above
10                to identify, evaluate, and prioritize Undergrounding Projects that are
11                expected to deliver substantial Wildfire Risk reduction and reliability
12                benefits and achieve our Plan Mitigation Objective. This approach is
13                based on:
14                1) Identifying the highest Ignition and Outage Program Risk Circuit
15                     Segments in our service territory using WDRM v4 and the Outage
16                     Program Risk Model; and
17                2) Making data-driven decisions about where it is appropriate to deploy
18                     undergrounding, compared to other Alternative Mitigations, using
19                     WBCA outputs, Screen 3 local risk review, and Project-specific
20                     feasibility information.
21                     This strategic targeting allows PG&E to focus undergrounding on
22                the portions of Circuit Segments where it is expected to provide the
23                greatest Overall Utility Risk reduction per mile, while using hybrid
24                mitigation approaches where appropriate to address localized
25                conditions. By applying this structured, data-driven process over the
26                10-year EUP period, PG&E will prioritize undergrounding that supports
27                achievement of the Plan Mitigation Objective, substantially reduces
28                Wildfire Risk, and significantly improves reliability.




     74 See Chapter 3, Section D.4 – Screen 4, Project Prioritization and Finalization, for further
        details of the Screen 4 prioritization approach.

 1   e. Overview of How the Project Acceptance Framework, Project
 2      Timelines, Workforce Development, Non-ratepayer Funding,
 3      Progress Report 0, Risk Modeling, and Reporting Metrics Support
 4      the Plan Mitigation Objective (EUP Guidelines, Section 2.3.1(e))
 5          PG&E’s EUP incorporates numerous programmatic elements that
 6      support the successful achievement of PG&E’s Plan Mitigation Objective
 7      and allow Energy Safety, the California Public Utilities Commission
 8      (CPUC or Commission), and stakeholders to monitor our progress
 9      towards achieving the Plan Mitigation Objective. Together, these
10      elements guide project selection, support efficient program execution,
11      quantify risk reduction, and provide transparent mechanisms for
12      measuring performance against the Plan Mitigation Objective.
13          PG&E’s Project Acceptance Framework supports the Plan Mitigation
14      Objective by identifying, evaluating, and prioritizing Undergrounding
15      Projects that provide the greatest reduction in Ignition Risk and Outage
16      Program Risk. Through the four-screen evaluation process described in
17      Chapter 3, PG&E focuses undergrounding investments on eligible
18      high-risk Circuit Segments that are expected to deliver the most
19      significant Overall Utility Risk reduction, thereby supporting achievement
20      of the Plan Mitigation Objective.
21          Risk modeling provides the analytical foundation to the Plan
22      Mitigation Objective. The Wildfire Distribution Risk Model, the Outage
23      Program Risk Model, and the Enterprise Bow Tie Models are used to
24      assess the risk associated with each EUP Project and evaluate the
25      corresponding risk reduction benefits. These models are used not only
26      to determine the Plan Mitigation Objective baseline but also support
27      project selection decisions throughout the Project Acceptance
28      Framework, and provide the basis for measuring progress toward
29      achievement of the Plan Mitigation Objective over the ten-year EUP
30      period. More information about PG&E’s Risk Modeling can be found in
31      Chapter 7.
32          Project completion timelines inform progress toward the annual,
33      5-year, and 10-year targets and objectives that culminate in achieving
34      the Plan Mitigation Objective. These milestones provide a structured

                                     -61-
 1   roadmap for delivering undergrounding projects and achieving the
 2   forecast risk reductions that underpin the Plan Mitigation Objective.
 3   Detailed reporting metrics will be used to track our progress towards
 4   meeting our Plan Mitigation Objective, allowing us to identify and
 5   remedy any issues if we are off track. Metrics include the number of
 6   miles installed underground, the number of overhead miles deenergized,
 7   Overall Utility Risk reduction, Ignition and Outage Program Risk
 8   reduction, and instantaneous and cumulative risk reduction values.
 9       Reporting metrics support the Plan Mitigation Objective by providing
10   measurable indicators of performance. Metrics such as overhead miles
11   de-energized, underground miles completed, Overall Utility Risk
12   reduction, Ignition Risk reduction, Outage Program Risk reduction, and
13   instantaneous and cumulative risk reduction values are used to evaluate
14   whether the EUP is achieving the forecast outcomes. In particular, the
15   Plan Tracking Objective metric “Risk Reduced per OH Mile
16   De-Energized” will be used to demonstrate how PG&E is tracking
17   toward the attainment of the Plan Mitigation Objective.
18       Workforce development supports the Plan Mitigation Objective by
19   ensuring PG&E has the trained workforce necessary to safely and
20   efficiently execute the forecast Portfolio of Undergrounding Projects.
21   We are continuing to work with our workforce development programs to
22   ensure we have the necessary workforce trained and available to deliver
23   on our targets and timelines, and ultimately on our Plan Mitigation
24   Objective. Further discussion is provided in EUP Chapter 5,
25   Section C.2.
26       Non-ratepayer funding supports the Plan Mitigation Objective by
27   reducing the cost to customers of achieving the forecast level of risk
28   reduction. While non-ratepayer funding does not change the amount of
29   risk reduction reflected in the Plan Mitigation Objective, it can reduce the
30   customer-funded investment required to achieve that objective and
31   improve the overall affordability of the EUP.
32       The information in Progress Report 0 and subsequent Progress
33   Reports will give Energy Safety, the CPUC, and stakeholders
34   transparent reporting of progress towards meeting our Plan Mitigation

                                  -62-
 1                 Objective, including tabular and geospatial data related to our risk
 2                 modeling methodology, Portfolio, and individual Undergrounding
 3                 Projects. This report will be used to monitor our progress and identify
 4                 any catch back or efficiency opportunities to remain on track to achieve
 5                 our Plan Mitigation Objective by the end of year 10.

 9                     PG&E presents our EUP metrics in the EUP Target/Timeline Table

 1            g. How Undergrounding Projects With Multiple Subprojects Will Be
 2                Reported and How the Risk Reduction Will Be Allocated Between
 3                Subprojects (EUP Guidelines, Section 2.3.1(g))
 4                     Undergrounding Projects with multiple Subprojects75 will be
 5                reported in the Subproject Table (C.14) with each Progress Report.
 6                Table C.14 includes all Undergrounding Subprojects created from
 7                Projects that have passed Screen 4.
 8                     PG&E will allocate risk reduction among the Subprojects on a
 9                pro-rata basis per mile considering the mitigation effectiveness for each
10                Alternative Mitigation and Additional Comparison.76
11                     Below we address the three requirements in EUP Guidelines
12                Section 2.3.1(g).

13                1) How the Project-Level Standard is Evaluated to Include the
14                     Effects of Both Undergrounding Subprojects and
15                     Non-Undergrounding Subprojects (EUP Guidelines
16                     Section 2.3.1(g)(i))
17                         PG&E evaluates the Project-Level Standard by accounting for
18                     the cumulative effects of all mitigation measures applied across a
19                     Circuit Segment, including Subprojects with Non-EUP mitigations
20                     (e.g., Overhead Hardening and/or Remote Grid).
21                         PG&E uses the term “Hybrid Project” to refer to a Project that
22                     includes undergrounding and non-undergrounding Subprojects on
23                     the same Circuit Segment. For Hybrid Projects, PG&E does not
24                     assess each mitigation in isolation. Instead, risk reduction is
25                     calculated by proportionally allocating pre-mitigation risk across the
26                     Circuit Segment based on the length treated by each mitigation type
27                     and then applying the applicable mitigation effectiveness to each
28                     portion. This approach ensures that the Project-Level Standard
29                     captures the combined performance of undergrounding and


     75 See EUP Guidelines, Appendix A, p. A-6. “‘Subproject’ means a delimited portion of
        work on a Confirmed Project. A Subproject must have a uniform set of mitigations
        applied to the entire Subproject. If a project does not have a uniform set of mitigations,
        it must be divided into more Subprojects.”
     76 See Attach. B, WP012 (Core Capability 5: Supporting Formulas).

                                                 -64-
 1          non-undergrounding Subprojects and reflects the total risk reduction
 2          achieved across the entire Circuit Segment.
 3          Example: 10-Mile Hybrid Mitigation Project (hypothetical
 4          scenario with example values)
 5               The example below illustrates the steps PG&E takes to assess
 6          each Project and Subproject against the required metrics, including
 7          the High-Risk Threshold and Project-Standard. The example
 8          includes six steps with hypothetical values and a discussion of the
 9          outcome. For Outage Program risks such as PSPS and EPSS,
10          mitigation effectiveness is modeled as a reduction in event
11          likelihood, while the consequences of such events remain
12          unchanged. Risk reduction is therefore applied proportionally based
13          on the extent a mitigation is applied to a Circuit Segment.
14          Example Step 1: Circuit Segment Configuration
15          •    PG&E implements a 10-mile Hybrid Project on a Circuit
16               Segment consisting of six miles of undergrounding and four
17               miles of overhead hardening.
18          •    Prior to mitigation, the Circuit Segment has $0.150 million of
19               Ignition Risk and $0.300 million of Outage Risk.
20          •    The pre-mitigated Overall Utility Risk per mile for this Circuit
21               Segment would be ($0.150 million Ignition Risk + $0.300 million
22               Outage Risk) / 10 miles = $0.045 million/mile.
23          •    PG&E accounts for the effects of both mitigation types
24               according to the simplified example below:

      4     Mitigation Ratio              60% underground/40% overhead
