 2                          In this example undergrounding is assumed to be 92 percent
 3                      effective in reducing Wildfire Risk. For PSPS and EPSS, mitigation
 4                      effectiveness is modeled as a reduction in the event likelihood, with
 5                      the consequence of such events remaining unchanged. Within the
 6                      risk modeling framework, undergrounding is assumed to eliminate
 7                      the likelihood of PSPS. For the purposes of forecasting, PG&E
 8                      assumes that undergrounding eliminates PSPS and EPSS events
 9                      on the underground portions of a Circuit Segment, resulting in 100
10                      percent effectiveness for those risk categories. For Circuit
11                      Segments that are only partially undergrounded, PSPS and EPSS
12                      risk reduction is applied proportionally based on the extent of
13                      undergrounding.
14                          Overhead Hardening demonstrates 45 percent Wildfire Risk
15                      reduction in this example. Overhead Hardening provides no PSPS
16                      risk reduction as PSPS events continue to be necessary to avoid
17                      Ignition Risk. Mitigation effectiveness for EPSS risk is assumed to
18                      be 52 percent for Overhead System Hardening. See Attach. B,
19                      WP001 (Mitigation Effectiveness Analysis) for detailed mitigation

 9   2) Measurement of the Plan Tracking Objectives and Plan
10      Mitigation Objective for Subprojects (EUP Guidelines
11      Section 2.3.1(g)(ii) and (iii))
12          Only Undergrounding Projects or Undergrounding Subprojects
13      count towards the Plan Tracking Objectives used to assess how the
14      Portfolio develops over time and whether it is on track to meet the
15      Plan Mitigation Objective explained in Section E below. PG&E will
16      apply a pro-rata allocation of Circuit Segment risk to the
17      Undergrounding Subprojects to determine the value of the
18      Portfolio-level metrics associated with them.
19          When measuring the Plan Tracking Objectives and the Plan
20      Mitigation Objective, PG&E isolates the performance of the EUP
21      Portfolio by excluding risk reduction associated with non-EUP
22      system hardening work (e.g., overhead hardening, Rule 20 projects
23      funded in the GRC, or other non-EUP mitigations). This ensures
24      that system-level metrics reflect progress toward the EUP’s
25      undergrounding-specific objectives and do not double-count risk
26      reduction achieved through other programs.
27          Similar to the Portfolio level approach described above, for
28      Circuit Segments where non-EUP system hardening work is
29      present, PG&E applies a pro-rata allocation of Circuit Segment risk
30      based on the length and scope of the non-EUP work to quantify the
31      portion of risk reduction attributable to those activities. That
32      allocated risk reduction is then explicitly excluded from the
33      system-level metrics used to track progress against the Plan
34      Tracking Objectives and the Plan Mitigation Objective.

                                 -69-
 1               As a result, system-level metrics measure only the incremental
 2          risk reduction associated with EUP Undergrounding Projects, while
 3          the effects of other system hardening work on non-Portfolio Circuit
 4          Segments are identified and reported in the Non-EUP Project Table
 5          (Attach. A, Table C.22). Non-EUP Project metrics are excluded
 6          from the EUP metrics.

1   E. Plan Tracking Objectives (EUP Guidelines, Section 2.3.2)

        To track and evaluate progress toward the Plan Mitigation Objective, the EUP
    must also include specific Plan Tracking Objectives. The Plan Tracking
    Objectives will be used to assess how the Portfolio of projects develops over time
    and whether the Large Electrical Corporation is on track to meet the Plan
    Mitigation Objective. The Plan Tracking Objectives must consist of
    forward-looking, quantifiable measurements and objectives, measured at the
    Portfolio-Level and System-Level, that will be used to assess progress toward the
    Plan Mitigation Objective. The list of Plan Tracking Objectives must:
    a. Be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and timely outcomes for the
       EUP.
    b. Include annual and 5-year tracking objectives.
    c.    Include tracking objectives based on total Overall Utility Risk Reduction.
    d. Include some tracking objectives based solely on Ignition Risk Reduction and
       some based solely on Outage Program Risk.
    e. Include tracking objectives measured by risk reduced per mile.
    f.    Include tracking objectives measured in miles of overhead line deenergized.
    g. Include tracking objectives measured in number of projects that have
       completed Screens 3 and 4.
        The Independent Monitor will use the Plan Tracking Objectives, and other
    EUP objectives to assess the Large Electrical Corporation's progress with
    implementation of its EUP. The Plan Tracking Objectives will be tracked in all
    Progress Reports pursuant to sections 8388.5(f)(3) and 8388.5(g).
        The Plan Tracking Objectives are the Large Electrical Corporation’s current
    forecast plan for meeting the Plan Mitigation Objective. Each Progress Report
    must use performance metrics to compare and update the Plan Tracking
    Objectives. The Progress Report must explain the reasons for any changes to the
    Plan Tracking Objectives.
        The EUP must contain a narrative setting forth the process the Large
    Electrical Corporation will use to compare and update Plan Tracking Objectives in
    each Progress Report.

 1       2. Process to Update the Plan Tracking Objectives in each Progress
 2           Report
 3               PG&E’s initial Plan Tracking Objectives are in Table 2-13 above. We
 4           will provide an updated Plan Tracking Objectives table in each Progress
 5           Report. The update will report actual values for completed years of the EUP
 6           and forecast values for the remaining years. Only EUP Projects count
 7           toward the Plan Tracking Objectives, which include Fire Rebuild Projects
 8           that have qualified for the EUP. Non-EUP Projects are excluded from the
 9           Plan Tracking Objectives. Core Capability 5 (described in Chapter 7,
10           Section G.5.a) details the methodology for the allocation of risk and risk
11           reduction to subprojects. Only the allocated risk reduction associated with
12           the Undergrounding Subprojects of a Circuit Segment will count towards the
13           Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives. Risk reduction
14           associated with non-undergrounding Subprojects is separately quantified for
15           Project-Level evaluations but excluded from Plan Mitigation Objective and
16           Plan Tracking Objectives attainment calculations. PG&E will compare each
17           updated Plan Tracking Objective table to the most recent table and not to
18           the original Baseline, to allow for more meaningful variance explanations
19           and align with the requirements of the EUP.79 In each Progress Report,
20           PG&E will provide an explanation for changes between planned and actual
21           values, as needed.
22               When PG&E updates our risk models, we will update the Plan Tracking
23           Objectives in the subsequent Progress Report and will backtest those
24           values to make the metrics comparable to the Plan Tracking Objectives
25           provided in Progress Report 0 that were based on the version of WBCA in
26           effect when we filed the EUP.
27               In each Progress Report, PG&E will review our progress against the
28           forecast Plan Tracking Objectives. We will also update our Plan Tracking
29           Objectives to more closely align them to the current EUP and our progress
30           towards achieving the 10-year objective.

31   F. Risk Calculations for Non-Undergrounding Subprojects (EUP Guidelines,
32        Section 2.3.3)

        If the Undergrounding Project includes non-undergrounding Subprojects, the
     non undergrounding work is counted as follows:
     a. Project Threshold (see Sections 2.4.3.2 and 2.7.5): for purposes of
        determining if the Circuit Segment meets a Project Threshold, use the risk
        score for the entire Circuit Segment (including any potential non
        undergrounding Subprojects).
     b. Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives (see Sections
        2.3.1, 2.3.2 and 2.7.5): for purposes of determining progress towards and
        compliance with the Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives,
        only use the risk reduction attributed to the Undergrounding Subprojects.
     c.       Comparative Metrics (see Section 2.7.10): for purposes of comparative
              metrics, use the risk reduction for the entire Circuit Segment when determining
              whether the project meets the Project Level Standard, but only apply the risk
              reduction attributed to the Undergrounding Subprojects towards the Plan
              Mitigation Objective.


33               PG&E describes how we account for non-EUP Subprojects included in an
34        Undergrounding Project in the following locations:
35        •      Project-Level Thresholds: Chapter 7, Section M.1 (EUP Guidelines
36               Section 2.7.9.1);
37        •      Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives: Chapter 2,
38               Sections D and E (EUP Guidelines Sections 2.3.1 and 2.3.2, respectively);
39               and
40        •      Comparative Metrics: Chapter 7, Section N (EUP Guidelines
41               Section 2.7.10).

42   G. Risk Calculations for Projects Extending Beyond a Confirmed Polygon
43        (EUP Guidelines, Section 2.3.4)

          If the scope of a project changes to include sections outside of the Confirmed
     Project Polygon (see Sections 2.4.2.4 and C.4.2), risk for the project is counted as
     follows:
     a. Expansion outside of a Confirmed Project Polygon: in the event that a
        portion of another Circuit Segment outside of the Confirmed Project Polygon is
        added to a project, use the risk reduction for the full (expanded) project for
        determining the contribution towards the Plan Mitigation Objective and use
        only the work inside the original Confirmed Project Polygon for determining
        whether the project meets the Project-Level Standard (see Section 2.7.9.2).



                                                 -80-
44                If a portion of another Circuit Segment outside of the Confirmed Project
45         Polygon is added to a Project, we will use the risk reduction for the full Project
46         (including the portion that extends beyond the confirmed polygon) to determine
47         the contribution towards the Plan Mitigation Objective. We will use only the work
48         inside the original Confirmed Project Polygon to determine whether the Project
49         meets the Project-Level Standard.

50   H. Risk Calculations for Projects in Fire Rebuild Areas (EUP Guidelines,
51         Section 2.3.5)

           If the Circuit Segment is in a Wildfire Rebuild Area (see Section 2.4.3.1), risk
      for the Circuit Segment is calculated as follows:
      a. Project Threshold (see Sections 2.4.3.2, 2.7.5 and Appendix C.1.10): The
         Pre-Wildfire distribution infrastructure and associated risk scores are used to
         determine if the Circuit Segment meets the Project Thresholds.
      b. Screen 3 Comparisons (see Sections 2.4.5 and 2.7.10): for purposes of the
         Screen 3 Comparative Metrics, the Pre-Wildfire distribution infrastructure and
         associated risk must be used as the comparison Baseline.
      c.       Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives (see
               Sections 2.3.1, 2.3.2 and 2.7.5): the risk reduction from a Wildfire Rebuild
               Area Undergrounding Project is compared to Pre-Wildfire distribution
               infrastructure and associated risk scores for purposes of determining progress
               towards the Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives.


52                PG&E describes how we account for risk if a Circuit Segment is in a Fire
53         Rebuild Area in the following sections of the EUP:
54         •      Project-Level Thresholds: Chapter 7, Section M.1;
55         •      Screen 3 Project Risk Analysis: Chapter 3, Section D.3; and
56         •      Plan Mitigation Objective and Plan Tracking Objectives: Chapter 2
57                Section D (Plan Mitigation Objective) and Section E (Plan Tracking
58                Objectives) above.

59   I.    Chapter Summary
60                This chapter explains how PG&E satisfies Section 2.3 of the EUP
61         Guidelines by demonstrating substantial Wildfire Risk reduction and improved
62         reliability. It describes the Plan Mitigation Objective, the risk framework used to
63         measure progress and the targets and timelines for achieving results over the
64         10-year plan period.

  66           PG&E will calculate and report risk reduction for undergrounding and related
  67           Project components, including non-undergrounding Subprojects, Projects
  68           extending beyond confirmed polygons, and Projects in Fire Rebuild Areas.
  69           Together, these sections provide the basis for tracking progress and
  70           demonstrating compliance with the EUP Guidelines.

 7       requirements in Sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.6 of the Electrical Undergrounding Plan

10       Circuit Segment scores for various risks.

12       Guidelines addressed in this chapter.

14       Acceptance Framework over time, including how Circuit Segments progress
15       through the screens and how changes are incorporated after the EUP is

17       information, Fire Rebuild areas, Project scoping details, Subprojects, and
18       physical changes to Circuit Segments through reapplication of screens where

20       used to maintain the framework that is current, consistent, and traceable
21       throughout the EUP period.

23       Framework. The Project Acceptance Framework of Screens 1 through 4
24       illustrates the process to screen Projects from the entire High-Fire Threat District
25       (HFTD) population to identify Confirmed Projects for the EUP Portfolio.80

27       Projects in Portfolio 0 were selected.

1        C. Project Acceptance Framework Requirements (EUP Guidelines
2             Section 2.4)

                Pursuant to section 8388.5(c)(2), the Large Electrical Corporation must
           identify Undergrounding Projects in its EUP. The Project Acceptance Framework
           is a multi-step process that the Large Electrical Corporation must establish and
           use to determine which Circuit Segments can be considered Undergrounding
           Projects, and, if undergrounded, will substantially increase electrical reliability and
           substantially reduce the risk of wildfire.
                The Large Electrical Corporation must list all Circuit Segments in its service
           territory (the “All Circuit Segment List”), apply the Project Acceptance Framework
           to that list, and include the results in the EUP as described below. The Large
           Electrical Corporation must demonstrate that projects successfully passing
           through the Project Acceptance Framework contribute to achieving the Plan
           Mitigation Objective. The Project Acceptance Framework has four screens:
               Screen 1: Circuit Segment Eligibility
               Screen 2: Project Information and Alternative Mitigation Comparison
               Screen 3: Project Risk Analysis
               Screen 4: Project Prioritization and Finalization


                                                     -86-
1          In Section D below, we describe how we use our Project Acceptance
2      Framework to determine which Circuit Segments can be considered Confirmed
3      Projects that will substantially increase electrical reliability and reduce Wildfire
4      Risk.

5      1. Project Progression Through Screens (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.1)

       The Project Acceptance Framework has a procedure for progressing a Circuit
    Segment through the four screens:
         Screen 1 Procedure. The EUP must apply Screen 1 (Circuit Segment
    Eligibility) to all Tier 2 or 3 High Fire Threat District (HFTD) and non-HFTD Circuit
    Segments and any Wildfire Rebuild Areas at the time of EUP filing. The Large
    Electrical Corporation must identify any Wildfire Rebuild Areas using the
    procedure described by the Large Electrical Corporation pursuant to
    Section 2.4.3.1 below. Circuit Segments that are not located in a Wildfire Rebuild
    Area or a Tier 2 or 3 HFTD (“Out of Area Circuit Segments”) are eliminated in
    Screen 1. Each Circuit Segment that is located in a Wildfire Rebuild Area or a Tier
    2 or 3 HFTD is then evaluated to determine if the Circuit Segment meets the risk
    score criteria for eligibility. In-Area Circuit Segments that meet the risk score
    criteria are “Eligible Circuit Segments” and proceed to Screen 2. In-Area Circuit
    Segments that do not meet the risk score criteria are “Ineligible Circuit Segments”
    and do not proceed to Screen 2.
        Screen 2 Procedure. The EUP must apply Screen 2 (Project Information and
    Alternative Mitigation Comparison) to all Eligible Circuit Segments. Circuit
    Segments that pass Screen 2 are considered “Undergrounding Projects” and can
    proceed to Screen 3. These Undergrounding Projects constitute the list of
    Undergrounding Projects that must be identified in the EUP pursuant to section
    8388.5(c)(2).
         Screen 3 Procedure. The EUP must apply Screen 3 (Project Risk Analysis)
    to all Undergrounding Projects for which the Large Electrical Corporation has
    sufficient information. Projects that pass Screen 3 are reported as “Confirmed
    Projects.”
       Screen 3 must be applied to a Portfolio of at least 25 individual
    Undergrounding Projects at the time of EUP filing.
       Screen 4 Procedure. The EUP must apply Screen 4 (Project Prioritization
    and Finalization) to all Confirmed Projects at the time of EUP filing. Projects that
    pass Screen 4 are “Prioritized Projects.”
         The Large Electrical Corporation must detail the implementation approach it
    will use for each screen. The general requirements of each screen, including the
    minimum data and information requirements, are further described in the Sections
    below.


6              Our description of the Project progression through the four screens is
7          discussed in Section D below.

                                              -87-
 1      2. Incorporating Changes (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.2)

 2          a. Changes to Circuit Segment (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.2.1)

          After the EUP is filed, the Large Electrical Corporation must account for new
     information (such as project-specific information obtained through scoping and
     other project work), model version and calibration changes (such as those detailed
     in Section 2.7.5.2), and updates to HFTD maps or new Wildfire Rebuild Areas.
         In each Progress Report, the list of Circuit Segments provided to Energy
     Safety, and associated risk scores, must be the same list and scores used at that
     time by the Large Electrical Corporation for risk modeling and decision-making.
     This list, at minimum, must include changes to risk scores through completion of
     Undergrounding Projects performed via the EUP, or any other wildfire mitigation
     activity.
         Additionally, risk scores for each Circuit Segment must be updated to account
     for modeled effects of application of the EUP and other wildfire
     mitigation/hardening, until such time as a model calibration or version update
     takes place and assigns new risk scores directly.
         If any changes occur on a Circuit Segment before it has passed Screen 3,
     then Screen 1 and Screen 2 must be reapplied. This could result in Circuit
     Segments being added or removed from the EUP. The Out-of-Area Circuit
     Segment list, In-Area Circuit Segment list, Eligible Circuit Segment list, Ineligible
     Circuit Segment list, and the list of Undergrounding Projects must all be updated.
     Information in the Screen 2 comparison must also be updated.
          The EUP narrative must describe the process the Large Electrical Corporation
     will use to update this information in Progress Reports.


 3                   In compliance with the EUP Guidelines, PG&E’s Progress Reports
 4              will account for new information, model changes and other updates that
 5              affect relevant Circuit Segments.
 6                   When PG&E performs risk model updates, we will update the
 7              Baseline risk values to account for changes to risk scores due to work
 8              implemented in all system hardening programs, including the EUP,
 9              non-EUP undergrounding, overhead hardening, and line removal.
10              PG&E will apply the risk reduction achieved from system hardening to
11              the pre-mitigation risk scores to account for the risk value change on the
12              Circuit Segment. Risk reduction achieved from Subprojects will be
13              applied on a pro-rata basis. PG&E will account for risk reduction only
14              after a Project has passed Quality Assurance (QA) review, which is a
15              key step in confirming the construction is complete and the underground



                                              -88-
 1   assets are operational. PG&E will provide annual updates to risk scores
 2   in our Progress Report.
 3       The Wildfire Distribution Risk Model (WDRM), Outage Program Risk
 4   Model (OPRM), and associated Wildfire Benefit Cost Analysis (WBCA)
 5   are based on a defined snapshot of system conditions, risk information,
 6   and mitigation status at a point in time. As new versions of these models
 7   are developed, the underlying snapshots are refreshed to incorporate
 8   updated information available at the time of the model update. Such
 9   updates may include revisions to High Fire Threat District (HFTD)
10   boundaries approved by the CPUC, updates to work completed in Fire
11   Rebuild Areas, completed mitigation activities, changes in asset
12   conditions or configurations, and other updates affecting model inputs.
13       PG&E may update Circuit Segment risk scores reported in Progress
14   Reports to reflect score changes due to updated model versions and
15   refreshed data snapshots in addition to risk reductions directly
16   attributable to EUP Undergrounding Projects or other system hardening
17   activities. To the extent that completed mitigation measures, whether
18   associated with system hardening programs or other risk reduction
19   programs, are reflected in the updated model snapshot, the resulting
20   risk score changes will be incorporated into the WDRM and OPRM and,
21   in turn, the WBCA outputs used for EUP reporting and decision making.
22   PG&E will incorporate the updated risk scores in future Progress
23   Reports.
24       If changes occur on a Circuit Segment before it has passed
25   Screen 3, we will re-evaluate the Circuit Segment risk scores by
26   reapplying Screen 1 and Screen 2 (to reconfirm eligibility and
27   Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) values for alternative mitigations). During the
28   Screen 3 review process, PG&E will determine if system hardening has
29   already occurred on a Circuit Segment or portion of a Circuit Segment
30   through a non-EUP system hardening Project. Any Circuit Segments or
31   portions of a Circuit Segment that have previously been hardened will
32   be removed from EUP eligibility (see Figure 3-5, High Level Feasibility
33   Review). Additionally, when PG&E issues a new version of the WBCA,
34   we will rerun Screen 1 and Screen 2 and re-evaluate Circuit Segments

                                  -89-
 1              that have not passed Screen 3. Once a Project has passed Screen 3,
 2              the Project will be considered a Confirmed Project and will be developed
 3              for construction. Any future updates, including risk model updates, will
 4              not change the status of Confirmed Projects.
 5                   PG&E describes our timing and process for issuing new versions of
 6              our risk models in Chapter 8, Section C (EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.6).

 7          b. Subprojects (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.2.2)

          During the scoping process, the Large Electrical Corporation may divide an
     Eligible Circuit Segment into one or more Subprojects. Subprojects may be
     created for operational reasons, such as differences in expected completion times
     of portions of the undergrounding work (referred to as Undergrounding
     Subprojects). Subprojects may also be created to reflect that a portion of the
     Circuit Segment will be treated with a different wildfire mitigation (referred to as a
     non-undergrounding Subproject). If a Circuit Segment does not have multiple
     Subprojects during the scoping process, then it should be reported as a single
     Subproject.
         The EUP narrative must include a detailed description of the decision-making
     process the Large Electrical Corporation will use to determine when to divide a
     Circuit Segment into Subprojects. This narrative must include a list of possible
     reasons for division, with a detailed explanation of each.


 8                   PG&E selects mitigations by looking at the Circuit Segment as a
 9              whole. These Circuit Segment level mitigations together are defined as
10              a System Hardening Project. We select the Project-level mitigations
11              using the process described in Section D.2 below. A Project that
12              includes more than one type of mitigation, or a hybrid of mitigations, is
13              segmented into Subprojects based on the type of mitigation. Thus,
14              while a Project may include multiple mitigations, a Subproject can only
15              involve one mitigation type. During Project scoping, PG&E may divide
16              an Eligible Circuit Segment into one or more Subprojects to differentiate
17              by mitigation and to record the cost of the Subproject to the correct
18              funding, as outlined below:
19              •    Funding Sources: Undergrounding will exclusively be funded
20                   through the EUP while non-EUP system hardening (i.e., Overhead
21                   Hardening, Remote Grid, and Line Removal) will continue to be
22                   funded in the General Rate Case (GRC). Projects are divided into
23                   Subprojects to identify and manage funding source differences.

                                              -90-
 1              •   Remote Grids: Remote Grids are implemented on small sections of
 2                  Circuit Segments. They are often developed, estimated, and
 3                  constructed with different resources than undergrounding or
 4                  overhead hardening and can have longer lead time dependencies
 5                  due to the type of customer interaction and agreements required.
 6              •   Different County: Cost and tax implications vary by county. We
 7                  separate Projects into Subprojects if the Project (i.e., Circuit
 8                  Segment) spans multiple counties so that county-specific accounting
 9                  requirements can be correctly applied.

10     3. Other Anticipated Changes (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.2.3)

         The Large Electrical Corporation must provide a narrative describing any other
     expected or known changes likely to occur and how those changes will be
     incorporated into the EUP.


11              PG&E does not currently anticipate any changes to the EUP other than
12          potential changes to the CPUC’s HFTD map discussed in Section D.1.a.3 if
13          PG&E files a Petition for Modification (PFM) that results in an expansion of
14          the HFTD. Expansion of the HFTD would potentially allow other
15          Undergrounding Projects to be included in the EUP.
16              Should new information arise or circumstances change, including
17          changes arising from the SPD-37 proceeding (A.26-02-005) or other
18          changes in regulatory requirements, changes to cost estimates, or the
19          development of new technologies, PG&E would seek to revise the EUP,
20          respond as directed to a regulatory request or requirement to modify the
21          EUP, and/or provide updated information in Progress Reports, as
22          appropriate. PG&E remains committed to ongoing evaluation and
23          transparency so that changes are documented and integrated in accordance
24          with EUP Guidelines, reporting requirements, and internal processes.




                                             -91-
 1      4. Physical Changes to a Circuit Segment (EUP Guidelines
 2          Section 2.4.2.4)

         The EUP must account for physical changes to a Circuit Segment such as
     relocating lines for operational reasons, the addition or removal of equipment that
     redefines the endpoints of a Circuit Segment, or changes in alignment due to
     undergrounding itself, among other factors. These changes are accounted for in
     three ways.
         First, the Circuit Segments must be represented by unique identification
     names, which are unique both spatially and temporally, meaning a name cannot
     be reused for a “new” Circuit Segment. A Circuit Segment is considered “new”
     and requires a new Circuit Segment ID if equipment that defines the boundaries
     between Circuit Segments (e.g., circuit breakers and reclosers) are moved,
     removed, or added. See the introduction of Appendix C.1 for details.
        Second, the evolution of Circuit Segments is tracked in the Circuit Segment
     Changelog table, linking the prior Circuit Segment ID to the new one (See
     Section C.1.7 of Appendix C).
         Third, a Confirmed Project is defined by the boundaries of the Confirmed
     Project Polygon that encompasses the entire Circuit Segment on which the
     Undergrounding Project is defined. The Confirmed Project Polygon is fixed once
     the Circuit Segment becomes a Confirmed Project. Further details on the
     Confirmed Project Polygons are defined in Appendix C.4.2. Changes to proposed
     work on each Undergrounding Project do not need to be re-evaluated or passed
     through the screens again due to a physical change to the underlying Circuit
     Segment unless the work would take place outside the Confirmed Project
     Polygon, in which case additional justification will be required. Any Project or
     Subproject which has assets outside of the Confirmed Project Polygon must have
     a justification in the C.1.14 Subproject Table.
          The EUP narrative must describe the process the Large Electrical Corporation
     will use to update this information in Progress Reports.


 3              PG&E will account for physical changes to a Circuit Segment. PG&E
 4          developed a mapping tool called the Circuit Segment Version Comparison
 5          tool for tracking changes to Circuit Segments between risk model versions.
 6          The tool considers comparative geometries and equipment asset
 7          relationships to determine how each Circuit Segment has changed between
 8          WDRM versions. For a WDRM version, each Circuit Segment is assigned a
 9          unique name which is reported as [circuit_segment_id]. Starting with
10          WDRM v5, all Circuit Segments will receive a new unique ID for each new
11          model version by appending the model version number to the end of the
12          Circuit Segment name, e.g., “circuit_segment_id” in WDRM v5 snapshot will
13          be represented as “circuit_segment_idv5”. Each new ID will be traceable to

                                             -92-
 1   the ‘parent’ Circuit Segment ID(s) in the previous risk model version
 2   snapshot.
 3       The output from the Circuit Segment version comparison tool will be
 4   used to populate the Circuit Segment Changelog Table (to be included in
 5   the Progress Report as Table C.7). This table will document significant
 6   changes in Circuit Segment configurations between model versions, as
 7   specified in the EUP Guidelines, by examining key attributes to identify and
 8   categorize changes.
 9       The Circuit Segment attributes used to determine configuration changes
10   between versions include:
11   •   Circuit Segment names;
12   •   Feeder Names/IDs;
13   •   Interrupting Device Operating IDs;
14   •   Primary and Secondary Overhead Conductor lengths; and
15   •   Conductor Asset IDs and counts.
16       To determine the change type for the Circuit Segment Changelog Table,
17   PG&E will compare conductor asset IDs on Circuit Segments between
18   snapshots. If conductors on a Circuit Segment appear on multiple Circuit
19   Segments in a subsequent snapshot, the change cause will be categorized
20   as a “split.” If conductors on multiple Circuit Segments appear on a single
21   Circuit Segment in a subsequent snapshot, the change cause will be
22   categorized as a “merge.”
23       We will provide the first Circuit Segment Changelog Table to Energy
24   Safety in the first Progress Report following an update to the WBCA model
25   (which includes the relevant WDRM and Outage Program Risk Model
26   updates).
27       Confirmed Project Polygons are included as part of our Geographic
28   Information System (GIS) data in Progress Report 0. (See Progress Report,
29   Attach. A-5, Table C.17). PG&E will not update a Confirmed Project Polygon
30   and will consider it fixed. In the event an update to a risk model adds
31   additional assets into the same area, that new Circuit Segment would be
32   evaluated based on our Screen 3 criteria, with the assets included in the
33   previously Confirmed Project, being excluded from the analysis. (See
34   discussion below in Section D.3.a)

16       1. Screen 1: Circuit Segment Eligibility (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.3)

           Screen 1 (Circuit Segment Eligibility) is the procedure within the Project
      Acceptance Framework that identifies relevant Circuit Segments and creates the
      List of Eligible Circuit Segments.


17                Figure 3-1 below shows the Screen 1 procedures within the Project
18           Acceptance Framework that we use to determine if a Circuit Segment is
19           eligible for the EUP.
20                Screen 1 begins by reviewing the list of all electric distribution primary
21           overhead Circuit Segments (also referred to as circuit protection zones or
22           CPZs) in PG&E’s service territory to determine which are relevant to the
23           EUP. Circuit Segments in Tier 2 or 3 of the HFTD or in a Fire Rebuild Area
24           are In-Area Circuit Segments and may be considered for the EUP. All other
25           Circuit Segments are excluded from consideration.
26                Next, to determine EUP eligibility, PG&E reviews the relevant Circuit
27           Segments against the following three risk thresholds: (1) the High-Risk
28           Threshold; (2) the High Frequency Outage Program Threshold; and the


     81 Attach. B, WP003 (Project Prioritization and Decision Tree).

                                                -94-
1   (3) Ignition Tail Risk Threshold. If a Circuit Segment meets one or more of
2   the thresholds, it is considered “high risk” and passes from Screen 1 to
3   Screen 2 for further evaluation.

1           a. Identification Of Circuit Segments Inside and Outside of a Tier 2
2               or 3 High Fire Threat Districts and Fire Rebuild Areas (EUP
3               Guidelines Section 2.4.3.1).

         In Screen 1, the Large Electrical Corporation must identify all Circuit Segments in
    its service territory (All Circuit Segments) and specify which Circuit Segments are
    located in a Wildfire Rebuild Area or Tier 2 or 3 High Fire-Threat District (“In-Area
    Circuit Segments”). If a Circuit Segment has portions both within and outside of a
    Tier 2 or 3 HFTD, each span crossing the Tier 2 or 3 HFTD boundary and up to two
    adjacent spans outside of a Tier 2 or 3 HFTD may be considered for undergrounding.
          For each Circuit Segment, the following risk scores must be reported: Overall
    Utility Risk Score; Ignition Consequence Score; and Outage Program Likelihood
    Score. Section 2.7.9 of these Guidelines details the requirements for these risk
    scores. Additionally, each Circuit Segment must be identified by location, indicating
    whether the Circuit Segment is in a Tier 2 or 3 High Fire-Threat District; in a Wildfire
    Rebuild Area; or not located in either a Tier 2 or 3 HFTD or a Wildfire Rebuild Area.
    Appendix C.1.6, Circuit Segment Identification Table, and C.1.8, Circuit Segment
    Risk Score Table, give instructions for the type of information required in Screen 1.
         The EUP narrative must describe the process the Large Electrical Corporation
    will use to identify Wildfire Rebuild Areas and the corresponding affected Circuit
    Segments. The Large Electrical Corporation must include a narrative in the Progress
    Reports describing identified Wildfire Rebuild Areas and providing information on the
    wildfire date, time, location, affected Circuit Segments and facilities impacted. The
    narrative must indicate if any distribution infrastructure damaged in the wildfire has
    already been rebuilt. Only Circuit Segments that have been damaged by wildfire and
    have not previously been rebuilt are eligible.
        The EUP must include the following information in the EUP narrative or an
    additional table:
    a. The total number of Circuit Segments within the Large Electrical Corporation
       service territory;
    b. The total number of Circuit Segments located within a Tier 2 or 3 HFTD;
    c.   The total number of Circuit Segments located within a Wildfire Rebuild Area; and
    d. The total mileage of lines in all Circuit Segments in each of the above groups.
        In the EUP narrative, the Large Electrical Corporation must create three lists of
    In-Area Circuit Segments sorted in descending order by:
    a. Overall Utility Risk Score;
    b. Ignition Consequence Score; and
    c.   Outage Program Likelihood Score. Each list should be shown as a table with
         only the top 20 highest scoring Circuit Segments, containing all three risk scores,
         the county where the Circuit Segment is located, and the Tier 2 or 3 HFTD Tier
         or Wildfire Rebuild Area that applies to the Circuit Segment.



                                             -97-
 1               1) Process Used to Identify Circuit Segments in a Tier 2 or 3 High
 2                    Fire-Threat District
 3                        PG&E identifies In-Area HFTD Circuit Segments by reviewing
 4                    electrical distribution assets within HFTD boundaries. This review is
 5                    conducted by overlaying our GIS system data (detailed spatial
 6                    information about the location and configuration of electrical
 7                    infrastructure) with the HFTD maps published by the California
 8                    Public Utilities Commission (CPUC or Commission). PG&E
 9                    identifies all Circuit Segments that are either fully or partially located
10                    within Tier 2 or Tier 3 HFTD areas. For Circuit Segments that
11                    traverse the boundaries of HFTD zones, each span that crosses into
12                    or out of a Tier 2 or Tier 3 HFTD is reviewed, and it is confirmed that
13                    only up to two adjacent spans outside the HFTD would be eligible
14                    for evaluation and potential undergrounding, consistent with the
15                    EUP Guidelines.82

16               2) Process Used to Identify Circuit Segments in Fire Rebuild
17                    Areas83
18                        PG&E implemented two processes to identify Circuit Segments
19                    damaged by wildfire. The first process identifies Circuit Segments
20                    where previous Fire Rebuild hardening work occurred. The second
21                    process identifies Circuit Segments with Electric Corrective (EC)
22                    tags from fires spanning 2015 to 2025.84 Taken together, the
23                    Circuit Segments from both processes represent the population of
24                    Circuit Segments with a PG&E asset that was damaged by wildfire.




     82 “If a Circuit Segment has portions both within and outside of a Tier 2 or 3 HFTD, each

        2.4.3.1, p. 16.
     83 While the EUP Guidelines reference “Wildfire Rebuild Areas,” PG&E uses the term “Fire

 4       Immediately after a wildfire, PG&E conducts a damage
 5   assessment and determines if damaged assets require hardening.
 6   Damaged assets that require hardening are considered for Fire
 7   Rebuild. System hardening is deployed where significant rebuilding
 8   is required (e.g., four or more spans and/or segments with
 9   intermittent damage). In this case, PG&E will add the Circuit
10   Segments to the population of Fire Rebuild Circuit Segments in the
11   HFTD and provide all required information about the wildfire and
12   impacted facilities in the Progress Report. Circuits Segments

 1                        In Sections D.2 through D.4 below (addressing EUP
 2                    Guidelines 2.4.4 to 2.4.6), we detail how we apply the four screens
 3                    to a Circuit Segment in a Fire Rebuild Area. There are several
 4                    differences in how Fire Rebuild Circuit Segments progress through
 5                    Screens 3 and 4 compared to a non-Fire Rebuild Circuit Segment.
 6                    •   Screen 1: No Difference – Fire Rebuild Circuit Segments are
 7                        eligible for the EUP if they meet one of the Project Level
 8                        Thresholds (see Chapter 7, Section M for details of Project
 9                        Level Thresholds).
10                    •   Screen 2: No Difference – Calculate BCR for: (1) 100 percent
11                        Underground; (2) Alternative Mitigation 1; (3) Alternative
12                        Mitigation 2; and (4) Additional Comparison. See Table 3-9
13                        below for a detailed description of the Screen 2 mitigation
14                        comparison types.
15                    •   Screen 3: If undergrounding has the highest BCR or is within
16                        the BCR uncertainty factor,85 PG&E proceeds through the full
17                        Screen 3 analysis to scope multiple mitigations and determine
18                        the appropriate, permanent mitigation. See Table 3-9 below for
19                        a detailed description of the Screen 3 mitigation comparison
20                        types.
21                    •   Screen 4: Fire Rebuild Projects are given priority over other
22                        Circuit Segments in Screen 4, regardless of the calculated
23                        priority of the Circuit Segment, due to the time sensitivity of
24                        rebuilding assets after they have been damaged by fire. Not all
25                        Circuit Segments in a Fire Rebuild Area are considered Fire
26                        Rebuild Projects, only those Circuit Segments that have been
27                        through the damage assessment process shown in Figure 3-2.

1           b. Identification of Risky Circuit Segments and Mitigation Standards
2               (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.3.2)

         Screen 1 (Circuit Segment Eligibility) ensures that the EUP limits eligibility to
    higher risk Circuit Segments. In the description of the Project Acceptance
    Framework, the EUP must present Project-Level Thresholds that establish the
    need for risk mitigation. Additionally, the Large Electrical Corporation must
    present Project-Level Standards that define a successful mitigation. Additional
    information on the required Project-Level Thresholds and Standards is provided in
    Section 2.7.9 of these Guidelines. The Project-Level Thresholds and Standards to
    be applied to Circuit Segments are:
    1. Eligible Circuit Segment Thresholds: the minimum risk score thresholds
       that will be used to identify Circuit Segments that are eligible for the 10-Year
       EUP. These thresholds are the High-Risk Threshold, Ignition Tail Risk
       Threshold, and High Frequency Outage Program Threshold. They are further
       detailed in 2.7.9.1. In-Area Circuit Segments that do not meet any of these
       thresholds are called Ineligible Circuit Segments.
    2. Mitigated Circuit Segment Standards: the Project-Level risk score that an
       Eligible Circuit Segment must reach to be considered sufficiently mitigated
       under the terms of the EUP. These standards are the High-Risk Project Level
       Standard, the Ignition Tail Risk Project-Level Standard, and the High
       Frequency Outage Program Project-Level Standard. They are further detailed
       in 2.7.9.2.
        After determining these Project-Level Thresholds and Standards, the Large
    Electrical Corporation must evaluate the list of In-Area Circuit Segments to
    determine eligibility and minimum mitigation needs.
         The following must be included in the narrative portion of the EUP:
    a. The Project-Level Thresholds and Standards;
    b. The total number of In-Area Circuit Segments;
    c.   The number of Eligible Circuit Segments, by category; and
    d. The number of In-Area Circuit Segments that are below the eligibility
       thresholds (Ineligible Circuit Segments).

                                                        -110-
 1            Screen 2 Process
 2               In Screen 2, PG&E calculates three high-level BCRs86 for each Circuit
 3           Segment on the Screen 2 Circuit Segment list using the BCR methodology
 4           approved in CPUC Decision 25-08-032,87 as well as an additional
 5           comparison:
 6           1) 100 percent Underground: 100 percent Undergrounding (100 percent of
 7               the primary distribution line is undergrounded);
 8           2) Alternative Mitigation 1: 100 percent Overhead Hardening (referred to
 9               as OH);
10           3) Alternative Mitigation 2: 100 percent Remote Grid with line removal;
11               and
12           4.) Additional Comparison 1: Hybrid (50 percent of the Circuit Segment is
13               undergrounded and the other 50 percent is overhead hardened).
14               Consistent with Energy Safety's requested baseline, the mitigation
15           alternatives are evaluated relative to a baseline that includes applicable
16           operational mitigations, including EPSS, DCD, and PSPS. Accordingly,
17           operational mitigations are not treated as separate infrastructure alternatives
18           or repeated in the name of each mitigation comparison. For example,
19           Alternative Mitigation 1 is identified as “Overhead Hardening” because that
20           name describes the permanent infrastructure treatment being evaluated. It
21           does not mean that EPSS, DCD, or PSPS are excluded from the analysis.
22           Rather, those operational controls are reflected in the baseline and continue
23           to be deployed with overhead facilities as appropriate. While
24           undergrounding eliminates the need for EPSS, DCD and PSPS on
25           undergrounded facilities, mitigations such as overhead hardening generally
26           continue to operate alongside EPSS, DCD, PSPS, and other operational
27           measures when warranted by system conditions and wildfire risk.
28               The comparison types are more fully described below in Table 3-9. The
29           costs included in the calculation are the capital construction costs and the
30           ongoing capital and expense operations and maintenance costs, including


     86 These high-level BCR values are calculated at the Circuit Segment level and will be

2            calculation include Ignition Risk reduction, Outage Program Risk reduction,

6            a. Common Set of Values and Assumptions (EUP Guidelines
7                Section 2.4.4.1)

         Screen 2 (Project Information and Alternative Mitigation Comparison) may use
     common values and assumptions to develop estimates for Circuit Segments when
     project-specific information is not available. Screen 2 includes calculation of risk
     and benefit scores; it applies to both undergrounding and Alternative Mitigations.
     The EUP must include a narrative summarizing the assumptions underlying the
     values and explaining the metrics used in Screen 2. This narrative summary must
     be clear, concise, and comprehensive. At a minimum, this summary must include:
     a. A description of the metrics required by the CPUC Guidelines for the SB 884
        Program.
     b. Detailed description of mitigations that the Large Electrical Corporation will
        use for these comparisons. Explanation of why these Alternative Mitigations
        are being considered. Description of the process and criteria that the Large
        Electrical Corporation will use for determining the best Alternative Mitigations
        for individual project comparisons. Description of the process for identifying
        and evaluating new mitigation technologies through the life of the EUP.
        Description of processes and resources that will be used for deploying each
        Alternative Mitigation.
     c.   Description of any assumptions for scope, cost, extent, and wildfire risk
          reduction and reliability improvements that are applicable to multiple
          Undergrounding Projects. These descriptions must be provided for all
          activities (undergrounding and Alternative Mitigations).
     d. Explanation of how the need for additional easements, permits, and CEQA
        review are accounted for in the assumptions for scope, cost, extent, and risk
        reduction and reliability improvements.

12   b) Process for Identifying and Evaluating New Mitigation
13      Alternatives/Technologies Through the Life of the EUP
14          PG&E interprets the reference to “new mitigation
15      technologies” to mean new mitigation alternatives that we would
16      consider in Screen 2 and Screen 3. There are numerous new
17      technologies aimed at increasing cost efficiency of existing
18      mitigations such as Fluid Free Steerable Boring, Native Slurry
19      Backfill, and Ground Level Distribution System/Minimum Cover
20      Distribution System (GLDS/MCDS), but these do not represent
21      new mitigations and therefore will not be discussed as part of
22      this response. (Please refer to Chapter 5, Section C.3.c, for
23      more information on new technologies aimed at increasing cost
24      efficiency of existing mitigations.)
25          During the 10-year EUP period, PG&E may add new
26      alternative mitigations into our Screen 2 and Screen 3 analyses
27      if we identify a viable Alternative Mitigation technology or
28      solution and have confirmed through product and pilot testing
29      that it is suitable for deployment in PG&E’s service territory.
30      PG&E has done this in the past, for example, when we included
31      Remote Grids in our 2020 Wildfire Mitigation Plan (WMP) as a
32      new technology that we identified as a viable alternative to
33      conventional post-fire rebuild work in some locations. Since


                             -116-
 1                       installing our first remote grid in 2021, we have completed
 2                       17 installations (as of the end of 2025) and now include Remote
 3                       Grids as one of our three core WMP system hardening
 4                       initiatives, along with overhead hardening and undergrounding.
 5                           Throughout the EUP period, PG&E will continue our current
 6                       practice of identifying and evaluating new wildfire and outage
 7                       mitigation technologies and solutions through a multi-pronged
 8                       approach that includes open innovation challenges, strategic
 9                       industry partnerships, industry benchmarking, and rigorous
10                       testing.

11                   c) New Mitigation Identification Process
12                           PG&E identifies new and emerging mitigation opportunities
13                       by actively soliciting solutions from the global technology
14                       community to address specific operational challenges. This
15                       includes publishing R&D Strategy Reports93 that outline “critical
16                       challenges” and inviting innovators to submit proposals. PG&E
17                       also hosts events such as the PG&E Innovation Summit to
18                       engage with technology leaders and startups, and sponsors
19                       competitions such as the XPRIZE Wildfire Competition to
20                       identify and test breakthrough mitigation technologies. PG&E
21                       participates in the Electric Program Investment Charge (EPIC)
22                       grant program by identifying promising startup projects and
23                       providing field expertise and real-world pilot opportunities.
24                       PG&E also meets with other utilities both within and outside the
25                       United States to exchange information, benchmark approaches,
26                       and share best practices for existing and emerging
27                       technological and operational mitigations.

 1                         Program Risk Threshold). Eligible Circuit Segments are ranked
 2                         from 1-to-N based on wildfire Risk Density.99 Projects are then
 3                         selected for Alternative Mitigation analyses sequentially starting
 4                         with the highest‑risk Circuit Segments.
 5                              PG&E considered the following metrics100 when developing
 6                         the BCR that is used to identify Projects to be included in the
 7                         Screen 2 list (Table C.11 Screen 2).
 8                         1) Ignition Risk Reduction: Ignition Risk reduction estimates
 9                              the amount of Ignition Risk that will be removed from
10                              PG&E’s distribution system when a mitigation is applied to a
11                              Circuit Segment or portion of a Circuit Segment. The risk
12                              reduction is comprised of the initial risk on a Circuit
13                              Segment based on the WDRM and PG&E’s estimated
14                              mitigation effectiveness.
15                         2) Outage Risk Reduction: Outage risk reduction estimates
16                              the amount of outage risk―EPSS, PSPS, and Baseline
17                              outage risk―that will be removed from PG&E’s electric
18                              distribution system when a mitigation is applied to a Circuit
19                              Segment or portion of a Circuit Segment. The risk reduction
20                              is comprised of the initial risk on a Circuit Segment that
21                              comes from the Outage Program Risk Model and PG&E’s
22                              estimated mitigation effectiveness.
23                         3) Safety Risk Reduction: Safety risk reduction quantifies the
24                              reduction in non-wildfire public safety risks associated with
25                              distribution infrastructure when a mitigation is implemented.
26                              The public safety risk reduction is comprised of the
27                              non‑wildfire hazards to the public, such as contact with
28                              energized conductors, and vehicle collisions with utility
29                              poles.

                                               -121-
 1   4) Assumptions Related to Easements, Permitting, and CEQA
 2      Review Affecting Scope, Cost, and Risk Reduction and
 3      Reliability Benefits (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.4.1(d))
 4          PG&E’s scoping process (Screen 3) and Project execution
 5      planning (Screen 4 and beyond) consider the requirements to obtain
 6      easements, permits, and CEQA review. The number of required
 7      easements is an element of overall Project cost and is considered
 8      when developing cost assumptions. Permitting requirements are
 9      considered during mitigation selection and may influence where
10      PG&E chooses to overhead harden or underground a distribution
11      line. For example, if PG&E cannot secure an easement, we may
12      need to re-route a hardening Project around that area.
13          Obtaining permits, easements, and CEQA reviews are
14      considered long-lead activities and may impact Project schedules
15      and the selection of undergrounding locations. The time required to
16      secure easements for a system hardening Project is highly variable
17      and permit acquisition times can be unpredictable. PG&E estimates
18      the time required to secure easements, permits and/or conduct
19      CEQA reviews based on prior history, and then works proactively to
20      shorten the lead time and reduce the risk of delays from these
21      activities. As the Project’s scope is further defined, we are usually
22      able to refine our estimates for securing easements, permits and/or
23      conducting CEQA reviews.
24          Wildfire Risk reduction and reliability improvements are not
25      impacted by additional easements, permits, and CEQA review other
26      than in terms of Project timing. If a Project is delayed, PG&E may
27      realize wildfire risk reduction and/or reliability improvements later
28      than originally planned.

 1      3. Screen 3: Project Risk Analysis (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.5)

 2          a. Screen 3 Procedure (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.5.1)

          Screen 3 (Project Risk Analysis) is the procedure for evaluating an individual
     Undergrounding Project in the context of the Portfolio of Undergrounding Projects
     and includes information obtained through the project development process.
     Screen 3 considers the expected wildfire risk reduction and reliability increase
     elements of the Plan Mitigation Objective of an Undergrounding Project and
     includes comparing risk metrics for undergrounding and Alternative Mitigations.
         Screen 3 must be completed for each Undergrounding Project when the Large
     Electrical Corporation has sufficient information to fulfill the modeling requirements
     in Section 2.7 for that Undergrounding Project. Appendix C.1.12, Screen 3 Table,
     and C.1.15, Project Index Table, give instructions for the type of information
     required for Screen 3.
          The EUP must contain a narrative detailing how the Large Electrical
     Corporation will use Screen 3 on individual Undergrounding Projects and describe
     the typical scoping process. The narrative must include the Screen 3 procedure
     for selecting Alternative Mitigations consistent with the instructions on Alternative
     Mitigation selection in Section 2.7.10. The narrative must include a description of
     how project-specific information will be incorporated into the selection of
     Alternative Mitigations. The narrative must include a description of how Baseline
     values will be determined per Section 2.7.5, Core Capability 6. The narrative must
     describe how the scoping process will be used to determine what portions of an
     Eligible Circuit Segment will be undergrounded.
         For each Undergrounding Project with Subprojects, Appendix C.1.14,
     Subproject Table, requires the mitigation for each Subproject and a narrative with
     the reason for dividing the Circuit Segment into Subprojects (using the Subproject
     process required by Section 2.4.2.2).
         An Undergrounding Project that has completed Screen 3 can proceed to
     Screen 4. Undergrounding Projects that have completed Screen 3 are reported as
     Confirmed Projects in Progress Reports.

 1   3) Refining the Screen 2 Proposed Project List
 2          PG&E begins the Screen 3 process by refining the Screen 2
 3      proposed Project list.
 4          First, we identify Circuit Segments where the BCR for
 5      100 percent Undergrounding is greater than or within 50 percent of
 6      the BCR for the Screen 2 Alternative Mitigation 1. The 50 percent
 7      assumption is implemented to support prioritization of Circuit
 8      Segments that have the highest likelihood of requiring
 9      undergrounding and ensures that the screening process does not
10      exclude Circuit Segments that warrant consideration for
11      undergrounding due to risk characteristics not fully captured in the
12      BCR calculations, such as tree-strike risk, ingress/egress risk, and
13      PSPS risk. Screen 3 calculations are based on engineering
14      estimates developed during scoping using a project complexity
15      assessment rather than a strict unit cost assumption. Through the
16      Screen 3 process, PG&E can thoroughly review the risks in the
17      Circuit Segments. The output from this refinement process is a list
18      of Circuit Segments that are prioritized for additional review.
19          Next, PG&E identifies Circuit Segments that are less than one
20      mile in length (Short Circuit Segments) and evaluates whether they
21      can be combined with adjacent Circuit Segments. Short Circuit
22      Segments may be combined with adjacent Circuit Segments that
23      are planned for system hardening, provided those adjacent
24      segments are expected to be included in the workplan within the
25      next few years. If no adjacent Circuit Segments are planned for
26      hardening, Short Circuit Segments are generally excluded from
27      further consideration. Prior to either combining or excluding these
28      Short Circuit Segments, PG&E conducts a review to evaluate
29      whether the Short Circuit Segment presents meaningful wildfire risk,
30      or whether the estimated risk is influenced by known modeling
31      phenomena that affect comparability with other Circuit Segments.
32      For example, a high concentration of modeled assets
33      (e.g., switches, transformers, or insulators) within a small
34      geographic area may result in disproportionately elevated Risk

2   Circuit Segments may consist only of single spans of conductor or
3   isolated pieces of equipment, for which modeling is not intended to
4   provide precise risk estimates and therefore warrant additional
5   review.

 1   4) High-Level Feasibility Review
 2          For Circuit Segments that were not excluded by the Project list
 3      refinement described in Figure 3-4, PG&E conducts a High-Level
 4      Feasibility Review.
 5          If the Circuit Segment or parts of the Circuit Segment are
 6      already included in the current Workplan or system hardening work
 7      is complete, the Circuit Segment or parts therein are excluded from
 8      consideration for undergrounding in the EUP.
 9          PG&E also determines if a distribution Circuit Segment is
10      associated with a transmission line. Circuit Segments constructed
11      under a transmission line (referred to as “T-line under-build”) are
12      generally only considered for overhead hardening. Similarly, electric
13      distribution lines in a transmission “guest position” (essentially built
14      to transmission standards and sharing a structure with transmission
15      lines but operated at a lower, distribution voltage) are excluded from
16      consideration for overhead hardening or undergrounding in the
17      EUP.
18          We also check if the Circuit Segment crosses the HFTD
19      boundary into non-HFTD. Circuit Segment spans that cross the
20      HFTD boundary and are up to two adjacent spans in non-HFTD may
21      be considered for undergrounding (EUP Guidelines,
22      Section 2.4.3.1.).
23          PG&E then documents the results of the high-level feasibility
24      review and creates internal Project management and tracking
25      documents including Planning Orders, Work Breakdown Structure
26      (WBS) Elements, Notifications and Project Management Orders.
27          After completing the high-level feasibility review, PG&E
28      conducts an Alternative Mitigation review as shown in Figure 3-6
29      below.

 1   5) Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation Review
 2          The Alternative Mitigation review starts by creating preliminary
 3      drawings in ArcGIS/Google Earth to show the proposed overhead
 4      and/or underground routes and the mainline/tap line designation.
 5      During this review, we also determine if there are any idle lines or
 6      redundant circuit ties that can be removed.
 7          If there are idle or redundant circuit ties, then we update the
 8      scope in ArcGIS/Google Earth. If there are no idle lines or
 9      redundant circuit ties that could be removed, then we begin a review
10      of Additional Comparison 2. This review of Additional Comparison 2
11      assesses the Circuit Segment and surrounding areas to determine if
12      one or more of the following conditions exist:
13      •   High Tree Strike Risk: In areas with high tree strike risk,
14          undergrounding permanently eliminates exposure to vegetation
15          contact, a leading wildfire ignition driver that cannot always be
16          fully mitigated through overhead hardening and/or vegetation
17          management. Our Grid Design engineers use the most recent
18          LiDAR information available and satellite imagery to review
19          whether the trees are tall enough to strike the lines and their
20          potential to strike and break hardened conductors. PG&E uses
21          six or more trees per span as the threshold for determining if
22          tree strike potential warrants further consideration of
23          undergrounding instead of overhead hardening.
24      •   Ingress/Egress Concerns: Where overhead facilities traverse
25          constrained roadways or evacuation routes, undergrounding
26          removes the risk of lines obstructing ingress and egress during
27          emergency conditions. Our Grid Design engineers conduct a
28          detailed analysis of local conditions at the street level to assess
29          ingress and egress. This granular approach allows them to
30          identify specific ingress and egress challenges that may not be
31          apparent in city or county-level data. For instance, they can
32          assess the condition of specific roads, the presence of potential
33          obstacles, and the overall accessibility of the area. This step



                                -131-
 1                         includes analysis by the Public Safety Specialist (PSS)103 in the
 2                         area. Input from these experts with local knowledge is
 3                         important because they can add insight on community factors
 4                         that allow us to determine whether undergrounding would be
 5                         more effective in reducing wildfire-related risks, including risks
 6                         related to ingress and egress during a wildfire.
 7                    •    PSPS Event Probability: PSPS events are driven by
 8                         geographically defined risk conditions that do not align with
 9                         circuit boundaries. If the PSPS polygon (area where
10                         climatological conditions warrant taking PSPS) covers only part
11                         of the Circuit Segment, targeted undergrounding of only the
12                         affected portion of a Circuit Segment provides a precise,
13                         risk-based means of reducing PSPS exposure without
14                         necessarily undergrounding all parts of that Circuit Segment.
15                         Undergrounding is the most appropriate mitigation where local
16                    conditions (i.e., presence of fall-in tree risk, ingress, and egress
17                    needs, and previous PSPS impacts) require a more effective
18                    mitigation for wildfire, reliability, and/or public safety risks than
19                    overhead hardening. If PG&E identifies one of these areas of
20                    impact, we will consider undergrounding as the preferred mitigation
21                    and consider implementing overhead hardening in those areas not
22                    impacted by these conditions and risks. Based on this review,
23                    Additional Comparison 2 would be made up of hybrid mitigations
24                    (Subprojects).
25                         PG&E then determines if the scope of Additional Comparison 2
26                    is the same as the scope for the 100 percent Undergrounding
27                    solution or Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation.
28                    •    If it is the same, we identify a viable location for a remote grid
29                         and create a combined mitigation alternative (with Remote Grid)
30                         to be considered as Additional Comparison 2.

 1                6) Benefit-Cost Comparison
 2                        The benefit-cost comparison determines which mitigation is
 3                    appropriate on a specific Circuit Segment based on several
 4                    iterations of BCR analyses.
 5                        First, PG&E determines which alternative has the best BCR (or
 6                    has a negative BCR).105 The first comparison of mitigations is
 7                    summarized below and further detailed in Table 3-9:
 8                    •   100 percent Undergrounding: Proceed with 100 percent
 9                        Undergrounding in the EUP.
10                    •   Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation: Conduct additional analysis to
11                        identify if localized risk factors are present.
12                    •   Additional Comparison 2: Proceed with Project as Scoped. The
13                        undergrounding work is included in the EUP and overhead
14                        hardening and/or remote grid is addressed in the GRC.
15                        PG&E reviews BCRs for comparison of each Alternative
16                    Mitigation and Additional Comparison (100 percent Undergrounding,
17                    Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation and Additional Comparison 2), if 100
18                    percent Undergrounding or Additional Comparison 2 have a BCR
19                    that is at least 70 percent of Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation. The 70
20                    percent assessment reflects an estimate uncertainty range applied
21                    to BCR results to account for known limitations and uncertainties in
22                    cost estimates and risk model outputs at the Project-selection stage.
23                    Specifically, PG&E applies a 30 percent estimate uncertainty range
24                    in the EUP application, which means that a more risk reducing
25                    mitigation alternative (e.g., undergrounding) may be considered
26                    when it has an estimated BCR that is at least 70 percent of the BCR
27                    for Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation. The 70 percent framing is simply
28                    100 percent minus the 30 percent uncertainty range and does not
29                    represent a separate or additional threshold. This estimate
30                    uncertainty range is based on:



     105 A BCR may be negative where the investment returns a net positive cashflow such that
         the “cost” is negative, making it a good economic investment even without consideration
         of the risk reduction related benefits.

                                               -135-
 1                    •   Industry‑standard estimating practice (ACEE Cost Estimate
 2                        Classifications), which recognizes that cost estimates developed
 3                        during Project scoping are not yet fully mature;
 4                    •   Energy Safety’s recommendation in its decision on PG&E’s
 5                        2026-2028 Base WMP to reduce the prior 50 percent estimate
 6                        uncertainty range to 30 percent, reflecting improvements in data
 7                        quality and modeling while still accounting for residual existing
 8                        uncertainty in the decision-making process;106 and
 9                    •   Inherent uncertainty in modeled risk point estimates, driven by
10                        compounding assumptions, variability in inputs, and structural
11                        limitations of quantitative risk models.
12                        Where the BCR results fall within this uncertainty range, PG&E
13                    evaluates site-specific factors that are not fully captured in
14                    quantitative models, namely the factors described in Section D.3.a.5
15                    above: ingress and egress constraints, tree-strike exposure, and
16                    PSPS risk, to determine whether a more risk‑reducing alternative is
17                    more prudent than overhead hardening.
18                        The estimate uncertainty range therefore provides appropriate
19                    flexibility to select the safer, more risk-reducing option when
20                    modeled BCRs are close and known uncertainty exists. Below is a
21                    numerical example of how the 70 percent factor will be applied, in
22                    this example:
23                    •   100 percent Undergrounding
24                    •   Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation
25                    •   Additional Comparison 2
26                        We consider the 100 percent Undergrounding or an Additional
27                    Comparison alternative when the BCR is at least 70 percent of the
28                    BCR for the Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation, as shown below:

29

         Wildfire Mitigation Plan (Feb, 5, 2026), pp. 19-20.

              Where BCR_x represents the BCR of either 100 percent Underground
     or Additional Comparison 2.
