10        risk mitigating alternative.

11        a) BCR Comparisons
12                 If Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation has the best BCR, PG&E
13            determines if the BCR for 100 percent Undergrounding or
14            Additional Comparison 2 is greater than or equal to 70 percent
15            of the BCR for the Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation.
16            •    If the BCR for 100 percent Undergrounding is the only
17                 alternative ≥ 70 percent of the Screen 3 Alternative
18                 Mitigation BCR: Proceed with 100 percent Undergrounding
19                 in the EUP.



                                    -137-
 1   •    If the BCR for Additional Comparison 2 is the only
 2        alternative ≥ 70 percent of the Screen 3 Alternative
 3        Mitigation BCR: Proceed with Additional Comparison 2.
 4   •    If the BCR for both the undergrounding solution and
 5        Additional Comparison 2 are ≥ 70 percent of the Screen 3
 6        Alternative Mitigation BCR: proceed with the alternative
 7        with the highest BCR between 100 percent Undergrounding
 8        and Additional Comparison 2.
 9   •    If neither the BCR for 100 percent Undergrounding nor the
10        BCR for Additional Comparison 2 are ≥ 70 percent of the
11        Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation BCR: Conduct Additional
12        Comparison 2 analysis, as described in the paragraphs
13        below.
14        If Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation is still the best BCR and no
15   other mitigation is within 30 percent (i.e., ≥ 70 percent), PG&E
16   conducts an Additional Comparison 2 analysis, essentially
17   creating a revised Additional Comparison 2 Project scope, as
18   described below.
19        First, we exclude targeted undergrounding for PSPS
20   impacted areas (allowing for overhead hardening in those
21   areas) from the current Project scope and determine if the BCR
22   for this revised Additional Comparison 2 is greater than or equal
23   to 70 percent of the BCR for Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation.
24        If the BCR for Additional Comparison 2 is greater than or
25   equal to 70 percent of the BCR for Screen 3 Alternative
26   Mitigation, we proceed with this revised Additional Comparison
27   2.
28   •    If the BCR for this revised Additional Comparison 2 is still
29        less than 70 percent of the BCR for Screen 3 Alternative
30        Mitigation, we exclude targeted undergrounding for
31        ingress/egress impacted areas (allowing for overhead
32        hardening in those areas) from the current Project scope.
33        We then test if the BCR for Additional Comparison 2 is




                          -138-
 1          greater than or equal to 70 percent of the Screen 3
 2          Alternative Mitigation BCR.
 3          If the BCR for Additional Comparison 2 is greater than or
 4      equal to 70 percent of the Screen 3 Alternative Mitigation BCR,
 5      proceed with Additional Comparison 2. If the BCR for Additional
 6      Comparison 2 is less than or equal to 70 percent of Screen 3
 7      Alternative Mitigation BCR, proceed with Screen 3 Alternative
 8      Mitigation. PG&E then conducts the Additional Comparison 3
 9      review shown in Figure 3-8 below and described below.

10   b) BCR Calculations
11          Occasionally, BCR calculations may result in a negative
12      number. There are two instances where this happens:
13      1) When the O&M cost savings of the selected mitigation (PV
14          over the life of the asset) exceeds the capital installation
15          costs of the Project (i.e., the BCR calculation would have a
16          negative denominator). Such outcomes represent
17          economically favorable mitigations, as they effectively have
18          no cost, and are therefore treated as exceeding the BCR ≥
19          1.0 threshold for EUP eligibility.
20      2) When the mitigation alternative introduces a net new risk
21          (e.g., EPSS risk) to the system that outweighs the wildfire
22          risk reduction. Such outcomes represent economically
23          unfavorable mitigations, as the risk introduced to the system
24          exceeds the potential benefits (i.e., the BCR calculation
25          would have a negative numerator).
26          PG&E may select alternatives with a negative BCR when
27      the negative BCR is driven by the difference in the net O&M
28      costs and capital installation costs. PG&E will not select a
29      mitigation where, as described in the second example above,
30      the mitigation would create a new net risk.

 1                    7) Additional Comparison 3 Benefit-Cost Analysis
 2                               The Additional Comparison 3 benefit-cost analysis consists of
 3                           further evaluating portions of Circuit Segments to determine if they
 4                           are candidates for the Remote Grid and/or the Line Elimination
 5                           Incentive Program (LEIP). Segments are considered for Remote
 6                           Grid and LEIP if they are end of line (or will be end of line after
 7                           system hardening mitigations are applied) and are relatively long
 8                           and serve only a small number of customers. Each Circuit Segment
 9                           that is being evaluated in Screen 3 goes through an Additional
10                           Comparison 3 analysis. This step is essential to evaluate the
11                           Remote Grid or LEIP alternative as this mitigation typically impacts
12                           only a small portion of the Project.
13                               If there are candidates for Remote Grid or LEIP in the Circuit
14                           Segment, PG&E completes a desktop screening process to identify
15                           any site-specific features that would render Remote Grid or LEIP
16                           infeasible and generate an expected cost for Remote Grid and/or
17                           LEIP. If it is determined through this initial screening process that
18                           Remote Grid is potentially feasible for the location(s), an additional
19                           BCR calculation is completed for Additional Comparison 3.
20                           Additional Comparison 3 would take the selected alternative from
21                           the previous steps (100 percent Undergrounding, Screen 3
22                           Alternative Mitigation, or Additional Comparison 2) and then

                                                                  -140-
 1      combine it with Remote Grid or LEIP in the confirmed portion of the
 2      Project. We then test if this BCR for this new Additional Comparison
 3      3 is greater than the Project as Scoped BCR, which results from the
 4      comparison of 100 percent Undergrounding, Screen 3 Alternative
 5      Mitigation and Additional Comparison 2.
 6      •   If the BCR for Additional Comparison 3 is greater than the
 7          Project as Scoped BCR derived from the previous analysis,
 8          Additional Comparison 3 becomes the new Project as Scoped.
 9      •   If the BCR for Additional Comparison 3 is less than the Project
10          as Scoped BCR, we do not proceed with Additional
11          Comparison 3.
12          If there are no opportunities for Remote Grid or LEIP, PG&E
13      proceeds to the desktop scoping meeting with the preferred
14      alternative mitigation based on the BCR results.

15   8) Desktop Scoping Meeting, Final Cost Analysis, Final DBM
16      Packaging
17          Once a preferred mitigation alternative has been identified,
18      PG&E prepares for a desktop scoping meeting. Prior to the
19      meeting, PG&E develops preliminary sketches, analyzes fire risk,
20      vegetation, and engineering requirements; identifies constructability
21      limitations; and completes necessary field visits. This information is
22      reviewed during the desktop scoping meeting.
23          Following the meeting, we update the proposed system
24      hardening route with a digital map file (a KMZ) and, for Hybrid
25      Projects, recommend segmentation into Subprojects. PG&E then
26      begins the final cost analysis and inputs updated scope and cost
27      information into the feedback loop calculations. We rerun the BCR
28      analysis with the updated mileages and unit costs, and we repeat
29      the BCR comparison described above for all alternatives as it is
30      possible that there are changes identified during the desktop
31      scoping meeting that could impact the final decision of which
32      Alternative Mitigation will be selected as the Project as Scoped.
33      Once PG&E identifies the preferred mitigation configuration through
34      the Screen 3 process, including consideration of both BCR results

                                -141-
 1                    and site-specific factors, BCR evaluation is complete and the scope
 2                    of the selected project advances through the remainder of the
 3                    Project Acceptance Framework.
 4                        The DBM documents the preliminary design and identifies
 5                    important information about the Project and documents key
 6                    engineering considerations and records decisions made. PG&E
 7                    then creates specific planning orders, reviews Subproject
 8                    segmentation, scope, and schedule, and updates key sketches and
 9                    work descriptions. To complete scoping, we route the DBM for
10                    approval and attach a scope document to each order in SAP, our
11                    system of record.
12                        The detailed scoping process is shown in the end-to-end Project
13                    Acceptance Framework diagram.107 For each Undergrounding
14                    Project with Subprojects, we list in Table C.14 to the Progress
15                    Report 0 the mitigation for each Subproject and a narrative with the
16                    reason for dividing the Circuit Segment into Subprojects (using the
17                    Subproject process required by EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.2.2).

18                9) Screen 3 Procedure for Selecting Alternative Mitigations
19                    Consistent With Section 2.7.10
20                        In Section D.3.a.1-8, above, PG&E describes our procedure for
21                    selecting Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons
22                    consistent with EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.10. The EUP
23                    Guidelines require us to consider the Wildfire Risk reduction and
24                    reliability improvement elements of the Plan Mitigation Objective of
25                    an Undergrounding Project and include comparing risk metrics for
26                    100 percent Undergrounding, Alternative Mitigations and Additional
27                    Comparisons. We also describe how we compare undergrounding
28                    to other Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons and use
29                    the outcome of these comparisons to select the appropriate
30                    mitigation for each Circuit Segment.

 1                10) Incorporating Project Specific Information Into the Selection of
 2                    Alternative Mitigations
 3                        PG&E incorporates specific cost and scope information into our
 4                    selection of Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons
 5                    through the scoping process described in Section D.3.a.1-8. During
 6                    scoping, we run different project variations through the Feedback
 7                    Loop and evaluate the BCR for the different project variations. After
 8                    the desktop scoping meeting, the final mitigation analysis includes a
 9                    review of the BCR using the proposed mileage and cost
10                    assumptions. The final benefit-cost analysis incorporates
11                    Project-specific cost and scope information gathered through the
12                    scoping process and confirms our final mitigation selection.

13                11) Determining Baseline Values
14                        PG&E establishes Baselines using the WDRM v4 asset
15                    configuration, which is anchored to a January 1, 2023 grid
16                    snapshot.108 Baseline values used for forward-looking evaluation
17                    are subsequently calibrated through postprocessing adjustments to
18                    reflect expected 2028 conditions, including recognition of historical
19                    hardening completed since the snapshot date and application of
20                    appropriate climate escalation factors.
21                        The Baseline scenario is a foundational element of the BCR
22                    calculation because it establishes the reference condition against
23                    which all costs and benefits are measured. Its purpose is to enable
24                    a consistent assessment of the incremental impacts of each of the
25                    proposed mitigations. As directed by Energy Safety in EUP
26                    Guidelines Section 2.7.10, PG&E will use a Baseline consisting of
27                    bare overhead wire paired with PSPS, EPSS and DCD capability.
28                        Core Capability 6 requires PG&E to describe how we establish
29                    and maintain Baselines and historical model calibrations used to
30                    evaluate system risk and compare Undergrounding Projects,
31                    Alternative Mitigations, and Additional Comparisons. In subsequent

         The filed EUP must include a Portfolio of at least 25 individual Undergrounding
     Projects considered under Screen 3. This Portfolio must include:
     a. at least one Circuit with multiple Undergrounding Projects.
     b. at least three Undergrounding Projects with multiple Subprojects (if
        Subprojects will be part of the EUP).
     c.   at least three Undergrounding Projects with non-undergrounding Subprojects
          (if non-undergrounding Subprojects will be part of the EUP).

        Outage Program Threshold (if High Frequency Outage Program will be part of
        the EUP).

        Threshold (if Ignition Tail Risk will be part of the EUP).

 1   c. How Prioritization Supports the Plan Mitigation Objective
 2          The Plan Mitigation Objective is the total amount of change in
 3      wildfire and reliability risk that is necessary to demonstrate that PG&E
 4      has substantially increased electrical reliability and substantially reduced
 5      the risk of wildfire through our EUP. PG&E’s Plan Mitigation Objective is
 6      defined as the monetized average Overall Utility Risk reduced per
 7      primary overhead mile removed. PG&E’s Screen 4 prioritization aligns
 8      with and supports the Plan Mitigation Objective because we are
 9      primarily identifying and prioritizing work on Circuit Segments with the
10      highest monetized Overall Utility Risk reduced per primary overhead
11      mile removed.

12   d. Consideration of Completion Time of Subprojects and the Effect of
13      Staggered Completion Timeline Requirements Consistent With
14      EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.5, Core Capabilities 4 and 5
15          Core Capability 4 requires PG&E to describe how we use estimated
16      Project timelines to model the reduction of risk and increase in reliability
17      over time.
18          Core Capability 5 requires PG&E to describe how we evaluate
19      Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk for Undergrounding Projects that
20      are completed in stages or have multiple mitigations on a single Circuit
21      Segment.
22          Undergrounding and Hybrid Projects that pass Screen 4 are already
23      initially prioritized for Ignition Risk, Reliability Risk, Cost Efficiency, and
24      Public Safety (as described above). At the time Screen 4 is applied to a
25      Project, the degree to which there will be staggered completion times for
26      the associated Subprojects within a Project is not well understood.
27      Completion times of Subprojects become better understood during the
28      estimating and dependency phases of the Subprojects. As part of our
29      Subproject planning process, PG&E considers how staggered
30      Subproject completion timelines affect Ignition Risk and Outage
31      Program Risk reduction. Subproject planning includes constraints
32      analysis at both a Portfolio level and the Subproject level. For instance,
33      Subproject constraints include permitting requirements, land rights,



                                      -154-
 1                resource availability, material availability, weather impacts, community
 2                impacts, and similar factors to build Subproject schedules. Portfolio
 3                constraints include cost recovery requirements that will be established in
 4                the CPUC Phase 2 Decision, as well as the Plan Mitigation Objective,
 5                Plan Tracking Objectives and other specific targets and objectives (as
 6                outlined in the EUP Guidelines Section 2.3). Throughout the Project
 7                and Subproject lifecycle, actual and forecasted execution timelines can
 8                change from the estimated timelines used initially to model Ignition Risk
 9                and Outage Program Risk reduction. These changes in the timing of
10                forecasted and actual risk reduction from Subproject completion are fed
11                back into our risk reduction model and are used to support updates to
12                the annual Plan Tracking Objectives.111 PG&E will adjust the workplan
13                for future years based on the work completed to meet the EUP and
14                CPUC Phase 2 Application targets and objectives. We will update the
15                Plan Tracking Objectives to reflect any changes.

16       5. Incorporating Previously Scoped Projects Into the EUP
17                Project scoping and implementation is a long-term effort that often
18           spans multiple years. PG&E incurs significant costs to develop an
19           Undergrounding Project scope. Over the past years, we have scoped
20           several Projects pursuant to the decision trees in approved WMPs. These
21           Projects may not meet certain EUP requirements—for example, certain of
22           the Projects may have been selected and scoped based on a previous
23           version of the risk model.
24                PG&E has Undergrounding Projects in progress that we anticipate will
25           be completed prior to the effective date of the EUP. These Projects are
26           reasonable as they were prudently selected under the existing Project
27           selection and decision-making process as vetted and approved in our
28           WMPs. If any of these Projects are incomplete when the EUP begins, we
29           would incorporate them into the EUP Portfolio and complete those Projects.
30                We expect only a small minority of the EUP mileage to be made up of
31           previously-scoped Projects, and we would expect that many of these



     111 Controls to mitigate these impacts are described more in Chapter 5, Section C.1.c
         Controls to Maintain Adherence to Schedules (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.1(c)).

                                               -155-
 1           Projects would meet the EUP eligibility criteria and significantly reduce
 2           Wildfire Risk. However, even If the Project does not meet all the EUP
 3           requirements, PG&E should be allowed to complete them because when
 4           they were selected and scoped PG&E forecasted that they significantly
 5           reduce wildfire risk based on the risk model at the time―the key factor in
 6           selecting and pursuing Projects in the EUP.
 7                Further, it would be very disruptive to customers and communities
 8           where planning for undergrounding has already begun, often including
 9           acquisition of land rights from local customers, coordination with the
10           municipality about paving plans and traffic controls plans, to cancel a Project
11           simply due to the transition from GRC funding to EUP funding.
12                Therefore, it is reasonable to include these previously-scoped Projects
13           in the EUP Portfolio. We would consider the risk reduction, miles, and unit
14           cost of these Projects in the annual values included in the Target/Timeline
15           Table.112

16   E. Chapter Summary
17           This chapter establishes PG&E’s Project Acceptance Framework for
18       identifying, evaluating, and prioritizing Undergrounding Projects. It explains how
19       Circuit Segments move through four screens and how PG&E applies statutory
20       and EUP Guidelines requirements at each stage. Overall, the chapter shows
21       that PG&E’s framework is designed to focus undergrounding where it can
22       provide the greatest wildfire risk reduction, reliability benefit, and public safety
23       value while remaining cost-efficient and operationally feasible. By combining
24       threshold-based screening, benefit-cost comparisons across undergrounding
25       and alternative mitigations, Project-level scoping, and Portfolio-Level
26       prioritization, PG&E creates a transparent and repeatable process for selecting
27       confirmed and Prioritized Projects. This framework supports development of
28       Portfolio 0 and provides the structure for future updates as Project conditions,
29       model outputs, and implementation constraints evolve.

 5   A. Introduction
 6          In this chapter, we address two issues required by Section 2.4.7 of the
 7      Electrical Undergrounding Plan (EUP) Guidelines: the preparation of the Circuit
 8      Segment Information Lists and information regarding other system hardening
 9      programs Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) conducts to reduce Wildfire
10      and Outage Program Risk in the High Fire Threat District (HFTD)/High Fire Risk
11      Areas (HFRA) outside of the EUP.
12          Section B lists the requirements in Senate Bill (SB) 884 and the EUP
13      Guidelines addressed in this chapter.
14          Section C explains how tabular data created in compliance with the Project
15      Acceptance Framework described in Chapter 3 is combined and sorted to create
16      the required Circuit Segment Information Lists.
17          Section D describes PG&E’s current system hardening programs that are
18      conducted to reduce or eliminate Wildfire and Outage Program Risk on Circuit
19      Segments outside of the EUP: (1) PG&E’s existing Undergrounding Program;
20      (2) Overhead System Hardening; and (3) Line Removal with or without Remote
21      Grids. For each program, we provide a Project description, the approximate
22      timeline for completion, Project status, and associated Wildfire Risk reduction.
23          Section E provides a chapter summary and Section F lists attachments
24      supporting this chapter.

25   B. Undergrounding Plan Requirements
26          In Tables 4-1 and 4-2 below, we identify each of the statutory and EUP
27      Guidelines requirements that are addressed in this chapter.

 1   C. Required Circuit Segment Information Lists (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.7)

 2      1. Instructions for Circuit Segment Information Lists (EUP Guidelines
 3          Section 2.4.7.1)

         The Project Acceptance Framework uses a series of screens to evaluate
     Circuit Segments for the EUP.
         As seen in Figure 1, Project Acceptance Framework Flowchart and described
     above, each screen requires the Large Electrical Corporation to create and review
     progressively smaller sets of Circuit Segments which satisfy various criteria and
     have different levels of information determined, until they finally become
     Confirmed Projects and Prioritized Projects. The full lists of Circuit Segments
     which have reached these stages can be generated from the data submission
     tables described in Appendix C. Each Progress Report, beginning with Progress
     Report 0 (see Section 2.6), will include the data submission for these lists in a
     tabular format that can be accessed by members of the public.
         The table below describes the lists utilized in the Project Acceptance
     Framework process, the relevant information they contain, and the tables that can
     be joined to generate the lists.


 4              As described in Chapter 3, PG&E applies the Project Acceptance
 5          Framework to evaluate Circuit Segments for the EUP, including the Project
 6          evaluation steps described in four consecutive screens. Consistent with
 7          Section 2.4 of the EUP Guidelines, this process applies standardized,
 8          risk-based criteria to progressively refine the population of the Circuit
 9          Segments and develop Undergrounding Projects, Confirmed Projects and
10          Prioritized Projects.
11              Section 2.4.7.1 of the EUP Guidelines, which is addressed in this
12          chapter, provides instructions for generating the full list of Circuit Segment
13          and Project information that have reached applicable stages of the Project
14          Acceptance Framework.
15              PG&E provides this information through Attachment B, Workpaper 032,
16          Circuit Segment List, and the data submission tables in Progress Report
17          Attachment A-2. Attachment B, Workpaper 032 Circuit Segment List
18          (WP032), provides the complete inventory of Circuit Segments in PG&E’s
19          service territory that serves as the foundational dataset for the Project
20          Acceptance Framework. For each Circuit Segment, the workpaper provides
21          the Circuit Segment ID, associated Circuit ID, segment length, Project ID
22          where applicable, county, HFTD tier, and indicators identifying whether the


                                             -161-
 1   Circuit Segment is within a Rebuild Area, is In Area, and is eligible for the
 2   EUP.
 3       Below describes the information in the Circuit Segment Information List.
 4   •   All Circuit Segments List: PG&E lists all Circuit Segments in our
 5       service territory.
 6   •   In-Area Circuit Segments List: PG&E develops this list by removing
 7       all Circuit Segments outside the Tier 2 or Tier 3 HFTD and Fire Rebuild
 8       Areas from the All Circuit Segments List.
 9   •   Eligible Circuit Segments List: PG&E develops this list by applying
10       the Project-Level Thresholds (outlined in Chapter 7, Section M.1) to all
11       In-Area Circuit Segments. Projects that are above the Project-Level
12       Thresholds are included in the list of Eligible Projects.
13   •   Ineligible Circuit Segments List: PG&E develops this list by applying
14       the Project-Level Thresholds (outlined in Chapter 7, Section M.1) to all
15       In-Area Circuit Segments. Projects that fall below the Project-Level
16       Thresholds are included in the list of ineligible Projects.
17       The Progress Report data submission tables in Attachment A-2 provide
18   the additional information needed to identify and track Projects as they
19   advance through the Project Acceptance Framework. The data in
20   Workpaper 032 may be joined with the applicable data submission tables
21   provided in Attachment A-2 Progress Report Tabular Data that generates
22   the lists of Circuit Segments that have reached the relevant framework
23   stages, including Confirmed Projects and Prioritized Projects. Table C.9, the
24   Screen History Table, identifies the screens that each Circuit Segment or
25   Project has passed. Table C.10, the Project Table, provides the Projects
26   that have advanced through Screens 2, 3, or 4, including the information
27   used to identify Undergrounding Projects, Confirmed Projects, and
28   Prioritized Projects. All information related to Circuit Segment eligibility and
29   EUP inclusion is provided in Table C.6. Non-EUP Projects located in Tier 2
30   or Tier 3 HFTD are listed in Table C.22. See below for more information
31   about each list:
32   •   Undergrounding Projects List: PG&E defines an Undergrounding
33       Project as a Circuit Segment that has passed Screen 2 and is eligible for
34       undergrounding. The list of Undergrounding Projects is the basis of


                                      -162-

 2       reviewed for those Circuit Segments in Table C.11 (see Chapter 3,
 3       Section D.2).
 4   •   Confirmed Projects List: PG&E develops the Confirmed Projects List
 5       as Projects progress through the Screen 3 assessment (outlined in
 6       Chapter 3, Section D.3.a.1-8). This list can be found in Table C.10.
 7   •   Prioritized Projects List: PG&E applies the Screen 4 prioritization

 1   D. Information on Non-EUP Projects (EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.7.2)

          The EUP must include information on any distribution undergrounding or other
     system hardening project in a Tier 2 or 3 High Fire Threat District that is funded or
     in the Project Planning or Construction Phases that is not included in the 10-Year
     EUP (“Non-EUP Project”). The Large Electrical Corporation must include this
     information in the Circuit Segment Identification Tables as described in
     Appendix C.1.6. The Large Electrical Corporation is not required to apply the
     screens to non-EUP Projects.
         The Large Electrical Corporation must also provide a brief overview of all
     non-EUP Undergrounding programs and all other distribution system hardening
     programs aimed at reducing Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk. The Large
     Electrical Corporation must include the timeline for completion of Non-EUP
     Projects, their Project Status, and their associated risk reduction. The overview
     must discuss how the selection process for these Non-EUP Projects and
     programs is different from the EUP and how they will be coordinated with the EUP.
         All of the information above must be updated in each Progress Report. The
     Large Electrical Corporation must also include a narrative describing how these
     projects are accounted for in the Risk Modeling Methodology.


 2          PG&E’s system hardening programs approved by the California Public
 3      Utilities Commission (CPUC or Commission) through the General Rate Case
 4      (GRC) include: (1) Undergrounding; (2) Overhead System Hardening; and
 5      (3) Line Removal with and without Remote Grids. Each program is specifically
 6      designed to reduce Ignition Risk and Reliability Risk. PG&E does not address
 7      Rule 20 Undergrounding Projects in our EUP as they are primarily completed for
 8      aesthetic purposes rather than reducing Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk.
 9          PG&E includes in the Progress Report a list of all non-EUP system
10      hardening Projects, including the timeline for completion, Project Status, and
11      associated risk reduction (see Progress Report 0 Table C.22).
12          Each non-EUP system hardening program (i.e. Overhead Hardening and
13      Line Removal), timeline for completion and estimated risk reduction are
14      described in detail below. In addition, PG&E deploys Hybrid Projects that
15      consist of a combination of undergrounding, overhead hardening, and/or line
16      removal. Depending on the mitigations selected for a Project, PG&E will follow
17      the steps for each mitigation and apply it to the selected portion of the Circuit
18      Segment.




                                             -164-
 1       1. GRC-Funded Undergrounding Program

 2           a. Program Description
 3                    PG&E’s existing Undergrounding Program is focused on mitigating
 4                Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk caused by distribution overhead
 5                assets. The primary benefits provided by undergrounding are: (1) near
 6                permanent ignition risk reduction from overhead electric distribution
 7                equipment; and (2) avoiding customer reliability impacts from deploying
 8                Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) and Enhanced Powerline Safety
 9                Settings (EPSS) to mitigate Ignition Risk on overhead lines.
10                    Undergrounding is PG&E’s preferred solution for mitigating Ignition
11                Risk in the highest-risk areas where the long-term benefits of
12                undergrounding include greater wildfire risk reduction, reliability
13                improvements, and ongoing vegetation management and operational
14                cost avoidance. Undergrounding also mitigates the potential for harm or
15                injury to members of the public by reducing the likelihood of contact with
16                an energized line.
17                    PG&E forecasts that we will underground 1,205 circuit miles during
18                the 2023-2026 period. PG&E’s plan to underground 307 circuit miles in
19                2027 was approved by Energy Safety in its decision on PG&E’s
20                2026-2028 WMP113 and is pending approval in PG&E’s 2027 GRC.

21           b. Timeline and Project Status
22                    A typical timeline for all Undergrounding Project activities over the
23                Project lifecycle is approximately four years (one to two years for
24                pre-construction activities, one year for construction and one year for
25                post-construction activities).

                                               -165-
 1                   Undergrounding electric distribution system assets follows the same
 2               general process as most utility construction work. The following
 3               describes the phases of an Undergrounding Project:
 4               (1) Project Planning and Scoping: The Undergrounding Program
 5                   focuses on circuits in the HFTD and Fire Rebuild Areas.114 Project
 6                   planning and scoping consists of identifying, developing, and
 7                   defining an Electric Distribution asset requiring undergrounding. In
 8                   scoping Projects, PG&E balances risk reduction, constructability,
 9                   and affordability.
10               (2) Engineering and Design: Engineering and design consists of
11                   developing a comprehensive design for the new assets to be
12                   installed underground and identifying materials needed to execute
13                   the Project. This includes designing the trench, bore tunnel, or other
14                   underground pathway for the conduit and electric cable, as well as
15                   the boxes, transformers or other connections needed to integrate
16                   with customer services. The Project scoping and design phases
17                   address and plan for constructability issues, which include the local
18                   geology (whether hard rock exists), existing underground utilities
19                   (including water, natural gas and drainage systems), plans for future
20                   road widening, sensitive environmental and/or cultural resources,
21                   and other factors.
22               (3) Material Acquisition: Material acquisition includes sourcing,
23                   purchasing, storing, and staging materials needed for
24                   Undergrounding Projects. Material acquisition also includes
25                   developing a sustainable supply chain to ensure availability of
26                   materials and securing favorable rates through long-term
27                   contracting.
28               (4) Permitting and Land Rights: Undergrounding Projects may
29                   encounter sensitive resources such as waterways, animal habitats,
30                   and cultural resources. PG&E implements construction impact
31                   mitigation measures and best management plans to mitigate



     114 The Undergrounding Program previously included circuits in the HFTD, HFRA and Fire
         Rebuild Areas.

                                             -166-
 1       disturbances and engages key agencies, cities, counties, tribes,
 2       individuals and other stakeholders early and often to mitigate risks
 3       and issues associated with permitting and environmental
 4       considerations. PG&E may adjust Project designs or construction
 5       plans as a result of this process. Additionally, for undergrounding
 6       work on private property, PG&E acquires the appropriate land rights,
 7       which generally involve easements. PG&E’s existing land rights for
 8       overhead power lines often do not grant the right to install
 9       underground assets in the same configuration and thus require new
10       or expanded land rights.
11   (5) Construction: The actual construction phase of an Undergrounding
12       Project is the most labor-intensive and community impacting phase
13       of the Project. Traffic control is often deployed to keep construction
14       crews and community members safe as undergrounding is
15       frequently performed in or adjacent to public roads. Construction
16       can also be subdivided into the following two phases (although the
17       phases may overlap): (1) civil construction including trenching and
18       installing the conduit and boxes; and (2) electric construction pulling
19       cable through the installed conduit and connecting the cable to
20       equipment installed inside the boxes. At the end of the construction
21       phase, service to impacted customers is converted from the existing
22       overhead powerlines to the new underground lines and the
23       deenergized overhead assets are removed.
24   (6) Quality Control and Inspections: Quality inspection of underground
25       assets is performed throughout the construction phase, including
26       when the trench is open or electric cables are being pulled and
27       connected to equipment. At the end of construction, PG&E
28       conducts a fire safe audit prior to energizing the new underground
29       line. Any quality validation or inspection activities must be carefully
30       timed and executed in partnership with construction activities.
31   (7) Mapping, Documentation, and Closeout: Mapping, documentation,
32       and closeout involves permanently documenting the assets that
33       have been installed as part of the Undergrounding Projects and




                                 -167-
 1                   removing from the active maps the overhead lines that have been
 2                   eliminated, and other administrative Project closeout activities.
 3                   PG&E engages with customers, property owners, and communities
 4               through the entire process of planning and executing an
 5               Undergrounding Project to partner, coordinate, and share
 6               information.115

 7           c. Risk Reduction
 8                   Relocating overhead distribution lines underground is the most
 9               effective way to achieve near permanent Wildfire Risk reduction and
10               significantly reduces Outage Program Risk from PSPS and EPSS.
11               PG&E assessed the effectiveness of each of Alternative Mitigation
12               (undergrounding, overhead hardening, overhead hardening with EPSS,
13               line removal) against more than 2,700 outage combinations that
14               occurred in PG&E’s HFTD during the 2015-2024 wildfire seasons.
15               Undergrounding primary distribution lines is approximately 98 percent
16               effective at mitigating Wildfire Risk.
17                   PG&E also analyzed the reliability performance on Circuit Segments
18               where undergrounding was performed in 2022 and 2023 to quantify
19               overall improvements to service reliability. PG&E’s analysis included
20               approximately 750 outages between 2021 and 2024 and showed an
21               approximate 90 percent reduction in faults that resulted in sustained
22               outages after the undergrounding work was completed.
23                   Our 2027 GRC forecast requests approval of 307 circuit miles of
24               undergrounding and estimates that this will achieve 2.8 percent of
25               Wildfire Risk reduction in 2027. If the Commission does not approve
26               307 miles in PG&E’s 2027 GRC, PG&E will update our 2027 risk
27               reduction forecast based on the number of miles approved.

28       2. Overhead System Hardening

29           a. Program Description
30                   Overhead System Hardening includes replacement of bare
31               overhead primary conductor and associated framing with conductor



     115 See A.25-05-009, PG&E Ex-04, pp. 7-25 to 7-28.


                                              -168-
 1   insulated with abrasion resistant polyethylene coatings (often referred to
 2   as “covered conductor” or “tree wire”) that can be an effective mitigation
 3   in certain instances to prevent ignitions caused by distribution lines.
 4   Installing covered conductor can help reduce the likelihood of faults in
 5   instances such as line-to-line contacts, tree branch contacts, and faults
 6   caused by animals. Installing covered conductor on secondary lines has
 7   similar resilience to faults or risk events as installing it on primary lines.
 8   In addition to replacement of conductor, Overhead System Hardening
 9   reduces Wildfire and Reliability Risk through the following foundational
10   activities: (1) primary and secondary covered conductor replacement;
11   (2) pole replacement, which may include adding additional poles, where
12   the poles are not strong enough for the covered conductor;
13   (3) replacement of non-exempt equipment; (4) replacement of overhead
14   distribution line transformers; (5) framing and animal protection
15   upgrades; and (6) vegetation clearing. Further detail of each of these
16   activities is outlined below:
17   (1) Primary and Secondary Covered Conductor Replacement:
18       Replacement of bare overhead primary conductor and associated
19       framing with conductor insulated with abrasion resistant
20       polyethylene coatings (covered conductor or tree wire) can be an
21       effective mitigation in certain instances to prevent ignitions caused
22       by distribution lines. Installing covered conductor can help reduce
23       the likelihood of faults including but not limited to: line-to-line
24       contacts, tree branch contacts, and faults caused by animals.
25       Installing covered conductor on secondary lines has similar
26       resilience to transient events to installing it on primary lines.
27   (2) Pole Replacements: Evaluating all existing poles where a system
28       hardening Project is planned is necessary to determine whether
29       those poles meet the strength requirements to withstand the new,
30       heavier covered conductor and associated equipment. PG&E then
31       replaces poles based on that evaluation. Often, most poles in the
32       scope of an overhead hardening Project will need to be replaced
33       because they do not meet PG&E standards. In addition, new poles




                                     -169-
 1      can be added as needed to support additional conductor weight and
 2      loading.
 3   (3) Replacement of Non-Exempt Equipment: Replacing existing
 4      primary line equipment such as fuses/cutouts and switches with
 5      equipment that is certified by the California Department of Forestry
 6      and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) as low fire risk is another
 7      component of PG&E’s System Hardening Program. This
 8      replacement work eliminates overhead line equipment and devices
 9      that may generate exposed electrical arcs, sparks, or hot material
10      during their operation.
11   (4) Replacement of Overhead Distribution Line Transformers:
12      Upgrading transformers with newer transformers that contain fire
13      resistant “FR3” insulating fluid to be consistent with PG&E’s current
14      equipment standards. “FR3” insulating fluid, a natural ester derived
15      from renewable vegetable oils, provides improved fire safety,
16      transformer life, increased load capability, and environmental
17      benefits. In addition, new transformers are manufactured to achieve
18      higher Department of Energy electrical efficiency standards.
19   (5) Framing and Animal Protection Upgrades: Replacing crossarms
20      with composite arms, wrapping jumpers, and installing animal
21      protection upgrades reduces animal contacts and pole-related
22      ignition risks.
23   (6) Vegetation Clearing: Clearing vegetation undergrowth to access
24      facilities to execute a Project and bring the vegetation clearance up
25      to standard for the newly-installed infrastructure is a critical
26      component of overhead hardening. Regulatory requirements
27      mandate four feet of clearance throughout the year. If there is a
28      change to a line’s profile, including using taller poles or wider cross
29      arms, the vegetation must be cleared to be consistent with any
30      profile changes and provide the required clearing for new overhead
31      lines. This clearance must be maintained over the life of the
32      overhead assets.




                                  -170-
 1           b. Timeline and Project Status
 2                    Overhead System Hardening Projects have similar cycle times as
 3               Undergrounding Projects as both project types navigate scoping,
 4               permitting, and pre-construction activities. Overhead System Hardening
 5               Projects take approximately 17 months from Project initiation (identified
 6               at the scoping phase of a Project) to Project completion (construction
 7               end).116
 8                    Overhead System Hardening is tracked and managed as part of
 9               PG&E’s System Hardening Program. Projects are tracked starting with
10               Project scoping when mitigations are first selected.
11                    PG&E’s System Hardening Program generally begins tracking
12               non-EUP Undergrounding Projects in the HFTD once a Non-EUP
13               Project has been identified and given a unique identifier for reporting.
14               When Non-EUP Projects reach this stage, we will report them in
15               Table C.22 of our Progress Reports.

16           c. Risk Reduction
17                    Overhead System Hardening provides benefits for Wildfire Risk
18               reduction. Based on an analysis of projected performance of overhead
19               hardened facilities on more than 2,700 outage types, PG&E estimates
20               that, on average, Overhead System Hardening can reduce 67 percent of
21               the distribution overhead asset ignitions caused by equipment failures or
22               external contact/strikes with energized lines, such as vegetation tree
23               strikes.117 When used in combination with EPSS and Downed
24               Conductor Detection (DCD), Overhead System Hardening can, on
25               average, reduce Wildfire Risk by approximately 79 percent. See
26               Workpaper 001, Mitigation Effectiveness Analysis, for additional
27               information on PG&E’s mitigation effectiveness methodology.
28                    PG&E forecasts in the 2027 GRC that we will achieve approximately
29               four percent of Wildfire Risk reduction from 2027 to 2030 by installing




     116 Analysis based on subprojects completed between 2018-2024, excluding Fire Rebuild
         work.
     117 PG&E 2026-2028 Wildfire Mitigation Plan R3, Vol. 1, (Dec. 30, 2025), Section 8.2.5.


                                              -171-
 1               approximately 760 miles of covered conductor.118 If the Commission
 2               does not approve our full 2027 GRC Overhead System Hardening
 3               forecast, PG&E will update our risk reduction forecast based on the
 4               number of covered conductor miles approved.

 5       3. Line Removal Program

 6           a. Program Description
 7                   The Line Removal Program is a cost-effective Wildfire Risk
 8               mitigation and a form of system hardening that may be considered
 9               where operationally feasible, as part of PG&E’s broader wildfire risk
10               mitigation strategy. Line removal is pursued when a distribution line is
11               no longer needed for operational or service reasons and its continued
12               presence increases Ignition Risk. Consistent with PG&E’s WMP,
13               targeted line removal may be enabled through several implementation
14               pathways.119 These include:
15               (1) Removal of Idle Facilities: Idle facilities are electric distribution line
16                   segments that are no longer serving customer load or operational
17                   needs. Where an idle facility is no longer required for future system
18                   operations or contingency use, PG&E may remove the line to
19                   permanently eliminate the associated Ignition Risk.
20               (2) Circuit Re-route: PG&E may evaluate a Circuit Segment for
21                   removal if system reconfiguration, new construction, or other
22                   infrastructure upgrades mean that its associated load is now
23                   permanently served through an alternate path and the original line
24                   segment is no longer required for normal operations, contingency
25                   support, or reliability purposes.
26               (3) Remote Grids: PG&E can remove overhead distribution lines by
27                   installing remote grids—standalone power systems that provide
28                   continuous, permanent electric service—to meet customer energy
29                   needs in remote locations serving a small number of customers.
30               (4) Line Elimination Incentive Program (LEIP): Through this program,
31                   PG&E enters into an agreement with a property owner in a wildfire


     118 A.25-05-009, PG&E Ex-04, p. 7-22, Table 7-6.
     119 2026-2028 WMP, Section 8.2.9.2.


                                               -172-
 1          risk area under which PG&E removes the electric line serving the
 2          property and provides compensation. Under the LEIP agreement,
 3          the customer assumes responsibility to provide their own energy
 4          supply, thereby allowing PG&E to permanently remove the
 5          distribution line to eliminate the associated Ignition Risk.
 6      (5) Land Purchases: In limited circumstances where Wildfire Risk
 7          cannot be reasonably mitigated through other system hardening
 8          measures, PG&E may purchase land from a property owner and
 9          discontinue electric service to the property.
10          Remote grids, LEIP, and land purchases are implementation
11      mechanisms that may enable line removal; these mitigations are
12      evaluated using the same underlying risk mitigation framework as other
13      system hardening mitigations.

14   b. Timelines and Project Status
15          The timeline of a Line Removal Project varies based on the
16      implementation method. Where the implementation method is
17      associated with installing infrastructure such as a Remote Grid, the
18      timeline is typically longer than for pathways where installation of new
19      infrastructure is not required. Remote Grid Projects can have similar
20      timelines as Undergrounding and Overhead System Hardening Projects
21      because Remote Grid Projects involve scoping, land rights and
22      permitting where applicable, and engineering and other pre-construction
23      activities. The end-to-end timeline for Remote Grid Projects is
24      approximately 24 months. Remote Grid Projects requiring discretionary
25      permitting can take longer.
26          To the extent that an idle facilities Project, circuit re-route, LEIP or
27      land purchase Project is not dependent on an associated infrastructure
28      installation Project (e.g., a LEIP Project and a Remote Grid Project
29      located on the same end-of-line Circuit Segment), these Project types
30      may have timelines shorter than 24 months.
31          In addition, all line removal implementation methods may have
32      permitting requirements for the line removal work that can impact the
33      timeline, in addition to the pre-construction activities and the line
34      removal work itself.

                                      -173-
 1                      Line removal Projects enabled by Remote Grid or LEIP are tracked
 2               and managed by PG&E’s Remote Grid Program Management team
 3               which implements standardized PG&E processes for evaluating,
 4               designing, deploying, and operating Remote Grids.

 5           c. Risk Reduction
 6                      PG&E forecasts that we will achieve approximately 0.04 percent of
 7               Wildfire Risk reduction from our line removal program from 2027-2030,
 8               based on our 2027 GRC target. Line Removal eliminates 100 percent of
 9               the risk associated with the former overhead distribution lines.120

10       4. Selection Process for Non-EUP Projects and Differences With EUP
11           Project Selection
12               Consistent with the requirements in the EUP screen process (see EUP
13           Guidelines Section 2.4), Overhead System Hardening and other system
14           hardening mitigations will be selected using the same methodology where a
15           Circuit Segment does not meet the requirements for an Undergrounding
16           Project.
17               For each Circuit Segment that is not selected for undergrounding, PG&E
18           will identify an Alternative Mitigation based on the results of economic
19           analyses (cost benefit analysis and net benefit) and the Project selection
20           framework, including the EUP decision tree. As a result of that process,
21           PG&E will designate a Circuit Segment for Overhead System Hardening or,
22           if appropriate, find an opportunity for Line Removal which could entail
23           deployment of a Remote Grid or the LEIP.

24       5. How Non-EUP Projects Are Accounted for in the Risk Modeling
25           Methodology
26               All system hardening Projects are modeled the same. There is no
27           difference in how we model non-EUP system hardening Projects compared
28           to EUP Projects.
29               Circuit Segments that have been hardened outside of the EUP could be
30           identified as Eligible Circuit Segments under the Screen 1 criteria (located in
31           the HFTD and meet one of the Project-level thresholds) but they would be



     120 2026-2028 WMP, p. 179, Table 8-1.


                                              -174-
 1           excluded from further consideration during Screen 3 filtering if the Circuit
 2           Segment or portions of the segment have already been hardened and thus
 3           would be excluded from consideration in subsequent screens. (See
 4           Chapter 3, Section D.3.a.) We also exclude any privately-owned distribution
 5           lines.
 6               Non-EUP Projects would be excluded when we report instantaneous
 7           and cumulative risk over various time periods since only Confirmed Projects
 8           are included in the instantaneous and cumulative risk calculations.121
 9           PG&E will account for the risk reduced by Non-EUP Projects when reporting
10           changes to Circuit Segment information as required by EUP Guidelines
11           Section 2.4.2.1 and when recording new baselines each year as required by
12           EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.5, Core Capability 6.

13       6. Coordination with the EUP Projects
14               Non-EUP system hardening work will be coordinated with EUP
15           Undergrounding Projects.
16               PG&E’s system hardening scoping process accounts for future grid
17           needs and includes collaboration with distribution planning and operating
18           engineers so we can ensure our Project scope reflects anticipated future
19           growth and operational needs. Specifically, PG&E’s planning and operating
20           engineers are included throughout the review and approval process from
21           when a Project is first identified for possible system hardening to when the
22           final job package is created and the Project design is estimated for
23           construction.
24               For Projects and Subprojects which may opportunistically be planned for
25           coordination during construction, PG&E also employs strategies to gain
26           efficiencies across non-EUP and EUP work. These include, but not limited
27           to, shared permits with local and state jurisdictions, shared contractor
28           resources and contracting strategies, shared outage windows limiting
29           customer impact, shared laydown or staging yards, material procurement
30           strategies, and shared Project and construction management.




     121 See EUP Guidelines, p. 36, Section 2.7.5, Core Capability 4: Approximating Future
         Risk and Accumulation of Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk Over Time.

 1   E. Chapter Summary
 2          This chapter explains how PG&E satisfies the EUP Guidelines requirements
 3      in Section 2.4.7 by producing the Circuit Segment Information Lists and by
 4      identifying other system hardening efforts in the HFTD/HFRA that are outside of
 5      the 10-Year EUP. It describes how the standardized data developed through
 6      the Project Acceptance Framework is combined and sorted to generate the full
 7      set of required lists, including all Circuit Segments, In-Area, Eligible/Ineligible,
 8      Undergrounding Projects, Confirmed Projects, Prioritized Projects, and
 9      Non-EUP Projects lists.
10          This chapter also provides a concise overview of PG&E’s non-EUP system
11      hardening programs—GRC funded undergrounding, overhead system
12      hardening, and line removal—by describing program scope, typical timelines
13      and Project status, and the associated wildfire and reliability risk reduction. By
14      documenting how these activities are tracked, reported, and incorporated into
15      risk modeling, and by explaining how non-EUP work will be coordinated with
16      EUP Projects, this chapter establishes transparency on both the EUP Project
17      pipeline and the broader portfolio of system hardening work that collectively
18      reduces Wildfire and Outage Program Risk.

 6   A. Introduction
 7          In this chapter, we address the following issues required by Section 2.5 of
 8      the Electrical Undergrounding Plan (EUP) Guidelines: (1) EUP Project timeline
 9      and targets; (2) our workforce development plan; (3) the costs and benefits of
10      undergrounding; and (4) the availability of non-ratepayer funding sources for
11      EUP Projects.
12          In Section B, we list the requirements in Senate Bill (SB) 884 and the EUP
13      Guidelines that are addressed in this Chapter.
14          In Section C, we provide a Target/Timeline table outlining the work we plan
15      to complete, unit costs, and changes in Wildfire and Reliability Risk for each
16      year of the EUP. We describe the Project Management Template we will use to
17      track and communicate each Project’s schedule and the controls in place to
18      adhere to the schedule.
19          We then describe our workforce development plan including resource
20      needs, recruiting and hiring strategy, training, third-party contracting, our plans
21      for addressing resource constraints, and how we will manage potential impacts
22      among the EUP and traditional safety and reliability work.
23          We next present an evaluation of project costs and benefits, the Benefit
24      Cost Ratio (BCR) calculation, inputs into the Wildfire Benefit Cost Analysis
25      (WBCA) model, and cost containment strategies.
26          In Section D, we describe our plan for identifying, applying for, and tracking
27      non-ratepayer funds to reduce ratepayer costs for the EUP.
28          Section E provides a brief conclusion and Section F includes a list of
29      attachments supporting this chapter.

      targets and mileage completion targets for each year covered by the plan.” To

                                                                                                               -184-
 1   c. Controls to Maintain Adherence to Schedules (EUP Guidelines
 2      Section 2.5.1(c))
 3          PG&E currently employs a structured change control process and
 4      Portfolio Management Framework to manage schedule risk within our
 5      Undergrounding Program. We establish annual undergrounding
 6      mileage and risk reduction targets and actively manage schedule risk to
 7      achieve these program objectives. We will continue the processes and
 8      controls described below for our EUP.
 9          To support schedule reliability, we develop an Annual
10      Undergrounding Portfolio that consists of both committed miles and
11      reserve miles. Committed miles comprise scoped Projects and
12      Subprojects that collectively represent the planned undergrounding
13      mileage in a given year (the Annual Project Portfolio). Reserve miles
14      consist of additional scoped Subprojects that may be incorporated into
15      the Annual Project Portfolio if a committed Subproject is determined,
16      through the change control process, to be at risk of missing its
17      scheduled energization date. Underground miles are considered
18      “complete” only upon completion of the following work: (1) energization
19      of new assets, (2) de-energization of existing assets where applicable,
20      and (3) successful quality assurance passage. This Portfolio structure
21      allows PG&E to maintain progress toward annual program targets
22      despite individual project-level schedule variability.
23          After Project selection and scoping, PG&E establishes a baseline
24      milestone schedule for each Project and Subproject. The baseline
25      milestone schedule includes planned dates for four key activities needed
26      to achieve Subproject completion (i.e., energization of newly installed
27      assets): (1) estimating, (2) dependencies (e.g., permitting), (3) civil
28      construction, and (4) electric construction. Project performance is
29      managed against these milestones throughout execution.
30          Any potential impacts to the scheduled electrification date are
31      tracked through PG&E’s change control process to ensure continued
32      alignment with program-level targets. If a PG&E project manager
33      identifies a risk to a scheduled milestone date, the project manager
34      evaluates the downstream impacts to the project and implements a


                                     -185-
 1               recovery plan to mitigate the potential delays. Common strategies for
 2               reducing potential schedule delays may include reallocating or adding
 3               resources, extending work hours, identifying alternative resources to
 4               relieve constraints, resequencing activities, or performing work in
 5               parallel to compress schedules.
 6                   In addition, PG&E may also address schedule risks by modifying
 7               project designs or subdividing Projects into smaller components to
 8               improve constructability and schedule performance. Through these
 9               controls, PG&E actively manages schedule risk at both the Subproject,
10               Project, and Portfolio levels to maintain adherence to approved
11               schedules, achieving annual program objectives.

12        2. Workforce Development Plan (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.2)

         Section 8388.5(c)(5) requires the EUP to include a “plan for utility and
     contractor workforce development.” To fulfill this component, the EUP must
     contain a description of how the Large Electrical Corporation will successfully
     secure the resources required to implement the EUP for the full 10 years. Some
     examples include:
     a. A list of the job classifications;
     b. Annual EUP workforce targets;
     c.   A description for workforce training, recruitment, and retention;
     d. A description of constraints and strategy for addressing those constraints; and
     e. A description of the potential impacts that EUP implementation could have on
        traditional safety and reliability related projects and programs that rely on the
        same field personnel.


13                   PG&E developed a plan for utility and contractor workforce
14               development to successfully secure resources to implement our EUP.
15               By executing on this plan, PG&E will have sufficient internal and
16               external resources to support the EUP while continuing to meet
17               traditional safety, reliability, and Fire Rebuild obligations, and will
18               continue to manage resource allocation to ensure that critical work
19               across all programs is appropriately prioritized and executed.
20                   PG&E considered the following key elements in developing our EUP
21               workforce plan: (1) the fundamental components of the Undergrounding
22               Program, (2) the resources needed to execute each program


                                               -186-
 1               component, and (3) the distribution of resources between internal PG&E
 2               team members and external contractors.
 3                   The workforce plan reflects the project life-cycle stages, from project
 4               identification through scoping, construction, and post-construction
 5               activities. PG&E’s internal and external resource needs to implement
 6               these stages are driven by the number of Undergrounding Projects in
 7               development, the number of undergrounding miles planned for
 8               construction for any given year, and the forecast for future years.
 9               PG&E’s resource plan for utility and contractor development is designed
10               to be flexible given the varying number of projects and miles, the
11               location of the miles, the differing project conditions, various work
12               methods, and different efficiency factors.
13                   PG&E worked with Jacobs Solutions Inc., an industry-leading
14               construction and engineering firm with expertise in delivering large-scale
15               projects, to develop an Excel-based resourcing model for our EUP
16               (Workpaper 007 Undergrounding Resource Model).124 The EUP
17               Resource Model calculates monthly and annual resource requirements,
18               based on undergrounding mileage targets and productivity estimates of
19               the resources critical to implementing the program. The EUP Resource
20               Model provides the estimated resource requirements for more than 30
21               job classifications, including, for example, project management,
22               estimating, and civil and electric construction.
23                   PG&E’s EUP Resource Model uses both historic and forecasted
24               project and workforce data inputs to calculate the projected annual
25               resource needs for the work proposed in the 2028-2037 EUP.
26               Specifically, the EUP Resource Model inputs include:
27               •   Historic Project Information: Mileage and project timeline data from
28                   undergrounding work constructed 2022-2025.




     124 Attach. B, WP007 (Undergrounding Resource Model).

 1                •   Project Schedule Progression (Workstream Progression):125
 2                    Schedule estimates126 for construction and non-construction
 3                    activities (scoping, estimating, and permitting) based on projected
 4                    undergrounding miles per month and per year (2028-2037) that will
 5                    progress through the project stages (scoping, design, permitting,
 6                    and construction).
 7                •   Estimated Project Resource Hours: Resource estimates are based
 8                    on average project size, working days per year, and assumed
 9                    productivity rates. Productivity rate assumptions reflect civil and

11                    categories and disciplines, quantifying their expected productivity
12                    rate using the Key Performance Indicator (KPI) of Full-Time
13                    Equivalent (FTE)/mile.127 For example, electric construction

15                    of underground cable pulled per day.

17                model intended to estimate program-level workforce needs based on
18                PG&E’s mileage forecast, average project characteristics, and assumed
19                productivity factors. The model relies on historic project data and
20                generalized assumptions and does not reflect final project scope,
21                sequencing, or staffing requirements for individual EUP Projects and
22                Subprojects. The number of internal or external FTE resources
23                generated by the EUP Resource Model is based on information
24                available as of May 2026. Actual workforce needs may vary over time
25                due to changes in authorized program scope, project locations and
26                complexity, permitting timelines, labor availability, contractor market

1               b. Workforce Training, Recruiting and Retention (EUP Guidelines
2                    Section 2.5.2(c))
3                        A key requirement for meeting EUP resource needs is to recruit and
4                    hire resources with the right qualifications and further develop their
5                    qualifications through training and on-the-job performance assessments.
6                    In addition, PG&E contracts with third parties who have the necessary


                                                  -190-
 1   qualifications and skills for undergrounding work. We will continue to
 2   build on the recruiting and hiring, training, and third-party contracting
 3   efforts described below to deliver on our EUP commitments.
 4       As shown in Table 5-4, PG&E has identified workforce positions for
 5   team members working on the delivery and execution of the work
 6   proposed in the EUP. For each of the identified positions, PG&E
 7   defines the minimum required qualifications and special certifications to
 8   establish a well-qualified workforce. The required qualifications for the
 9   different workforce positions vary but include items such as minimum
10   education requirements; relevant experience in areas such as project
11   management, project controls, electrical, mechanical or civil
12   engineering, estimating, design, distribution planning, land surveying,
13   and traffic control; and special certifications or qualifications such as
14   Project Management Professional, Professional Engineer, licensed
15   California Land Surveyor, Journeyman Lineman, and American Traffic
16   Safety Services Association certification.
17       PG&E will use the EUP’s 10-year workforce plan to balance existing
18   internal staff, hiring additional resources and external resources
19   (e.g., staff augmentation, contractors, consultants, etc.) and continue to
20   develop the workforce. PG&E’s recruiting team utilizes the FTE and
21   resource estimates from the EUP Resource Model and identifies internal
22   and external resourcing strategies. The team also partners with PG&E’s
23   Labor Relations experts to ensure that workforce planning adheres to
24   applicable labor agreement guidelines.
25       PG&E’s internal resourcing strategy focuses on finding qualified
26   resources to fill open positions, when and where they are needed.
27   PG&E’s internal recruiting team works with Undergrounding Program
28   management team to develop a plan for identifying and hiring the right
29   resources. PG&E’s recruiting team may work with community colleges,
30   universities, trade schools, career sites, trade associations, and job
31   boards to locate interested and qualified resources.
32       In addition to traditional recruiting methods, PG&E established the
33   PowerPathway program to offer training to individuals interested in
34   entry-level careers at PG&E and the construction-energy industry.


                                  -191-
 1   PowerPathway is a nationally recognized workforce development model
 2   that works with community organizations, schools, and local
 3   governments to develop a sustainable pipeline of candidates for PG&E
 4   and the industry. More than 1,300 students have graduated from this
 5   program from 2008 through 2025. Many PowerPathway students come
 6   from communities impacted by wildfires and where Undergrounding
 7   Projects are occurring. In addition, the program focuses on recruiting
 8   military veterans and individuals who are currently unemployed.
 9       The PowerPathway training program is a free multi-week training
10   that includes both classroom and hands-on learning. Since 2017,
11   approximately 86 percent of the program graduates have been hired by
12   PG&E or within the utility industry, providing an opportunity for often
13   disadvantaged community members to build a career.
14       As an example of PowerPathway’s relevance to the proposed EUP,
15   in June 2023, PowerPathway held an all-military veteran
16   undergrounding training program. To ensure our workforce is
17   representative of the communities we serve, all of the participants lived
18   within 50 miles of a work headquarters in the Sacramento North Valley
19   area. Upon graduating, all 20 military veterans were placed in careers
20   at PG&E supporting Undergrounding Projects; of this number eight were
21   construction utility workers and 12 were traffic control professionals.
22       PG&E intends to leverage the PowerPathway program to fill civil
23   and electrical construction crew needs to support the proposed EUP.
24   We expect the program to expand our civil and electrical crews who live
25   and work in our hometowns and help create a pipeline for leadership
26   and journey-level positions that are difficult to fill. After graduating
27   PowerPathways, these individuals can be promoted based on their
28   career interests, location, and the needs of the program, via progression
29   tracks that are already in place for the Undergrounding Program.

28          PG&E developed a multi-year third-party contractor sourcing
29      strategy to support our Undergrounding Program resource needs
30      and meet the EUP mileage, safety, and cost targets.

32      Services Agreements (MSA) in place with nine undergrounding

34      in-place to fulfill proposed mileage targets through at least 2029 and

 3                   approaches include:
 4                   •   Adjusting the size of the contractor pool over the life of the
 5                       program to manage internal and external workforce resources,
 6                       while maintaining the flexibility to scale as needed;
 7                   •   Preparing a pipeline of construction-ready work (e.g., designed
 8                       and permitted projects) to facilitate bundling work for

17                   •   Sourcing multi-year MSAs with flexible delivery models
18                       (e.g., direct negotiation, lump sum, unit pricing and quick bid).
