27   c. Description of and Strategy for Addressing Resource
28      Constraints (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.2(d))
29          Given the complexities of an Undergrounding Program and the
30      typical shifts in individual project schedules, there are times when more
31      resources are needed to complete scheduled work than were previously
32      identified. In the event additional resources are needed, solutions can
33      include extending working days/hours of construction crews, reassigning
34      work amongst construction vendors and/or PG&E crews, adding

                                    -195-
 1      additional construction vendors for short-term needs via Standalone
 2      Agreements, and adjusting project schedules.

 3   d. Managing Potential Impacts Among the EUP and Traditional
 4      Safety and Reliability Projects (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.2(e))
 5          Traditional safety and reliability projects and programs include work
 6      such as vegetation management, system inspections, pole replacement
 7      and other electric maintenance activities, that rely primarily on electric
 8      and vegetation management crews and less on civil construction crews.
 9      PG&E’s EUP work will be executed by civil construction crews who
10      typically perform 80 percent of the work and electric crews who perform
11      approximately 20 percent of the work. This is because the longest
12      duration undergrounding construction work is related to the civil
13      substructure work, i.e., digging the trenches and installing conduit into
14      which the electric lines will be pulled. Given the reliance on different
15      crews, it is unlikely that the most frequently used field personnel
16      supporting the EUP will represent a resource constraint for routine
17      safety and reliability work.
18          At times, PG&E may need to respond to wildfire events that require
19      activities in Fire Rebuild Areas. Fire Rebuild work is prioritized to
20      support customer restoration and public safety and may require the
21      temporary reallocation of certain civil construction and electric
22      resources, including resources that also support the EUP. When such
23      conditions arise, PG&E may shift resources to prioritize Fire Rebuild
24      activities. PG&E manages these potential overlaps through a structured
25      change control process and Portfolio management framework. As
26      described in Section C.1 above, PG&E actively manages the EUP
27      Project Portfolio, including the use of committed and reserve projects,
28      and change control processes to mitigate schedule risks and maintain
29      progress toward annual program targets. To the extent resource
30      constraints arise due to Fire Rebuild or other priorities, PG&E will adjust
31      project sequencing, deploy reserve projects, and/or supplement
32      resources through additional hiring or contracting, as appropriate.
33          Based on current staffing levels and contracting arrangements,
34      PG&E has sufficient internal and external resources to support the EUP

                                       -196-
 1               while continuing to meet traditional safety, reliability, and Fire Rebuild
 2               obligations, and will continue to manage resource allocation to ensure
 3               that critical work across all programs is appropriately prioritized and
 4               executed.

 5        3. Costs and Benefits (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.3)

           Section 8388.5(c)(6) requires the EUP to include “an evaluation of project
     costs, projected economic benefits over the life of the assets, and any cost
     containment assumptions, including the economies of scale necessary to reduce
     wildfire risk and mitigation costs and establish a sustainable supply chain.” To
     fulfill this component, the EUP must contain a narrative for each of the following:
     a.    Evaluation of project costs;
     b. Projected economic benefits over the life of the assets;
     c.   Cost containment assumptions (including economies of scale necessary to
          reduce wildfire risk and mitigation costs); and
     d. Strategies for achieving a sustainable supply chain and the economies of
        scale necessary to reduce costs over time.


 6           a. Evaluation of Project Costs (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.3(a))

 7               1) Mitigation Alternative BCR Analysis
 8                        PG&E uses our WBCA model to evaluate project costs and
 9                   benefits for the Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons
10                   that we analyze in Screen 2 and Screen 3. The WBCA model
11                   methodology, key inputs and outputs are detailed in Chapter 7,
12                   Section D.6. We use the WBCA model to conduct the BCR analysis
13                   to assess Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons in
14                   Screen 2 that are listed below and further described in Chapter 3,
15                   Section D.2. See Chapter 3, Section D.2 and Table 3-9 for a
16                   description of the comparison types described below.
17                   1) 100 percent Underground
18                   2) Alternative Mitigation 1
19                   3) Alternative Mitigation 2
20                   4) Additional Comparison
21                        The BCR values for Alternative Mitigations and Additional
22                   Comparisons are further refined in Screen 3. In Screen 3, PG&E
23                   generates BCRs for the “Project as Scoped” and the

                                              -197-
 1                   “Undergrounding as Scoped” mitigation scenarios. The Project as
 2                   Scoped is all work in the final project design including all
 3                   undergrounding and non-undergrounding portions of the project.
 4                   The Undergrounding as Scoped includes only the portion of the
 5                   Circuit Segment that will be undergrounded.
 6                       The cost and benefit inputs into the WBCA are described below.
 7                   For each Circuit Segment, the WBCA provides the forecasted cost
 8                   to build and maintain each of the Alternative Mitigations and
 9                   Additional Comparisons and an estimated BCR.
10                       The BCR is PG&E’s first but not only consideration when
11                   selecting a system hardening mitigation. The California Public
12                   Utilities Commission (CPUC or Commission) has stated that “the
13                   utility is not bound to select its Mitigation strategy based solely on
14                   the Cost-Benefit Ratios produced by the Cost-Benefit Approach.”130
15                   Consistent with this direction, PG&E uses the BCR and other factors
16                   to select Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons. PG&E
17                   considers multiple factors in selecting alternatives because an
18                   over-emphasis on the BCR may devalue projects that are both high
19                   cost and high benefit. The BCR does not reflect the magnitude of
20                   benefits and value of permanent risk mitigation and, when used as
21                   the sole criteria, may result in situations where significant risk is
22                   permanently left on the system. As a hypothetical example,
23                   Project A could have total risk reduction benefits of $10 million with
24                   a lifetime cost of $5 million, while Project B could have a total risk
25                   reduction benefit of $1 million with a lifetime cost of $0.5 million.
26                   Both Projects would have a BCR of 2, but Project A has the highest
27                   magnitude of benefits. PG&E’s Screen 3 analysis considers the full
28                   range of benefits, including mitigation of tree strike risks, reliability
29                   risks created by operational mitigations, and ingress/egress
30                   concerns.131 A utility must be able to consider multiple factors


     130   Decision (D.) 22-12-027, Appendix A, p. A-16, Row 26.
     131 Per ACI PGE-26B-07, the process for consideration of these risks may change when
         PG&E adopts WDRM v5 or makes other changes to our risk modeling approach in
         future.

                                               -198-
 1                   when selecting a mitigation and not be limited in its decision-making
 2                   to just a single factor.

 3               2) Calculating BCRs
 4                        The BCR is the ratio of benefits to costs. It is the present value
 5                   of the lifetime benefits of a project divided by the present value of
 6                   the lifetime costs. The BCR measures how much benefit is gained
 7                   per dollar spent. A BCR greater than 1.0, or a negative BCR,
 8                   indicates that the benefits of a project outweigh the costs. The BCR
 9                   is calculated by dividing Lifetime Benefit by the Lifetime Costs for
10                   each Alternative Mitigation and Additional Comparisons.132

15               3) Project Cost Inputs into the WBCA
16                        PG&E uses the WBCA model to estimate the present value of
17                   capital costs over the life of the asset for each Alternative Mitigation
18                   and Additional Comparison 1. Total project costs consist of: (1) the
19                   capital costs to construct the project (Initial Capital Spend); (2) the
20                   capital and expense amounts to operate and maintain the asset
21                   relative to the existing baseline assets (net operations and
22                   maintenance (O&M) costs); (3) vegetation management costs
23                   (Lifetime Vegetation Management Expense); (4) project financing
24                   costs; and (5) a climate adjustment factor. The basis and values for
25                   each of these project costs are used as an input into the WBCA
26                   model. PG&E proposes to review the validity of these input values
27                   at the time of the WBCA model update (see Chapter 8 Section C).

 2                      Initial capital spend consists of the installation costs to
 3                  implement a system hardening project. Cost types include: scoping
 4                  and surveying; project design and estimating; pre-construction
 5                  preparations such as ordering materials, acquiring permits and land

13              5) Lifetime Capital and Expense O&M Spend
14                      O&M costs are needed to operate and maintain an asset over
15                  its lifetime. The categories of O&M costs that are included in
16                  PG&E’s project cost analysis are as follows:
17                  •   Patrols and Inspections: PG&E regularly inspects our overhead
18                      and underground electric facilities to proactively identify areas of
19                      deterioration and degradation, including any pending failures of
20                      asset components and issues caused by outside forces or
21                      third-party contact that may create unsafe conditions, outages,
22                      or lead to an ignition.
23                  •   Maintenance and Repair: Maintenance programs consist of
24                      expense and capital repair/replacement work to address
25                      overhead maintenance conditions identified by PG&E’s patrol
26                      and inspection process. PG&E uses a risk-informed
27                      prioritization approach to address the highest risk issues on our
28                      system. Maintenance tags are assigned a priority based on the
29                      potential safety impact, in accordance with CPUC General
30                      Order (GO) requirements (e.g., GO 95 and GO 128). PG&E’s
31                      maintenance of our Electric Distribution facilities improves public
32                      safety, employee safety, and reliability. Almost all the


     134 Attach. B, WP006 (WBCA Whitepaper).


                                             -200-
 1       maintenance activities involve facilities which, if they failed,
 2       could potentially disrupt or degrade service, cause an ignition or
 3       pose a risk to the public or PG&E workers. Maintenance of
 4       Electric Distribution facilities is also required for regulatory
 5       compliance.
 6   •   EPSS: Distribution Control Center operators (Operators)
 7       receive daily instructions to enable and/or disable EPSS based
 8       on Wildfire Risk for the day. When outages occur on PG&E
 9       distribution circuits, the entire Circuit Segment that experienced
10       the outage must be patrolled before power can be restored to
11       customers. A patrol involves a visual examination of applicable
12       overhead facilities to identify obvious structural problems and
13       hazards that may have caused the outage and a possible
14       ignition if not cleared prior to reenergization. Post-outage
15       patrols on EPSS-enabled circuits ensures the system is safe to
16       facilitate restoration of the outage as quickly as possible. In
17       addition to enabling EPSS settings, the Operators are
18       responsible for monitoring outages when EPSS settings are
19       activated and coordinating with field personnel and engineering
20       on the safe patrol and restoration of circuits.
21   •   Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS): PSPS event costs consist
22       of the cost for activities directly associated with PG&E’s
23       proactive de-energization of overhead electric distribution lines
24       following a determination of weather-related imminent threats to
25       power line assets and increased risk of catastrophic wildfire.
26       This includes the sequence of activities associated with
27       activating the Emergency Operations Center (EOC), sending
28       customer and agency notifications, de-energizing power lines to
29       reduce the risk of those lines igniting a wildfire during a
30       weather-related event, patrolling the deenergized overhead
31       lines to ensure there are no hazards on the line that could have




                              -201-
 1                         caused an outage or ignition, and re-energizing the lines once it
 2                         is safe to do so.135
 3                     •   Routine and Major Emergency: Electric emergencies are
 4                         created when outages occur and require immediate response
 5                         by PG&E to restore customer service and protect the
 6                         community from potential safety hazards. Emergency outages
 7                         can range from Routine Emergencies resulting from equipment
 8                         failures and day-to-day weather conditions to Major and
 9                         Catastrophic Emergencies arising from major storms or natural
10                         disasters. PG&E’s response to electric emergencies is a
11                         fundamental part of operating an electric distribution system and
12                         is subject to the requirements of GO 166. PG&E prepares an
13                         electric emergency response plan that defines staffing levels,
14                         roles and responsibilities, emergency incident assessment
15                         guidelines, and communication plans. The response plan
16                         supports PG&E’s activation of emergency centers and
17                         mobilization of crews and other resources to respond to routine
18                         and major emergencies. Since underground lines are largely
19                         protected from weather-related hazards we forecast significantly
20                         reduced emergency response activities needed on underground
21                         system throughout the life of the asset.
22                         O&M costs are expressed as a unit cost specific to the activity
23                     type and vary depending on the mitigation. For example, PG&E will
24                     not incur EPSS-related O&M costs where lines are underground but
25                     will continue to incur them where covered conductor is installed.
26                     PG&E also does not incur PSPS-related operational costs in areas
27                     where lines are undergrounded.
28                         To develop the O&M costs for each mitigation, PG&E evaluated
29                     Maintenance Activity Type (MAT) cost forecasts in our 2023 General

20                        The WBCA also incorporates certain financing elements to

22                    costs and benefits by mitigation.
23                    •   Asset Life: The asset life period determines how many years of
24                        O&M costs and expected benefits are included in the BCR
25                        calculations. The WBCA model uses the Overhead and
26                        Underground Asset Life in PG&E’s 2023 GRC decision139 with
27                        a benefit life of 55 years for underground assets and 48 years
28                        for overhead assets.
29                    •   Present Value Rate of Return (PVRR): PVRR represents the
30                        present value of revenue that must be collected from customers
31                        to pay for the costs incurred on a Project, including a fair and

 3                    •    Discount Rates: In compliance with the Risk-Based
 4                         Decision-Making Framework Phase (RDF) II Decision, PG&E
 5                         shows the numerator and denominator of the BCR as present
 6                         values.140 In the RDF Phase III Decision, the Commission
 7                         directed utilities to use three different discount rates in their

 2                        The CBA Reliability Conversion in the WBCA is a Cost per
 3                    Customer Minutes Interrupted (CMI) output from the Lawrence

 9                9) Climate Assumptions
10                        PG&E includes two climate-related impacts in its WBCA.
11                    •   Fire Weather Index (FWI): The FWI variable measures the
12                        projected annual number of days per circuit segment that
13                        exceed the historical 95th percentile FWI value at that segment.
14                        The 95th percentile threshold is defined using a 20-year
15                        historical baseline centered on 2004 (1995-2014), a reference
16                        period commonly used in climate analyses. Future exceedance
17                        counts are derived from climate projections146 averaged over
18                        20-year windows centered on 2030, 2050, and 2080. The FWI
19                        is a generalized measure of fire potential that incorporates both
20                        fuel aridity and fire weather conditions, regardless of fuel type or
21                        abundance. It is calculated using daily maximum temperature,
22                        minimum relative humidity, average wind speed, and
23                        precipitation. Changes in the frequency of high-FWI days
24                        impact the probability that an ignition occurs during Red Flag
25                        Warning (RFW) conditions. Since ignitions associated with
26                        RFW conditions have higher per-event consequences than
27                        non-RFW ignitions, a risk multiplier for RFW outcomes is
28                        calculated at the Circuit Segment level. This multiplier scales
29                        proportionally with increases in annual days exceeding the
30                        historical 95th percentile FWI.



     145 A.24-05-008, Exhibit (PG&E-2), p. 2-12, Section C.5.b.
     146 Projections use the ensemble average of Wildfire Risk simulations driven by
         eight downscaled Global Climate Models under SSP3-7.0 scenario.

                                                -206-
 1                  •   Heat Day Analysis: Based on historical experience, equipment
 2                      failure rates increase roughly proportionally with the frequency
 3                      of continued heat events. These events are defined as periods
 4                      of three consecutive days exceeding 92°F where both daily
 5                      highs and lows surpass their respective 10-year averages. A
 6                      heat-based equipment-failure frequency multiplier is calculated
 7                      at the Circuit Segment level to capture climate-driven changes
 8                      in sustained heat exposure.
 9                      Climate assumptions also impact EPSS and PSPS programs.
10                  The frequency of events in these outage programs is likely to
11                  increase as environmental conditions are conducive to wildfire
12                  increase.

13          b. Projected Economic Benefits over the Life of the Assets (EUP
14              Guidelines Section 2.5.3(b))

15              1) Benefits Included in the BCR Calculation
16                      The benefits included in BCR calculation are described below
17                  and are explained in greater detail in Chapter 7, Section D.6 and in
18                  the WBCA Whitepaper.147
19                  •   Wildfire Benefit: The wildfire benefit quantifies the Wildfire Risk
20                      reduced by calculating the existing Wildfire Risk on the system
21                      (assuming existing infrastructure and PSPS is present)
22                      associated with each Circuit Segment before a particular
23                      mitigation is implemented. The wildfire benefit takes into
24                      account changes over time due to climate change from
25                      2028-2082. (See Chapter 7, Sections G.4.c and G.6.e for
26                      details regarding the climate change factors.)
27                  •   Public Safety Benefit: The public safety benefit quantifies the
28                      non-wildfire safety impacts that a Circuit Segment poses to the
29                      public. The main component of the public safety benefit is
30                      referred to as the public contact with intact energized electric
31                      equipment (PCEEE) which is the risk of serious injury or fatality
32                      to members of the public or contractors resulting from

     147 Attach. B, WP006 (WBCA Whitepaper).


                                            -207-
 1       interaction with intact, energized electric assets, where the
 2       event does not originate from asset failure. We refer to the
 3       public safety benefit as “Safety Risk Reduction.”
 4   •   Reliability Benefits: Reliability benefits quantify the reduction in
 5       customer service interruptions associated with implementing a
 6       mitigation. CMI measures the total amount of time a PG&E
 7       customer’s electricity access is interrupted. CMI is a cumulative
 8       sum of the interruption time for all affected customers and is
 9       calculated at the Circuit Segment level. Generally, to calculate
10       the reliability benefits, the total CMI is multiplied by the Value of
11       Service (VoS) per minute from the ICE calculator. In the
12       WBCA, reliability benefits are composed of three distinct
13       components:
14       −   Baseline Reliability Benefit: The baseline reliability benefit
15           reflects the reduction in CMI under normal operating
16           conditions, excluding interruptions associated with EPSS
17           and PSPS programs. This component captures
18           improvements in system performance resulting from
19           reduced outage frequency and duration due to the
20           mitigation.
21       −   EPSS Benefit: The EPSS benefit quantifies the reduction in
22           outages attributable to EPSS exposure for each Circuit
23           Segment when a particular mitigation is implemented.
24           EPSS risk is a function of CMI and reflects only those
25           customer minutes interrupted attributable to EPSS.
26           Calculation of this benefit is described in Chapter 7,
27           Section D 3.
28       −   PSPS Benefit: The PSPS benefit quantifies the reduction in
29           PSPS exposure for each Circuit Segment when a particular
30           mitigation is implemented. PSPS risk is a function of CMI
31           and reflects only customer minutes interrupted attributable
32           to PSPS. Calculation of this benefit is described in
33           Chapter 7, Section D 4.

 1               2) Mitigation Effectiveness
 2                        Project Variable Modifiers (PVM) are used in the WBCA to
 3                    determine the effectiveness and therefore the resulting benefits
 4                    (i.e., risk reduced) for each mitigation. (See Chapter 7, Section K,
 5                    PVMs, for the details of how these values are calculated.)

 6           c. Cost Containment Strategies Including Economies of Scale
 7               Necessary to Reduce Wildfire Risk and Mitigation Costs (EUP
 8               Guidelines Section 2.5.3(c))
 9                    Managing undergrounding costs is an integral part of PG&E’s
10               Undergrounding Program. Our cost containment strategy includes
11               two key components: (1) sourcing strategies; and (2) work execution
12               strategies. By implementing many of the sourcing and work execution
13               strategies detailed below, PG&E has already reduced the unit cost of
14               undergrounding by more than $1 million per mile. As certainty of
15               long-term undergrounding plans increases through approval of our EUP,
16               PG&E expects to be able to generate greater economies of scale with
17               internal crews, contractors, materials suppliers, designers and others.
18               We anticipate continuing to drive cost savings over the 10-year period,
19               saving approximately $220,000 per mile by 2037. When scaled across
20               the thousands of miles being proposed in the EUP, these efficiencies
21               are estimated to reduce unit costs by $746 million over the 10-year
22               period, before escalation. (See Target/Timeline Table for the declining
23               annual unit cost targets over the EUP period.)148
24                    Specific cost containment strategies are described in more detail
25               below.

26               1) Sourcing Strategies to Reduce Program Costs
27                        PG&E is testing and validating how different sourcing
28                    approaches can reduce undergrounding costs. As noted above,
29                    approval of the EUP will increase certainty in the volume of
30                    undergrounding work over the 10-year EUP:



     148 The Target / Timeline Table is provided in Progress Report 0 as Table A-2 (in
         Attach. A), and as required in EUP Guidelines Section 2.3.1.k, PG&E has included an
         excel workbook in Attach. B, WP002 (EUP Target / Timeline Table).

                                              -209-
 1   •   Competitively Bid Lump Sum Fixed Price: Competitively-bid
 2       lump sum fixed price sourcing strategies provide cost savings
 3       opportunities for a variety of reasons. For instance, in
 4       comparison to unit price sourcing strategies, lump sum fixed
 5       price sourcing strategies shift the potential risk of cost increases
 6       occurring during construction onto the contractor as opposed to
 7       the ratepayer. Additionally, by soliciting multiple offers
 8       (i.e. competitively bidding), PG&E can compare costs and
 9       ensure they receive the best value. In 2025, the program
10       achieved approximately 15 percent cost savings by leveraging
11       this pricing and delivery model. Competition encourages
12       contractors to offer their most competitive pricing and creates an
13       environment where a contractor with unique experience, skills or
14       tools to offer the lowest price and win the work. It is worth
15       noting that lump sum fixed price contracts require the timely
16       development of construction ready work to give bidders more
17       certainty in the scope of work prior to taking on the risk of cost
18       increase that may materialize during construction. The certainty
19       provided by an approved 10-year EUP enhances PG&E’s ability
20       to prepare construction-ready work and encourages contractors
21       to invest in tools, training and experience development to
22       continually execute work more efficiently.
23   •   Directly Negotiated Fixed Price: Negotiated lump sum fixed
24       price sourcing strategies offer similar cost savings advantages
25       as competitively bid lump sum fixed price contracts in that the
26       fixed price component of the contract shifts potential cost
27       increases during construction onto contractors. However,
28       directly negotiated lump sum fixed price contracts do not offer
29       the potential for additional savings from competition. For this
30       reason, directly negotiated lump sum fixed price contracts are
31       used opportunistically with contractors identified through the
32       competitive lump sum process to further reduce the price with
33       crews already mobilized in/near the location.




                             -210-
 1      •   Design Build – Engineering, Procurement, Construction (EPC):
 2          This sourcing strategy involves selecting one supplier to design,
 3          procure materials, and construct a Project. This approach may
 4          allow a contractor to harvest efficiencies from the integration of
 5          design and construction resource groups to lower the overall
 6          Project cost. Typically, this methodology also places the risk of
 7          scope changes and many other unexpected conditions on the
 8          supplier to the benefit of PG&E and our customers. PG&E is
 9          currently piloting this strategy on several Projects.
10      •   Production Paving: PG&E implemented a new paving
11          contracting approach in 2025 to leverage economies of scale
12          with other PG&E paving and restoration work. Since
13          implementing this approach, PG&E has achieved a 30 percent
14          savings in paving costs for Undergrounding Projects.
15      •   Traffic Control: Traffic control is normally subcontracted by the
16          electric and civil construction vendors using rates agreed upon
17          by the construction vendor and the traffic control provider and
18          often includes a markup for these services which PG&E pays as
19          a pass-through cost. PG&E’s undergrounding team has piloted
20          an approach in partnership with other PG&E teams to
21          coordinate scheduling, dispatching, and invoicing for Traffic
22          Control services and to leverage new rates negotiated by
23          PG&E’s Sourcing team directly with the traffic control providers.
24          This effort has resulted in a 20 percent reduction in cost for
25          traffic control.
26          As these, and more, sourcing strategies are tested, PG&E will
27      standardize those that generate cost savings while continuing to
28      look for additional opportunities to reduce costs through sourcing.

33      innovative construction methods, and implementing technological

 1   d. Strategies for Achieving Sustainable Supply Chain and the
 2      Economies of Scale Necessary to Reduce Costs Over Time
 3      (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.3(d))
 4          Regulatory certainty associated with PG&E’s EUP is critical to
 5      establishing and maintaining a sustainable supply chain and achieving
 6      the economies of scale necessary to reduce costs over time. PG&E has
 7      established a supply chain to deliver on our current pace of
 8      undergrounding which is adequate to support the program through at
 9      least 2029. However, a longer-term, clearly defined program would
10      provide supply chain participants with the confidence needed to invest in
11      capacity, workforce, and manufacturing capabilities aligned with growing
12      program needs. Long-term regulatory approval would enable PG&E to
13      transition from short‑term procurement to more strategic, multi‑year
14      sourcing arrangements to further capture economies of scale.
15          With regulatory certainty around program scope and funding, PG&E
16      will be able to pursue long‑term agreements with key suppliers and
17      manufacturers for materials such as cable, conduit, vaults, enclosures,
18      and related equipment required for large‑scale undergrounding. These
19      longer‑term agreements support unit cost reductions through volume
20      commitments, reduced procurement volatility, and improved production
21      planning. In several cases, suppliers have evaluated capital
22      investments—including facility expansions—based on the trajectory of
23      PG&E’s growing Undergrounding Program. As undergrounding mileage
24      scales over time, PG&E’s purchasing power increases, creating
25      meaningful economies of scale that are reflected in lower per‑unit
26      pricing and reduced transaction costs. Creating confidence around the
27      10-year outlook through an approved EUP will encourage suppliers to
28      make those investments and reduce costs.
29          As the Undergrounding Program has expanded, PG&E has
30      experienced material availability challenges, largely driven by broader
31      upstream supply chain disruptions following the COVID‑19 pandemic.
32      These constraints have been addressed through a combination of
33      production prioritization with incumbent suppliers, qualification and
34      onboarding of additional vendors, and the use of approved alternate

                                    -217-
 1   materials where appropriate. Establishing a 10‑year Undergrounding
 2   Plan will enable PG&E to more confidently forecast demand, coordinate
 3   with suppliers over a longer planning horizon, and reduce exposure to
 4   short‑term market disruptions.
 5       Long‑term regulatory approval also supports continued refinement
 6   of PG&E’s enterprise sourcing and delivery strategies, including
 7   standardization of new materials and technologies across programs,
 8   and integration of undergrounding material forecasts with other capital
 9   programs where appropriate. These approaches further enhance
10   economies of scale, reduce variability, and support consistent execution
11   as the program matures.
12       In parallel, PG&E remains committed to advancing supplier diversity
13   as part of a sustainable and resilient undergrounding supply chain.
14   Consistent with our Supplier Diversity Program, PG&E actively engages
15   woman‑owned (WBE), minority‑owned (MBE), service‑disabled
16   veteran‑owned (DVBE), and LGBT‑owned (LGBTBE) business
17   enterprises. Participation by diverse and small businesses supports
18   local economic development, expands the qualified supplier base, and
19   enhances overall program flexibility. PG&E will continue to identify
20   opportunities for diverse suppliers to participate in the EUP.
21       Taken together, regulatory certainty, long‑term planning, supplier
22   diversification, and scale‑driven sourcing strategies position PG&E to
23   manage costs responsibly while delivering undergrounding in a manner
24   that is sustainable and resilient.

 1   D. Non-Ratepayer Funding Sources (EUP Guidelines Section 2.5.4)

         Section 8388.5(j) requires the Large Electrical Corporation participating in the
     program to “apply for available federal, state, and other nonratepayer moneys
     throughout the duration of its approved undergrounding plan” and use acquired
     funds to reduce the program’s costs to ratepayers. To fulfill this component, the
     EUP must contain:
     a. List of existing nonratepayer funding opportunities;
     b. A plan for identifying additional sources of nonratepayer funding and plans for
        tracking and applying for nonratepayer funding opportunities that may become
        available; and
     c.    A plan for tracking nonratepayer funds received to ensure the funds are used
           to reduce ratepayer costs.


 2            PG&E is committed to maximizing opportunities that will reduce the costs of
 3        the EUP, including applying for external funding, such as federal and state
 4        funding, to offset program costs.
 5            In this section we: (1) list the non-ratepayer funding opportunities PG&E
 6        has already pursued or is currently pursuing as of the date of the EUP
 7        submission; (2) describe our plan for identifying and tracking additional sources
 8        of non-ratepayer funding opportunities; and (3) describe our process for applying
 9        for those funds to PG&E’s Undergrounding Program. PG&E anticipates
10        updating this information in our Progress Reports to provide Energy Safety with
11        information on relevant external funding opportunities applied for or received.
12        This section also includes a brief discussion of PG&E’s plan to comply with the
13        SB 884 CPUC Guidelines adopted in Resolution (Res.) SPD-37 and the tracking
14        requirements of CPUC Res. E-5254.

13   on-going state legislation. Because these opportunities are dependent on
14   external parties, the number of external funding opportunities and
15   associated amounts will vary.
16       When PG&E identifies a potential funding opportunity, we evaluate its
17   alignment with our business strategy, the benefits it would provide, the costs
18   necessary to pursue the funding, and whether PG&E has the ability and
19   resources available to prepare the application, and if awarded, to execute
20   the Project and comply with funding requirements. In considering whether
21   to pursue non-ratepayer funding opportunities for our Undergrounding
22   Program, PG&E evaluates the following specific criteria:
23   •   Strategic Alignment: Assess the alignment of the funding opportunity’s
24       goals with those of PG&E’s Undergrounding Program. Goal alignment
25       is imperative to delivering competitive Project proposals.
26   •   Positive Impact on Benefits: Evaluate if the fund’s desired outcomes
27       deliver positive benefits to PG&E’s Undergrounding Program and our
28       customers. Apply for only those opportunities where this is true.
29   •   Reduction in Costs: Determine if the net impact of the opportunity
30       (discounting additional fund application and compliance costs) will
31       reduce program costs.

 1          When PG&E identifies an opportunity using these criteria, we develop

 8   3. PG&E’s Plan for Tracking Non-Ratepayer Funds Received to Ensure
 9      the Funds are Used to Reduce Ratepayer Costs (EUP Guidelines
10      Section 2.5.4(c))
11          PG&E cannot reliably forecast the type or scale of external funding
12      opportunities that will be available during the EUP period, which of our
13      third-party funding applications will be successful, how much external
14      funding we may receive in any given year, or how much of that funding we
15      would be able to use for EUP work. Thus, for ratemaking purposes, PG&E
16      will need to evaluate the best method to reduce or refund customer costs
17      received from third-party funding and will propose an efficient method to do
18      this in our CPUC Phase 2 Cost Recovery Application. PG&E notes that



                                         -222-
 1          Generally Accepted Accounting Principles and the Federal Energy
 2          Regulatory Commission Uniform System of Accounts do not provide explicit
 3          rules or instructions for how companies should account for third-party
 4          funding such as government grants or loans. Like many other public
 5          companies, PG&E has referred to the International Financial Reporting
 6          Standards and their specific guidance under IAS 20, Accounting for
 7          Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance for
 8          accounting guidance related to governmental assistance. PG&E also notes
 9          that different processes may be necessary to true-up – and thus reduce
10          ratepayer costs – depending on any specific requirements of a particular
11          loan or grant.
12          Process for Tracking Non-Ratepayer Funding Via the DOE Loan
13              PG&E has received approval from the CPUC to confirm the process of
14          how savings will be returned to customers after we receive advances for
15          eligible Projects costs under the DOE LGA. Within 60 days of a loan
16          advance, PG&E will submit a Tier 2 Advice Letter calculating the resulting
17          interest cost savings once draw down occurs. The savings will be returned
18          to customers as a revenue credit though the Annual Electric True-Up and
19          Annual Gas True-Up Advice Letters submitted each December for the
20          following year.

21   E. Chapter Summary
22          Chapter 5 summarizes PG&E’s approach to meeting four core topics:
23      (1) Project timelines and annual targets for undergrounding work; (2) PG&E’s
24      workforce development plan to support delivery over the plan period;
25      (3) evaluation of undergrounding costs and benefits (including benefit-cost
26      analysis methods and cost containment strategies); and (4) identification and
27      pursuit of non-ratepayer funding sources to reduce customer costs.
28          The chapter outlines how PG&E will present and manage schedules through
29      a Target/Timeline table and a Project/Subproject management tracking
30      template, along with controls to maintain schedule adherence. It also describes
31      workforce planning assumptions, hiring and training approaches. Finally, it
32      describes how PG&E evaluates costs and benefits using modeling
33      (e.g., WBCA/BCR concepts) and sets out a process for finding, applying for, and



                                            -223-
1          tracking external funding opportunities so that awarded funds can be used to
2          offset ratepayer impacts.

23                         Portfolio submitted with future Progress Reports, resulting in two
24                         rows of data for the current risk model version and calibration.

27                         model or calibration, the previous risk models and calibrations

31                         modeling conditions; the KDMM value by applying the specified

 1                       risk model to the specified Portfolio; and the KDMM uncertainty
 2                       under these modeling conditions for that specific Portfolio.
 3                       Baselines will be updated annually,160 and updated Baseline
 4                       values will be shown in the first Progress Report of every

17                   b) Assumptions and Limitations
18                           There are currently limitations on PG&E’s ability to backtest
19                       new risk model versions and/or calibrations against old risk
20                       model versions that would yield accurate risk outputs. Circuit
21                       Segment geometry and Circuit Segment names are generated
22                       from the risk model using a snapshot of the distribution grid at a
23                       specific point in time. The snapshot of the Circuit Segment is a
24                       critical component in how risk is modeled from attribute data
25                       that is aligned in time with the grid configuration. Each new risk
26                       model version is developed using the latest and most useful
27                       attribute information available and the specific attributes used to
28                       produce the best risk estimations will not necessarily have
29                       equivalents when the prior risk model version was developed.
30                           Due to the limitations in our ability to use new model
31                       versions to make predictions on historic asset and

12          Mitigation 2, or Additional Comparison 1, the Portfolio ID, the
13          Circuit and Circuit Segment IDs, a description of the mitigation
14          work that will be performed, the safety, reliability, and financial
15          benefits, the total risk reduction, unit cost per overhead mile
16          deenergized, unit cost per mile of undergrounding, total

19          methodology). Table C.11 is submitted with Progress Report 0
20          and each subsequent Progress Report.

21      b) Assumptions and Limitations
22              Unit Cost Per Overhead Mile De-Energized represents the
23          initial capital installation cost divided by the primary overhead
24          HFTD miles removed or replaced by the mitigation. Note,
25          PG&E is populating cells for Additional Comparison 1, in
26          addition to 100 percent Undergrounding.
27              Unit Cost Per Circuit Mile Energized represents the initial
28          capital installation cost divided by the energized primary
29          overhead miles installed as part of the mitigation. For
30          undergrounding, a conversion factor is applied, reflecting the
31          assumption that each mile of overhead line replaced requires
32          approximately 1.25 miles of underground installation. No
33          conversion factor is applied to non-undergrounding mitigations.


                                -243-
 1              PG&E presents Total Costs as the capital costs to install the
 2          mitigation measure and the associated operations and
 3          maintenance (O&M) costs over the life of the asset. These
 4          values do not include baseline costs (e.g., O&M expenditures
 5          for existing infrastructure). Accordingly, they differ from the
 6          costs used in the Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) calculation, which
 7          are calculated as lifetime costs net of the baseline.

 4      a) Table Description
 5              PG&E provides a supplementary table (Table C.24) to the

 9          there is completed or ongoing Fire Rebuild work associated with

11          outlined in EUP Guidelines Section 2.4.3.1.

12      b) Assumptions and Limitations
13              PG&E does not maintain a comprehensive inventory of all
14          wildfire events occurring within our service territory, nor the
15          facilities and Circuit Segments impacted by those incidents. To
16          comply with the requirements of Section 2.4.3.1 of the EUP
17          Guidelines, PG&E provides a list of wildfire events associated
18          with current or historical (2015-2025) Fire Rebuild work.
19          Because the underlying historical data sources are not
20          comprehensive, the information presented in this table may not
21          reflect all wildfire events or associated impacts within PG&E's
22          service territory.
23              PG&E’s records do not consistently include wildfire name,
24          date, and location data for every wildfire event in our service
25          territory. Accordingly, for consistency in producing this table, we
26          are relying on CAL FIRE’s records, where available, to provide
27          wildfire name, date, and locations. If a wildfire event cannot be
28          identified with a CAL FIRE record, the Wildfire event is reported
29          with an unknown date or location information.
30              Circuit Segments reported within this table are limited to
31          Circuit Segments which are named within the most recent
32          WDRM. This ensures that only Circuit Segments which are
33          reported in Table C.6 are reported in this table. Facilities data is

 2                        historical Fire Rebuild Area dataset.

 6                        hardening. For the Rebuild Status field in Table C.24, the status

 5   f.   Confirmed Project Polygon (Polygon Feature Class) (GIS
 6        Feature C.4.2)

 9        Project will be associated with one Circuit Segment in the GIS data, and

11        avoid overlap between crossing or adjacent Circuit Segments where
12        possible, but some overlap may be unavoidable, as in cases where
13        circuit segments intersect or are in close, parallel alignment. The
14        Project Polygons will encompass the pre-mitigation geometries of the
15        constituent Subprojects.

22   g. Pre-Mitigation Overhead Conductor (Line Feature Class) (GIS
23        Feature C.4.3)

26        that will be replaced with overhead covered conductor, removed, or
27        replaced with underground conductor will be represented in this feature.

29        pre_mitigation_alignment_id which will map to the Subproject Table.
30        Pre_mitigation_alignment_id will start at 0 and increase if and when the
31        endpoints of available geospatial data move. Pre-Mitigation geometry is
32        expected to always fall within the Project Polygon. In the event that a
33        Subproject’s Pre-Mitigation Geometry falls outside the bounds of the

 1      associated Confirmed Project Polygon, we will provide an explanation in

 3      1) Pre-Mitigation Overhead Conductor GIS Data (Table C.18)

 5          Conductor GIS feature. It will contain the Utility Name, the
 6          Subproject ID on which the Overhead Conductor geometry is based,
 7          the version of the Overhead Conductor Geometry (the
 8          Pre-Mitigation Alignment ID Field), the Plan ID, Project ID, Circuit

10          This table will also identify the class of conductor that is selected for

15   h. Pre-Mitigation Assets (Point Feature Class) (GIS Feature C.4.4)
16          Pre-mitigation overhead conductor geometries are based on
17      scoping or design drawings that are created in a different system than
18      GIS (PG&E system of record). As such, they will not be perfectly
19      aligned with existing mapped Circuit Segment geometry. Therefore, we
20      will use a buffer analysis that relies on the Subproject’s Pre-mitigation
21      Overhead Conductor line feature data to capture assets within a 24-foot
22      buffer, or within 12 feet of that conductor geometry in any direction. This
23      is the optimal extent for capturing all relevant assets while minimizing
24      the capture of assets not associated with the Subproject’s geospatial
25      scope. This data must be regarded as a close approximation of the
26      pre-mitigation assets in scope and may capture assets that belong to
27      parallel or adjacent circuit segments. PG&E does not currently attribute
28      the assets with their Circuit Segment in the GIS system of record.

29      1) Pre-Mitigation Assets GIS Data (Table C.19)
30              Table C.19 is the attribute table of the Pre-Mitigation Assets GIS
31          feature. It contains the Utility Name, Subproject ID, Project ID, Plan
32          ID, Portfolio ID, Circuit ID, and Circuit Segment ID that an individual
33          asset data point is associated with via the geospatial analysis


                                     -257-
 1            described above. This table will also be updated with the
 2            pre- mitigation alignment id (geometry version) of the affiliated
 3            Subproject. This table will identify the asset type of each data point
 4            including: capacitor bank, fuse, switchgear, transformer, or support
 5            structure. Assets will be associated with a single Subproject ID.
 6            This table is submitted as confidential due to the identification of
 7            utility infrastructure locations.

 3   j.   Post-Mitigation Assets (Point Feature Class) (GIS Feature C.4.6)
 4            Post-mitigation assets including transformers, switches, fuses, and
 5        capacitor banks can be drawn in the scoping phase and will be provided
 6        for Subprojects when geometry is first provided. However, poles are not
 7        identified in the scoping phase and will not be included in this feature

11        1) Post-Mitigation Assets GIS Data (Table C.21)
12                Table C.21 is the attribute table of the pre-mitigation assets GIS
13            feature. It contains the Utility Name, Subproject ID, Project ID, Plan
14            ID, Portfolio ID, Circuit ID, and Circuit Segment ID that an individual
15            asset data point is associated with via the initial scoping drawing (if
16            the Subproject has not been fully mapped), or the GIS system of

20            each data point, including: capacitor bank, fuse, switchgear,
21            transformer, or support structure. Asset type data for capacitor
22            banks, fuses, switchgears, and transformers will be available after a

 5   A. Chapter Introduction
 6           This chapter explains Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s (PG&E) Risk
 7       Modeling Methodology consistent with the requirements in Section 2.7 of the
 8       Electrical Undergrounding Plan (EUP) Guidelines.
 9           Section B lists the requirements in Senate Bill (SB) 884 and the EUP
10       Guidelines addressed in this chapter.
11           Section C summarizes PG&E’s Risk Modeling Methodology. PG&E’s Risk
12       Modeling Methodology consists of our Wildfire Distribution Risk Model (WDRM),
13       Outage Program Risk Model (OPRM), Enterprise Bow Tie Model, and Wildfire
14       Benefit-Cost Analysis (WBCA) model. The WDRM, OPRM, and WBCA are
15       supported by several sub-models.176
16           The WDRM identifies the highest Wildfire Risk on PG&E’s distribution
17       system by estimating Circuit-Segment-Level Ignition Likelihood and potential
18       wildfire consequences. The outputs from the WDRM and OPRM, along with
19       cost, benefit, mitigation effectiveness and financial inputs are used in the WBCA
20       to calculate Benefit-Cost Ratios (BCR) for a variety of system hardening
21       mitigations at the Circuit Segment level. In parallel, the OPRM quantifies the
22       reliability impacts associated with wildfire mitigation outage programs by
23       estimating the likelihood and customer impacts of Enhanced Powerline Safety
24       Settings (EPSS) and Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) events. Together,
25       these models provide a view of wildfire risk and reliability impacts across the
26       system.


     176 These four key models describe PG&E’s overall risk modeling methodology. The seven
         model chapters outlined in Sections D.1 to D.7 below provide the required model-by-
         model detail underlying the risk modeling methodology, this includes models that are
         inputs to the key models. WDRM is documented through separate Ignition Likelihood
         and Ignition Consequence chapters (Model Report Chapters 1 and 2); OPRM is
         documented through separate EPSS and PSPS chapters (Model Report Chapters 3
         and 4); and the remaining chapters explain the Overall Utility Risk calculation (Model
         Report Chapter 4), the WBCA (Model Report Chapter 5), and the Enterprise Bow Tie
         Model (Model Report Chapter 6).

 1      C. Risk Modeling (EUP Guidelines Section 2.7)
 2
               This section describes the requirements for the Risk Modeling Methodology
           that the Large Electrical Corporation must employ to establish the Plan Mitigation
           Objective and to perform the analysis required in Screen 3 (Project Risk Analysis).
               The Large Electrical Corporation must justify its methodology in a narrative
           section of its EUP submission.
 3
 4                          We use our risk models to conduct analyses of Project-Level Risk and
 5               Ignition Risk. We conduct these analyses separately and look at them
 6               collectively to prioritize the locations and best mitigations for system hardening
 7               projects. Our risk modeling methodology enables us to estimate future risks and
 8               accumulation of risk over time, account for Undergrounding Projects with
 9               multiple mitigations and Subprojects, establish Baselines and historical
10               calibrations, and compare Alternative Mitigation strategies. This integrated
11               approach allows PG&E to make consistent, quantitative, and risk-informed
12               decisions about undergrounding and Alternative Mitigations across our system.
13               Figure 7-1 below is a high-level summary of the relationships between the key
14               risk models.

 1       1. Overview of Risk Modeling Methodology (EUP Guidelines
 2           Section 2.7.1)
 3
           The Large Electrical Corporation must provide an overview narrative that
      explains the key elements of its risk modeling approach and definitions. The
      narrative must detail how the Large Electrical Corporation will compare the
      potential wildfire risk and reliability impacts of Undergrounding to Alternative
      Mitigations. The overview must describe the methodology and underlying intent of
      the Large Electrical Corporation’s risk assessment in no more than five pages,
      inclusive of all narratives, bullet point lists, and any graphics. The overview
      narrative should also include any additional Key Decision-Making Metrics
      (KDMMs) proposed by the Large Electrical Corporation and the enterprise
      diagram as required by Section 2.7.3 below.
 4

 5           a. PG&E’s Risk Assessment Methodology and Underlying Intent
 6                   As summarized in Figure 7-1 above, PG&E’s risk assessment
 7               methodology begins with the quantification of Baseline risk across the
 8               electric distribution system. This Baseline risk is estimated using a
 9               combination of bottom-up risk models that together provide both spatial
10               detail and enterprise-level valuation.
11                   At the Circuit Segment level, the WDRM and OPRM estimate where
12               risk is concentrated by assessing Wildfire and Reliability Risk across the
13               system. Additional detail regarding the methodologies and algorithms
14               underlying these models is provided in the RaDA Algorithms and
15               Methodologies Whitepaper (Attach. B. WP0023). At the enterprise level,
16               the Enterprise Bow Tie Model translates these risks into monetized
17               impacts. Together, these models provide a view of where risk is
18               concentrated and the magnitude of potential impacts.
19                   To assess wildfire and safety risk impacts, PG&E uses historic acres
20               burned, structures destroyed, loss of life and serious injuries, and
21               California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE)
22               suppression data to value the wildfire risk associated with the electric
23               system. To assess reliability risk impacts, PG&E uses Lawrence
24               Berkeley National Laboratory’s (LBNL) Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE)
25               calculator to monetize the impact of outages on customers.177



     177 Resolution SPD-37 (Dec. 10, 2025).

                                              -267-
 1          Once Baseline monetized risk is established, PG&E uses the WBCA
 2      to evaluate Alternative Mitigations for high-risk Circuit Segments. The
 3      WBCA applies mitigation-specific effectiveness values to estimate the
 4      amount of risk each mitigation is expected to reduce over its lifetime.
 5      These estimated risk reduction benefits are then compared to lifetime
 6      costs to support quantitative, risk-informed selection of preferred
 7      mitigation solutions.
 8          This integrated approach allows PG&E to prioritize mitigation
 9      investments based on their ability to deliver meaningful risk reduction in
10      a cost-effective manner, while recognizing that different locations, asset
11      conditions, and risk drivers may warrant different mitigation solutions.

12   b. PG&E’s Risk Models and Risk Model Landscape
13          PG&E’s EUP Model Risk Landscape consists of the: (1) WDRM;
14      (2) OPRM; (3) WBCA; and (4) Enterprise Bow Tie Model. Together,
15      these models quantify Baseline risk, translate risk into monetized
16      impacts, and evaluate mitigation alternatives to support risk-informed
17      decision making. The enterprise diagrams are provided in Section E
18      below. In the Model Reports below, PG&E describes the vintage of the
19      models and plans to update the models. PG&E retires prior versions of
20      the risk models after an update. However, the model update does not
21      invalidate the prior model version or the planning and risk-informed
22      decisions that were based on that model version.

23      1) WDRM
24              The WDRM produces relative Circuit Segment values for
25          Ignition Risk (also referred to as Wildfire Risk, defined as the
26          product of Ignition Likelihood of a Risk Event (LoRE) and Ignition
27          Consequence of Risk Event (CoRE). Ignition Likelihood represents
28          the expected count of ignitions during wildfire season (June through
29          November) based on asset-specific failure modes and Ignition
30          Consequence represents the expected impact based on calibrated
31          wildfire spread simulations. Detailed descriptions are provided in
32          Sections D.1 and D.2.




                                    -268-
 1         Ignition Risk and Ignition Likelihood at the Circuit Segment level
 2     are calculated by aggregating the corresponding results across all
 3     asset locations within a Circuit Segment. Circuit Segment
 4     consequence is calculated as a probability‑weighted average, such
 5     that locations with a higher likelihood of ignition contribute more,
 6     reflecting the consequence most relevant to where ignitions are
 7     most likely. The Circuit Segment Consequence is derived by
 8     dividing Circuit Segment Ignition Risk by Circuit Segment Ignition
 9     Likelihood.
10         The WDRM produces a static baseline wildfire season dataset
11     aligned to a defined system configuration until a new version is
12     produced. WDRM version 4 (WDRM v4), based on a January 1,
13     2023 configuration, produces outputs at the asset, pixel, composite,
14     and Circuit Segment levels. Circuit Segment Ignition Risk, Ignition
15     Likelihood, and Ignition Weighted Consequence are used to
16     prioritize mitigation, inform Ignition Tail Risk thresholds, and serve
17     as direct inputs into the Circuit Segment Overall Utility Risk value.
18     Additional details are provided in Attach. B, WP026.

19   2) OPRM
20         The OPRM produces three distinct Circuit Segment-level
21     outputs: (1) EPSS Risk, (2) PSPS Risk, and (3) Baseline Outage
22     Risk. EPSS Risk and PSPS Risk represent outage impacts directly
23     attributable to these programs and are combined to calculate
24     Outage Program Risk, consistent with the EUP Guidelines. Detailed
25     descriptions of the EPSS and PSPS models are provided in
26     Sections D.3 and D.4 below.
27         Outage Program Likelihood is calculated as the sum of EPSS
28     and PSPS Likelihood, and Outage Program Risk as the sum of
29     EPSS Risk and PSPS Risk. The Outage Program Likelihood is
30     used to establish the High Frequency Outage Program Threshold,
31     which identifies additional Circuit Segments with significantly
32     elevated likelihood of frequent or prolonged service disruptions.
33     Outage Program Consequence is derived by dividing Outage
34     Program Risk by Outage Program Likelihood.

                               -269-
 1                        EPSS Outage Likelihood estimates the expected incremental
 2                    annual outage duration (in minutes per year) from enabling EPSS.
 3                    EPSS Outage Consequence quantifies the expected cost (in dollars)
 4                    of a Circuit Segment outage based on the number of affected
 5                    customers and Value of Service (VoS).
 6                        PSPS Outage Likelihood estimates the expected annual outage
 7                    duration (in minutes per year) based on a Circuit Segment’s
 8                    historical exposure to PSPS events. Circuit Segment PSPS
 9                    exposure is determined by a combination of PSPS event data and a
10                    historical lookback analysis that applies current PSPS criteria to
11                    past weather conditions. Outage Consequence represents the total
12                    expected cost (in dollars) of outages attributed to a Circuit Segment,
13                    including both direct and downstream customer impacts.
14                        Baseline Outage Risk represents residual risk of sustained
15                    outages not attributable to EPSS or PSPS, i.e., outage impacts that
16                    would be expected to occur absent these wildfire mitigation
17                    programs. While EPSS Risk, PSPS Risk, and Baseline Outage Risk
18                    are all incorporated into the WBCA to capture total customer outage
19                    impacts, only EPSS Risk and PSPS Risk are included in the Outage
20                    Program Risk KDMM and Overall Utility Risk KDMM used to inform
21                    mitigation selection decisions.
22                        The OPRM version 1 (v1) 178 produces a static dataset of
23                    Circuit Segment Outage Risk aligned to the same defined system
24                    configuration as WDRM v4. Model inputs are described in
25                    Section H.2 and Attach. B, WP019 (See Sections D.3 and D.4.for
26                    additional details.)
27                        PG&E uses the WBCA to perform Circuit‑Segment‑level
28                    evaluations of Alternative Mitigations and Additional Comparisons
29                    within the Project Acceptance Framework. The WBCA quantifies
30                    and compares the costs and benefits of each mitigation, including
31                    capital (construction) costs, ongoing operations and maintenance


     178 The underlying data of the OPRM is based on a data vintage date of January 1, 2023.
         The PSPS Risk Model also includes PSPS customer and event data from the 2024
         PSPS lookback study, which is the most recent PSPS lookback study available.

                                              -270-
 1                    (O&M) costs, projected climate change impacts, public safety
 2                    benefits, Wildfire Risk reduction, and reliability improvements.
 3                         WBCA version 1 (data as of January 2026) integrates output
 4                    from the WDRM and OPRM with inputs described in the WBCA
 5                    documentation (Attach. B, WP006) to calculate BCRs for each
 6                    mitigation evaluated in Screen 2. These mitigation configurations
 7                    include: (1) 100 percent Undergrounding, (2) 100 percent Overhead
 8                    Hardening, (3) 100 percent Remote Grid, and (4) hybrid
 9                    configurations (50 percent undergrounding/50 percent overhead
10                    hardening).
11                         The WBCA estimates total wildfire, reliability, and safety risk
12                    reduction over the expected life of each asset using monetized risk
13                    values derived from WDRM and OPRM, supplemented by inputs
14                    from the Enterprise Bow Tie Models. PG&E assumes asset lives of
15                    55 years for undergrounding and 48 years for overhead hardening.
16                    The resulting lifetime risk reduction is compared to total lifecycle
17                    costs relative to the No‑Build Baseline179 are used to calculate
18                    Project BCRs.
19                         Assumptions and inputs are further refined during the Screen 3
20                    scoping process (see Chapter 3, Section D.3), to support more
21                    detailed comparisons of Alternative Mitigations and identification of
22                    the appropriate system hardening strategy for each Circuit Segment.
23                    The use of model outputs in these evaluations is described in
24                    Chapter 3, Sections D.2 (Screen 2) and D.3 (Screen 3), consistent
25                    with EUP Guidelines Sections 2.4.4 and 2.4.5.

26                3) Enterprise Bow Tie Model
27                         The Enterprise Risk Bow Tie Model serves as the top-down
28                    component of PG&E’s Model Risk Landscape, converting ignition
29                    and outage-related risks into enterprise risk values used in
30                    downstream analysis. The model consists of three integrated Bow
31                    Tie models: a Wildfire Bow Tie, a PSPS Bow Tie, and an EPSS Bow
32                    Tie. For brevity, the discussion below focuses primarily on the


     179 See Attach. B, WP006 for further details.

                                                -271-
 1                    Wildfire Bow Tie. The model is developed under PG&E’s
 2                    standardized Bow Tie methodology consistent with the CPUC
 3                    Risk- Based Decision-Making Framework (RDF).180
 4                         The model integrates historical ignition and outage data,
 5                    post-event observations such as PSPS hazards and damages, and
 6                    external data sources (e.g., CAL FIRE records), along with
 7                    monetization parameters such as the Value of Statistical Life (VSL)
 8                    and VoS to quantify safety and reliability impacts in dollar terms.
 9                         Using these inputs, the model estimates event frequency by
10                    combining observed ignitions with avoided ignitions attributable to
11                    mitigation programs, allocates frequency across outcome categories
12                    using conditional probabilities, and characterizes consequences
13                    across safety, reliability, and financial attributes. These
14                    consequences are expressed in natural units (equivalent fatalities,
15                    customer minutes interrupted, and dollars), monetized, and
16                    aggregated into a single consequence value (CoRE), which is
17                    combined with frequency to calculate annual risk.
18                         The Enterprise Bow Tie Model produces standardized
19                    enterprise-level outputs, including expected annual frequency,
20                    expected consequences by attribute, and risk values expressed in
21                    both risk-neutral and risk-adjusted dollars.181 These risk-adjusted
22                    dollars are used as the quantified risk values in WBCA BCR
23                    calculations and provide the monetized risk foundation that
24                    integrates with WDRM and OPRM outputs.
