1   D. Model Reports (EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.2)
2
         The Large Electrical Corporation must present a Model Report consisting of a
    collection of report chapters on each individual model used in the Risk Modeling
    Methodology. A model is defined as a distinct part of the larger Risk Modeling
    Methodology that has explainable units. These distinctions must be at least as
    granular as in the enterprise diagram described in Section 2.7.3.1 of these
    Guidelines. At a minimum, these models must include an Ignition Likelihood
    model, an Ignition Consequence model, an Outage Program likelihood model, an
    Outage Program consequence model, and an overall utility risk model. For each
    model, the Large Electrical Corporation must describe the methodology and
    numerical calculations involved at a level of detail that would allow for verification
    and replication in a self-contained chapter. Each chapter of the Model Report
    must be no more than four pages, inclusive of all narratives, bullet point lists, and
    any graphics. A Model Report may reference additional, publicly available
    documents published by the Large Electrical Corporation or third-party vendors.
    Each Model Report must also attach a technical workbook as an appendix. The
    technical workbook must demonstrate the numerical calculations and contain the
    toy problems referenced below.
        Each chapter of the Model Report must be formatted into the following
    subsections addressing different aspects of the modeling methodology and
    implementation.
    a. Model Usage: For each chapter, the Model Usage section must describe the
       model’s scope, how often the model is utilized, what aspects of the electrical
       system’s risk profile are evaluated by this model, and specifically identify what
       risk or risk component the model is evaluating.
    b. Model Type: For each chapter, the Model Type section must describe the
       model’s taxonomy (e.g., physics simulation, mathematical model, machine
       learning classification).
    c.   Key Inputs: For each chapter, the Key Inputs section must describe the data
         that is fed into a calibrated model, including a description of the original data
         collection when applicable.
    d. Model Solution: For each chapter, the Model Solution section must describe
       the method used to calibrate, train, simulate, optimize, or implement the model
       from a mathematical standpoint. The model solution must include relevant
       information. For example:
         i.    If the model is based on a historical frequency table, briefly describe the
               data procurement and weighting of the decision function.
         ii.   If the model is based on a general linear model, Bayesian regression or
               other under-parameterized model, describe the training data and
               validation accuracy of the model.
         iii. If the model is based on solving a non-convex problem, briefly describe
              the optimization procedure and potential pitfalls of local minima.




                                              -273-
          iv. If the model is based on an overparameterized network, briefly describe
              the optimization procedure, including the number of learnable parameters,
              training technique, and the size and origin of the training and testing sets.
          v.    If the model is based on a physical simulation, describe the simulation
                evolution algorithm, spatial and temporal resolution, and any subgrid
                effects considered.
          vi. If the model is based on Monte Carlo simulations, describe the
              assumptions made to build the component distributions and the outcome
              uncertainties
    e. Model Outputs: For each chapter, the Model Outputs section must describe
       how the data produced by the model is fed into other models or used by the
       Large Electrical Corporation to make risk-related decisions. The Large
       Electrical Corporation must describe the mathematical type of output (e.g.,
       distribution, average value, score, probability), the spatial resolution (e.g., per
       Circuit, per segment, per county) and temporal resolution (e.g., per day, per
       season, per year).
    f.    Uncertainty: For each chapter, the Uncertainty section must describe the
          amount by which a calculated value output by the model might differ from the
          actual value when the input parameters are known. Additionally, this section
          must address any methods the Large Electrical Corporation uses to account
          for missing input data in its Risk Modeling Methodology. Lastly, this section
          must address the sensitivity analysis used to determine the relationships
          between the uncertainty in the inputs used in an analysis and the uncertainty
          in the resultant dependent variables due to numerical instability or stiffness of
          the underlying equations.
    g. Toy Problems: For each chapter, the Toy Problems section must describe
       three examples, specifying input and output values, using synthetic data. One
       input must lead to a low-risk (or low-probability, low-consequence) output, one
       for a medium-risk case, and one for a high-risk case. In each case, the Large
       Electrical Corporation must describe the magnitude and units of the inputs and
       outputs as well as the prevalence of each scenario in real-world data. These
       examples must also be presented numerically in a workbook attached to the
       end of the Model Report.
    h. Shelf-Life: For each chapter, the Shelf-life section must describe the length or
       period the model is expected to be used. This section must describe if/how
       the model is expected to be updated, both regarding new calibration data and
       new project input data. This section must describe if/when the model is
       expected to be retired or replaced by an entirely new model. Sections 2.7.5.2
       and 2.7.7 of these Guidelines detail further requirements for updating the Risk
       Modeling Methodology.
1
2              In this section, PG&E presents a model report that consists of chapters on
3        each of the individual models used in our Risk Modeling Methodology. Each
4        model report describes the methodology and numerical calculations at a level of
5        detail that allows for verification and replication. Due to page limitations for this

                                               -274-
 1   section, PG&E also refers the reader to the relevant sections of the model
 2   documentation for additional detail.
 3       PG&E has taken a “bootstrapping” approach to uncertainty for most model
 4   reports, as discussed in subsection f of each Model Report Chapter below. This
 5   approach involves repeatedly resampling the Circuit Segment level value from
 6   the risk model, with replacement, computing the statistic of interest for each
 7   resample. The computed values for the statistic form an estimate of the
 8   sampling distribution of the statistic. The 95 percent confidence interval is then
 9   taken as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of this bootstrap distribution. Models
10   that use alternative uncertainty methodologies are described separately in their
11   respective chapters.

12   1. Model Report Chapter 1 – Ignition Likelihood Model
13           PG&E’s Ignition Likelihood Model for the WDRM is implemented through
14       the Distribution Event Probability Models (DEPM), which is comprised of
15       23 cause-specific Probability of Outage models and a final Probability of
16       Ignition Given Outage model. The DEPM v4 documentation provided as
17       Attach. B, WP015 describes the model types, key inputs, model solutions,
18       and outputs for these 23 models.

19       a. Model Usage
20               The Ignition Likelihood Model estimates wildfire-season ignition
21           probability for overhead electric distribution asset locations and provides
22           the likelihood input to WDRM Wildfire Risk calculations that are
23           aggregated to the Circuit Segment level. WDRM Wildfire Risk estimates
24           are used routinely for informing work plan prioritization to monitor and
25           mitigate risk. An overview of the DEPM suite of models is provided in
26           Sections 1 and 3.1 of the DEPM documentation.

27       b. Model Type
28               The Ignition Likelihood model is comprised of a suite of supporting
29           failure/outage event-probability models and a Probability of Ignition
30           Given Outage model. The supporting failure/outage models are
31           Machine Learning models that use either XGBoost or Maximum
32           Entropy, while the Probability of Ignition Given Outage model uses
33           logistic regression. Section 3 of the DEPM documentation describes


                                            -275-
 1      each model’s taxonomy in the corresponding “Algorithm Selection”
 2      subsection.

 3   c. Key Inputs
 4          Each of the asset, contact-from-object, and ignition event probability
 5      models use many input datasets providing information about the
 6      equipment type, equipment attributes, and the surrounding weather and
 7      environmental conditions. Section 3 of the DEPM documentation
 8      describes each of the asset, contact-from-object, and ignition event
 9      probability model’s input data (see “Covariate Selection”).

10   d. Model Solution
11          Each event-probability model is developed using historical failure,
12      outage, and ignition data from the peak wildfire season months of June
13      through November 2015-2022. Model performance is evaluated using
14      an out-of-sample test dataset. Section 3.2.1 of the DEPM
15      documentation describes the performance metrics used to evaluate the
16      models, including Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the
17      Curve (ROC AUC), precision-recall, and 20 percent concentration factor.
18      Section 3 then describes each of the 24 asset, contact-from-object, and
19      ignition event probability models. For each model, the “Model Data,”
20      “Key Developments,” “Performance,” “Algorithm Selection,” and
21      “Covariate Selection” sections describe the development and solution.

22   e. Model Outputs
23          The Ignition Likelihood model outputs wildfire-season probabilities of
24      ignition. For equipment asset models, outputs are produced at the
25      individual asset level; for contact-from-object models, outputs are
26      produced at the 100m x 100m-pixel level. The 23 probability-of-outage
27      model outputs are used as inputs to the Probability of Ignition Given
28      Outage model to estimate ignition likelihood. Ignition probabilities are
29      combined with wildfire consequence values to calculate Wildfire Risk for
30      the WDRM and aggregate to Circuit Segments. Section 3.6 of the
31      DEPM documentation describes how the failure/outage model outputs
32      are used to produce overall Ignition Likelihood.



                                    -276-
 1   f.   Uncertainty
 2            Due to ignitions and failures occurring infrequently, there is limited
 3        direct evidence about the true risk of any single asset or location. This
 4        makes it difficult to calculate a precise uncertainty range for each
 5        individual model prediction. Accordingly, uncertainty for the Ignition
 6        Likelihood model is characterized primarily through individual
 7        event-probability model performance metrics, feature diagnostics, and
 8        documented model limitations, rather than through formal uncertainty
 9        bounds for each output.
10            For the asset-based models, missing input data was less limiting
11        because XGBoost was selected in part for its ability to handle missing
12        values. For other models, records with insufficient attribute or covariate
13        data were excluded from model development and prediction. In
14        practice, this was uncommon because records missing key attributes
15        were generally screened out during data preparation.
16            PG&E has taken a bootstrapping approach to produce a 95 percent
17        confidence interval for the median Circuit Segment Ignition Likelihood
18        per primary overhead High Fire Threat District (HFTD) or High Fire Risk
19        Area (HFRA) mile. The results of this analysis are included in EUP Risk
20        Model Backtesting Table (Table C.5), discussed in Chapter 6,
21        Section C.1.b.5.
22            For Ignition Likelihood, PG&E evaluates uncertainty more broadly by
23        comparing out-of-sample model performance and using feature
24        diagnostics, such as feature importance plots and SHAP plots, to
25        understand which inputs most strongly influence model results. These
26        diagnostics also help assess model sensitivity by showing how changes
27        in input variables are associated with changes in predicted outcomes.
28        Model performance metrics and feature diagnostics are described in
29        DEPM Section 3.2.1, while model-specific performance results are
30        provided in the “Performance” subsections of DEPM Section 3.5 for the
31        failure/outage models and DEPM Section 3.6.1.2 for the Probability of
32        Ignition Given Outage model. Model-specific feature importance and
33        SHAP results are provided in the “Covariate Selection” subsections.



                                      -277-
 1   g. Toy Problems
 2          To illustrate how the Ignition Likelihood model combines the
 3      likelihood of a failure or outage with the conditional likelihood of ignition
 4      given that failure/outage, three conceptual synthetic toy problems are
 5      presented in the Ignition Likelihood Workpaper (Attach. B, WP029)
 6      using the equipment-caused primary conductor wire down failure
 7      sub‑model. These examples are illustrative only. The machine‑learning
 8      models are non‑linear and are designed for inference rather than
 9      causality; the relationships described below rely on feature‑importance
10      metrics to demonstrate model behavior under low‑, medium‑, and
11      high‑risk conditions.
12          The low‑risk case represents benign operating conditions with less
13      dry fuels and fewer conductors. Both the primary conductor failure
14      likelihood and the probability of ignition given failure are lower than
15      those in the high-risk case, resulting in a lower overall wildfire season
16      ignition likelihood.
17          The medium‑risk case reflects elevated conditions driven by dry
18      fuels and many conductors but is moderated by the non-burnable land
19      surface. The primary conductor failure likelihood is moderately elevated
20      due to increased exposure of conductors, while the probability of ignition
21      given failure is elevated due to dry fuels. Together, these inputs
22      produce a mid‑range wildfire‑season ignition likelihood.
23          The high‑risk case reflects elevated conductor failure conditions
24      characterized by a low soil erodibility factor and unfavorable relative
25      humidity. In this scenario, the probability of ignition given failure is
26      driven by moderately dry fuels and moderate wind speed with majority
27      shrub groundcover, producing an elevated wildfire‑season ignition
28      likelihood. The combination of elevated failure likelihood and elevated
29      ignition given failure likelihood results in a high likelihood of ignition.




                                      -278-
 1      h. Shelf-Life
 2             WDRM v4 is expected to be used until the next update. Model
 3         updates are generally performed to support major deliverables, such as
 4         the WMPs and GRCs. WDRM v4 supported the 2026–2028 WMP and
 5         2027–2031 GRC.
 6             PG&E intends to release an update to the WDRM in 2028 to support
 7         the 2031–2034 WMP and GRC. The update is expected to include a
 8         model refresh using new calibration data, refreshed input datasets, and
 9         enhancements to model structure and methodology.

10   2. Model Report Chapter 2– Ignition Consequence Model

11      a. Model Usage
12             The model estimates the expected outcome of a wildfire initiated at
13         the location of overhead distribution lines and provides the consequence
14         component of WDRM v4 Wildfire Risk calculations aggregated to the
15         Circuit Segment level to inform work plan prioritization to monitor and
16         mitigate risk. The model evaluates the consequence portion of the
17         electrical system’s Wildfire Risk profile by estimating the severity of
18         potential wildfire outcomes—including acres burned, buildings
19         destroyed, and fatalities—by converting those outcomes into a single
20         consequence value through a Multi-Attribute Value function (MAVf).
21         (See also Wildfire Consequence Model WP, Attach. B, WP025.)

22      b. Model Type
23             The model combines a Base Consequence Model with two
24         adjustment models for wildfire suppression and public egress. The
25         Base Model assigns historical daily fire conditions to eight partitions and
26         estimates an average MAVf-based consequence score for each
27         partition. Suppression and Egress are fit as Binomial generalized linear
28         models with a logit link that adjust those scores to produce the final
29         location-specific consequence value used in WDRM v4 risk calculations.
30         (See also Attach. B, WP025 Sections 3 and 4.)




                                        -279-
 1            c. Key Inputs
 2                     The model uses historical wildfire outcomes and location-based
 3                indicators to estimate ignition impacts at each modeled location. Key
 4                inputs are NASA VIIRS detections, CAL FIRE Red Books, and CPUC
 5                Safety and Enforcement Division (SED) reports for acres burned,
 6                structures destroyed, and fatalities. Base scores are determined from
 7                HFRA status,182 Dry Wind Conditions, and Predicted Destructive
 8                conditions, with the latter informed by 24-hour wildfire simulations and
 9                Fire Potential Index (FPI) outputs used for PSPS decision-making.
10                Adjusted consequence uses Technosylva’s Terrain Difficulty Index (TDI)
11                for suppression difficulty and PG&E’s AFN index to model egress
12                challenges (see Sections 3.2 and 3.3 of Attach. B, WP0025 and
13                Attach. B, WP028 (Ignition Consequence Toy Problem).

14            d. Model Solution
15                     The model is implemented in two stages: a base consequence
16                sub-model and an adjustment for public egress and wildfire suppression.
17                The sub-model uses 2012–2022 records to assign each historical fire
18                one of eight condition partitions based on three true/false criteria—
19                HFRA status, Dry-Wind Conditions, and Predicted-Destructive
20                conditions; and a consequence score calculated using the MAVf to
21                convert acres burned, structures destroyed, and fatalities into a single
22                value. The model then derives an average MAVf consequence score for
23                each of the eight partitions.
24                     The adjusted consequence calculation applies wildfire suppression
25                and public egress models to refine the base consequence values. The
26                suppression model was fit using historical fire data with the dependent
27                variable represented as the portion of buildings survived. The egress
28                model was fit using the same historical fire data with fractional fatalities
29                as the dependent variable, meaning the model estimates the expected
30                fatality rate associated with the number of structures destroyed rather
31                than a fatality count. The model-fit diagnostics for the regression



     182 High Fire Risk Area (HFRA) refers to utility-identified areas considered at high risk for
         wildfire. When used in “HFRA status,” the term HFRA includes both HFRA and HFTD.

                                                  -280-
 1        models can be expressed in terms of deviance ratios relative to a null, or
 2        non-existent, model. The full model deviance ratios for suppression is
 3        0.755 versus 1.000 for the null model and for egress it is 0.898 versus
 4        1.000 for the null model.
 5            After the suppression and egress adjustments are estimated, the
 6        model constructs adjusted consequence tables that are referenced
 7        during application to grid asset locations. For each location, the model
 8        calculates daily consequence values across 11 wildfire seasons from
 9        2012 through 2022 and then averages those daily values to produce the
10        final location-specific consequence score used in WDRM. The final
11        day-weighted average consequence scores in the WDRM were
12        evaluated on a performance curve displaying the model’s ability to
13        capture the worst historical fire outcomes (acres burned, structures
14        destroyed, and fatalities) within the highest rank ordered pixel locations.
15        (See also Attach. B, WP026 (Wildfire Consequence v4 Performance
16        Figure 16).)

17   e. Model Outputs
18            The model produces a location-specific consequence score
19        representing the expected consequence of an ignition at each modeled
20        location. The model calculates daily consequence values for each
21        100m-by-100m grid pixel across 11 wildfire seasons (2012-2022) and
22        then averages those values to produce the final consequence score.
23        The score is used as the consequence component in WDRM, where risk
24        is calculated by combining ignition probability and wildfire consequence.
25        (See also Consequence Model WP, Attach. B, WP025, Sections 3.5 and
26        4.3.2.)

27   f.   Uncertainty
28            The WFC v4 model produces fire season daily averaged
29        consequence outcomes for historical ignitions in 100m x 100m pixels. It
30        is unlikely that an ignition event will result in the predicted seasonal
31        average consequence for that location due to variations in daily
32        conditions, which make rigorous uncertainty evaluations difficult. The
33        only known ignition outcomes are those for historical wildfires with


                                       -281-
 1      different causes of fire and local conditions at the time of ignition. PG&E
 2      used historical wildfire outcomes to calibrate the consequence model
 3      decision table used to predict a base consequence value for any given
 4      pixel for the daily conditions during a fire season.
 5          PG&E has taken a bootstrapping approach to produce a 95 percent
 6      confidence interval for the median Circuit Segment Ignition
 7      Consequence per primary overhead HFTD or HFRA mile. (See
 8      Progress Report 0, Risk Model Backtesting Table C.5.)
 9          For the Ignition Consequence sub‑models, records with insufficient
10      attribute or covariate data were excluded from model development and
11      prediction. In practice, this has occurred infrequently because key
12      inputs, such as weather variables, have broad spatial and temporal
13      coverage through reanalysis and because other inputs, including the fire
14      simulations, TDI, and AFN, are derived for all grid locations.

15   g. Toy Problems
16          The three Ignition Consequence Toy Problems correspond directly
17      to the Base Consequence Model condition partitions—HFRA status, Dry
18      Wind Conditions, and Predicted Destructive conditions—and to the
19      suppression and egress adjustment models that modify base
20      consequence outcomes. (See also Ignition Consequence Toy Problem,
21      Attach. B, WP028.)
22          The Low‑Risk example corresponds to locations outside
23      HFTD/HFRA that do not meet the threshold criteria for Dry Wind
24      Conditions or Predicted Destructive Conditions and have favorable
25      access and terrain characteristics. Wildfire suppression is generally
26      effective (low TDI) and public evacuation is less constrained (low AFN),
27      resulting in a low consequence score. Such conditions are most
28      common during typical operating periods outside of HFTD/HFRA.
29          The Medium‑Risk example corresponds to HFTD/HFRA locations
30      that do not meet the criteria for Dry Wind Conditions or Predicted
31      Destructive Conditions and have moderate access and terrain
32      characteristics. These conditions are associated with moderate fire
33      spread potential and partial reductions in suppression effectiveness.
34      These moderate TDI values increase the likelihood of structures

                                     -282-
 1         destroyed while moderate AFN values may modestly increase
 2         evacuation challenges and expected fatalities. Together these factors
 3         produce a mid‑range consequence score and occur frequently during
 4         wildfire season in HFTD/HFRA under elevated but not extreme
 5         conditions.
 6             The High‑Risk example corresponds to HFTD/HFRA locations that
 7         meet the criteria for both Dry Wind Conditions and Predicted Destructive
 8         conditions, representing the most severe Base Consequence partition.
 9         These conditions are combined with high TDI, indicating challenging
10         terrain and reduced suppression effectiveness, and high AFN, reflecting
11         greater evacuation challenges and higher expected fatalities. Together,
12         these factors result in the highest consequence scores and occur
13         infrequently during wildfire season.

14      h. Shelf-Life
15             Chapter 7, Section D.1.h (Ignition Likelihood Model Shelf-Life)
16         details the shelf-life methodology applicable to this model.

17   3. Model Report Chapter 3A – OPRM: EPSS

18      a. Model Usage
19             The OPRM quantifies in dollars the risk resulting from EPSS and
20         PSPS caused outages. This chapter describes the EPSS risk model.
21         The EPSS Risk Model and the PSPS Risk Model produce risk and
22         likelihood values that feed into the OPRM. The EPSS Risk Model
23         quantifies (in dollars) the expected impact of sustained outages on a
24         Circuit Segment when EPSS is enabled. It also evaluates
25         the incremental reliability risk introduced by enabling EPSS (see also
26         Outage Program Risk Model Documentation, Attach. B, WP019).

27      b. Model Type
28             The EPSS Risk Model is a deterministic mathematical model. It
29         uses a rule-based formulation to compute the expected number and
30         duration of sustained outages that include: (1) Historical outage rates;
31         (2) EPSS enablement schedules; (3) Empirical sustained outage
32         fractions; (4) Outage duration; (5) Number of affected customers; and
33         (6) Economic VoS interruption.

                                       -283-
 1   c. Key Inputs
 2          EPSS likelihood considers the probability of an outage that is based
 3      on the probability of failure from WDRM sub-models. It also considers
 4      the expected duration of that outage derived from the Distribution
 5      Reliability Value Model when EPSS is enabled. Inputs are derived from
 6      internal models (WDRM v4 and IGP) and historical outage data, filtered
 7      for HFTD/HFRA areas. (See also EPSS Risk Model Documentation,
 8      Attach. B, WP018.)
 9          Key inputs include:
10      •   N_outages,s,cs: Expected number of outages by WDRM subset
11          and Circuit Segment
12      •   D_outages,s,cs: Expected duration of an outage on a Circuit
13          Segment, which is derived by a weighted average for each modeled
14          asset type (conductor and support structures) and the protective
15          devices they are downstream from (breaker, dynamic protective
16          device, fuse, switch), on a Circuit Segment mapped to WDRM v4
17          subsets
18      •   f_EPSS_enabled: Fraction of wildfire season during which EPSS is
19          enabled, based on EPSS lookback and historical enablement data
20      •   f_sustained,s: Fraction of outages that are sustained (vs.
21          momentary) for each subset when EPSS is disabled. When EPSS
22          is enabled, it assumes that all outages are sustained outages.
23              The consequence component of the model quantifies the impact
24          of a sustained outage on a Circuit Segment when EPSS is enabled.
25          It is used to estimate customer impacts in terms of the VoS lost for
26          the number and types of customers impacted. Key inputs for the
27          consequence calculation include:
28      •   VoS: VoS from the Interruption Cost Estimate calculator, version
29          2.0 (dollars per minute); and
30      •   Incremental customer count: The count of customers
31          downstream of each EPSS-enabled protective device compared to
32          the count of customers impacted by a non-EPSS outage. There are
33          typically more downstream customers of an EPSS device than those
34          downstream of a traditional protective device, because EPSS

                                    -284-
 1          devices are generally installed on upstream portions of the circuit
 2          and de-energize a larger section. As a result, customers impacted
 3          by a non-EPSS outage would generally represent a subset of the
 4          customers impacted by an EPSS outage.

 5   d. Model Solution
 6          The EPSS Risk Model estimates the reliability risk introduced by
 7      enabling EPSS during wildfire season. It is applied at the Circuit
 8      Segment level and is designed to estimate the expected impact of
 9      sustained outages in monetary terms. The model evaluates the
10      expected number and consequence of sustained outages on a Circuit
11      Segment when EPSS is enabled, which is then compared to a
12      counterfactual scenario where EPSS is disabled. This approach
13      isolates the reliability impact associated with EPSS enablement.
14          To quantify the incremental reliability risk introduced by EPSS, the
15      model compares two scenarios: when EPSS is enabled and when it is
16      not. We evaluate these scenarios over the same period for consistency.
17      This allows PG&E to isolate the additional Outage Program Risk
18      attributable solely to EPSS and exclude other seasonal or operational
19      factors. A full derivation of the model’s solution is in the EPSS Outage
20      Risk Model Documentation (see EPSS Outage Program Risk Model
21      Documentation, Attach. B, WP019).

22   e. Model Outputs
23          The EPSS Risk Model output is a scalar value representing the
24      expected impact of sustained outages per Circuit Segment during the
25      EPSS-enabled portion of wildfire season. The following data outputs
26      are captured in the EPSS Risk Model: (1) Annual dollarized risk per
27      Circuit Segment; (2) Incremental increase in annual Customer Minutes
28      Interrupted (CMI) per Circuit Segment from EPSS; (3) Annual likelihood
29      per Circuit Segment in outage minutes per year; and (4) Consequence
30      per Circuit Segment in dollars per outage minute. This output feeds into
31      the overall OPRM in combination with data from the PSPS Risk Model.




                                    -285-
 1   f.   Uncertainty
 2            PG&E has taken a bootstrapping approach to produce a 95 percent
 3        confidence interval for the median Circuit Segment total outage program
 4        risk per primary OH HFTD or HFRA mile. The total outage program risk
 5        is the sum of PSPS and EPSS outage program risks. The results of this
 6        analysis are included in EUP Risk Model Backtesting Table (Table C.5),
 7        discussed in Chapter 6, section C.1.b.5.

 8   g. Toy Problems
 9            PG&E provided the data for three example toy problems (low,
10        medium, high risk) in the EPSS OPRM. Attach. B, WP016 details the
11        calculation methodology for the EPSS OPRM. The low-risk case
12        represents a Circuit Segment with minimal incremental exposure from
13        EPSS enablement. The segment has a low EPSS enablement rate
14        and/or low underlying failure probability, resulting in a low number of
15        momentary outages converted to sustained outages per wildfire season.
16        The segment also serves a small number of customers downstream of
17        EPSS protective devices, producing a low level of incremental CMI. The
18        combined low likelihood and low impact result in a low overall risk, which
19        represents the majority of EPSS enabled Circuit Segments in our
20        service territory.
21            The medium-risk case reflects a Circuit Segment with moderate
22        incremental outage exposure from EPSS enablement. The segment
23        experiences a moderate number of conversions per wildfire season,
24        driven by moderate failure probability and EPSS enablement history.
25        Each segment serves a moderate customer base, producing a
26        mid-range level of incremental CMI per converted event. Together,
27        these inputs yield a medium overall risk. Conditions of this type occur
28        on a meaningful subset of segments in areas with higher EPSS
29        utilization.
30            The high-risk case reflects a Circuit Segment with significant
31        incremental outage frequency from EPSS enablement. The segment
32        serves a large customer base downstream of EPSS protective devices,
33        with each event producing substantial incremental CMI due to the wider
34        EPSS isolation footprint and outage duration. The combination of high

                                      -286-
 1               likelihood and high impact yields a high overall risk. Such conditions
 2               occur on a small number of segments concentrated in PG&E's most
 3               EPSS-active circuits with dense customer populations.

 9         4. Model Report Chapter 3B – OPRM: PSPS

10            a. Model Usage
11                     The PSPS Risk Model calculates dollarized risk and outage
12               predictions (minutes of interruption) at the Circuit Segment level. Risk is
13               based on the historical likelihood of a segment being present within a
14               PSPS polygon over the seven-year lookback period of the input data
15               (2018-2024). Customer outage costs originate at each segment and are
16               then redistributed to upstream segments using mileage-weighted
17               coefficients. This reflects that de-energizing an upstream segment
18               causes outages on all downstream segments. Segments with more
19               exposed mileage within a PSPS event polygon receive proportionally
20               more redistributed risk. In effect, this model calculates the risk that
21               could be averted by undergrounding a given Circuit Segment.183




     183 Attach. B, WP019 provides further details on the Outage Program Risk Model.

                                              -287-
 1   b. Model Type
 2          The PSPS Risk Model is a deterministic mathematical model. It
 3      uses a rule-based formulation to compute the expected number of
 4      sustained outages that include: (1) circuit geometry; (2) aggregated
 5      customer value-of-service data; and (3) historical PSPS event polygons.
 6      The PSPS Risk Model does not involve simulation, machine learning, or
 7      statistical inference.

 8   c. Key Inputs
 9          Key inputs to the PSPS Risk Model include:
10      •   The PSPS Lookback Study: This dataset provides seven years of
11          PSPS event data including event polygons, outage duration in
12          minutes, and affected Circuit Segments and Service Point IDs
13          starting in 2018.
14      •   The WDRM v4: The WDRM is the PSPS Risk Model’s source of
15          record for Circuit Segment geometry.
16      •   PG&E Customer Segmentation Data: This data identifies the
17          customer service classes and critical customer factors for SPIDs
18          affected by PSPS events.
19          These inputs are derived from historic PSPS lookback event data
20      over the last seven years and WDRM data about the geometry of
21      affected circuits. The PSPS lookback includes all potential weather
22      events and the number of customers impacted and the duration. The
23      lookback also identifies the event type. For the PSPS model Distribution
24      only and Distribution/Transmission are the only events considered.

25   d. Model Solution
26          The PSPS Risk Model used in the OPRM is a circuit-based/
27      source-based mileage-weighted risk model. It is derived from the risk
28      associated with customer loss of service on a Circuit Segment. To
29      account for the downstream impact of de-energization triggered by
30      PSPS conditions upstream on a circuit, the customer experienced risk
31      on downstream Circuit Segments is distributed upstream to Circuit
32      Segments within PSPS weather event polygons based on the Circuit




                                   -288-
 1        Segment’s exposure to PSPS conditions, i.e., the length of the Circuit
 2        Segment within the polygon.
 3            The outage risk of each downstream Circuit Segment is modeled as
 4        a risk rate per mile: Ri/MA, where Ri is the customer-experienced risk on
 5        a given downstream Circuit Segment i and MA is the total exposed
 6        mileage of its ancestor (upstream) segments within the PSPS event
 7        polygon. The risk rate is then attributed to each upstream Circuit
 8        Segment in proportion to its exposed mileage: Rcs = Mcs *(Ri/MA), where
 9        Mcs is the length of segment cs within the event polygon. The total risk
10        on a given Circuit Segment is therefore the sum of all downstream
11        mileage-weighted risk attributed to it.
12            A full derivation of the model’s solution and example calculations are
13        in the PSPS Risk Model Documentation, Attach. B, WP020.

14   e. Model Outputs
15            The PSPS Risk Model output is a scalar-value dataset representing
16        the expected risk of sustained outages per Circuit Segment during a
17        year of PSPS events. The following data outputs are captured:
18        (1) Annual dollarized risk per Circuit Segment; (2) Annual likelihood per
19        Circuit Segment in outage minutes per year; (3) Annual CMI per Circuit
20        Segment; and (4) Consequence per Circuit Segment in dollars per
21        outage minute. This output feeds into the overall OPRM in combination
22        with data from the EPSS model.

23   f.   Uncertainty
24            PG&E has taken a bootstrapping approach to produce a 95 percent
25        confidence interval for the median circuit segment total outage program
26        risk per primary overhead HFTD or HFRA mile. The total outage
27        program risk is the sum of PSPS and EPSS outage program risks. The
28        results of this analysis are included in EUP Risk Model Backtesting
29        Table (Table C.5).
30            Because there is no machine learning component to this
31        deterministic model, uncertainty arises primarily from the use of variable
32        historical PSPS events as a proxy for the likely location and frequency of




                                       -289-
 1               future PSPS events. This uncertainty is mitigated by using seven years
 2               of PSPS event history.

 3           g. Toy Problems
 4                   To illustrate how the PSPS model categorizes Circuit Segment risk,
 5               PG&E provided the data for three example toy problems (low, medium,
 6               high risk) in the PSPS OPRM. PG&E has attached the calculation
 7               methodology for the PSPS OPRM.184 By looking at the historical
 8               likelihood of a circuit segment being de-energized and the typical
 9               severity of those de-energizations in terms of total customer-minutes of
10               interruption, we can produce a combined risk category.
11                   The low-risk case represents a Circuit Segment with minimal
12               exposure to PSPS event polygons over the seven-year lookback period.
13               The segment serves a small number of customers and is rarely included
14               in PSPS scoping, with limited customer-minutes of interruption in the
15               rare case an event does occur. The combined low likelihood and low
16               impact result in a low overall risk category, which represents most
17               Circuit Segments across PG&E’s system.
18                   The medium-risk case reflects a Circuit Segment with moderate
19               exposure to PSPS event polygons. The segment experiences a
20               moderate frequency of PSPS events and serves a medium-size
21               customer base, producing a mid-range level of customer-minutes of
22               interruption per event. Together, these inputs yield a medium overall
23               risk category. Conditions of this type occur on a meaningful subset of
24               segments in HFTD/HFRA areas.
25                   The high-risk case reflects a Circuit Segment within high-wind
26               corridors and fire-prone areas, with significant historical PSPS exposure
27               and a large or critical-customer-heavy customer base. The segment is
28               frequently included in PSPS scoping, with each event producing
29               substantial customer-minutes of interruption due to the customer count
30               and outage duration. The combination of high likelihood and high
31               impact yields a high overall risk category. Such conditions occur on a




     184 See Attach. B, WP017 for more details on the PSPS Toy Problem.

                                             -290-
 1           relatively small number of Circuit Segments concentrated in PG&E's
 2           highest-risk geographic areas.

 6   5. Model Report Chapter 4 – Overall Utility Risk Model

 7      a. Model Usage
 8               PG&E calculates Overall Utility Risk (OUR), a required KDMM, by
 9           combining Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk at the
10           Circuit-Segment level. The Overall Utility Risk calculation is presented
11           in this Model Report consistent with the EUP Guidelines’ requirement for
12           an Overall Utility Risk model. OUR is used as the top-level combined
13           risk metric at the project level, Portfolio level, and system level, enabling
14           project-level comparisons, Portfolio aggregation, system-level risk
15           assessment, and KDMM reporting. It provides a single, monetized
16           composite metric, allowing for standardized comparison across projects,
17           Portfolios, and the electric distribution system.

18      b. Model Type
19               The Overall Utility Risk calculation is a deterministic, rule-based
20           aggregation of Ignition Risk and Outage Program Risk (EPSS and
21           PSPS risks). Rather than serving as a primary risk estimation model, it
22           integrates outputs from the WDRM and OPRM, applying defined climate
23           adjustment factors and escalation parameters to produce a consolidated
24           view of utility risks. As a deterministic algebraic framework, calculations
25           are not independently calibrated and instead inherit underlying

                                           -291-
 1        assumptions, methodologies, and input dependencies from the
 2        upstream risk models, ensuring consistency with the foundational risk
 3        frameworks.

 4   c. Key Inputs
 5            The Key inputs to Overall Utility Risk include:
 6        •   Ignition Risk: monetized Circuit Segment Wildfire Risk
 7        •   Outage Program Risk: monetized Circuit Segment outage risk
 8            associated with Outage Programs.
 9        •   Climate change factors: Project-level multipliers applied over time
10            to reflect changing future conditions
11        •   Escalation factors: multipliers used to express future values in
12            comparable nominal terms.
13            Escalation and climate change factors are described in Section G.4
14        below (Core Capability 4), Core Capability 4 Workpaper (Attach. B,
15        WP011) and WBCA Whitepaper (Attach. B, WP006).

16   d. Model Solution
17            Overall Utility Risk is the sum of Ignition and Reliability Risk and
18        incorporates climate change and escalation.

19   e. Model Outputs
20            The calculation produces an Overall Utility Risk for each distribution
21        Circuit Segment in PG&E’s service territory.

22   f.   Uncertainty
23            PG&E has taken a bootstrapping approach to produce a 95 percent
24        confidence interval for the median Circuit Segment Overall Utility Risk
25        per primary overhead HFTD or HFRA mile. The results of this analysis
26        are included in EUP Risk Model Backtesting Table (Progress Report
27        Table C.5), discussed in Chapter 6, Section C.1.b.5.

28   g. Toy Problems
29            The Overall Utility Risk Toy Problem (Attach. B, WP031) provides
30        the toy-model inputs, outputs, and calculations.




                                       -292-
 1      h. Shelf-Life
 2             The Overall Utility Risk Calculation Shelf-life is directly dependent
 3         on the shelf-life of the contributing models for Ignition Risk and Outage
 4         Program Risk. (See Section D.1.h. and D.3.h for the applicable model
 5         Shelf-life for all relevant input models.)

 6   6. Model Report Chapter 5 – WCBA Model

 7      a. Model Usage
 8             The WBCA evaluates and compares different system hardening
 9         mitigations at the Circuit Segment level by estimating the costs and
10         benefits of implementing a particular mitigation at a specific location,
11         and the resulting reduction in safety, ignition and outage risk. Unlike
12         PG&E’s ignition and OPRMs, the WBCA ingests information from the
13         ignition and OPRMs, along with public safety risk, baseline reliability
14         risk, mitigation effectiveness, cost, and financial information, and
15         performs calculations that inform PG&E’s mitigation selection.

16      b. Model Type
17             The WBCA is built in the Foundry platform. PG&E aggregates
18         Ignition Risk data from the WDRM v4, outage program and baseline
19         outage risk data from the OPRM, public safety risk data, lifetime costs
20         and benefits, and mitigation effectiveness information to calculate
21         Circuit-Segment level BCRs. (See Attach. B, WP006.)

22      c. Key Inputs
23             The key inputs into the WBCA are:
24         •   Ignition Risk Data: Ignition Risk data from WDRM v4.
25         •   Outage Program Risk Data: Outage Risk data from OPRM.
26         •   Baseline Outage Risk Data: From a branch of PG&E’s OPRM that
27             accounts for the non-EPSS outage risk using WDRM probabilities of
28             failure.
29         •   Public Safety Risk Data: Also referred to as Public Contact with
30             Energized Electric Equipment (PCEEE), this input estimates the
31             likelihood and consequences of public contact with intact energized
32             equipment and prioritizes safety-driven investments using both



                                         -293-
 1       quantitative results and qualitative regulatory and operational
 2       considerations. (See PCEEE Risk WP, Attach. B, WP022)
 3   •   Cost Data: Includes the estimated present value capital costs for
 4       the capital project costs plus the estimated present value lifetime
 5       O&M costs. Estimated capital costs are based on historic values for
 6       similar activities adjusted for inflation and other factors. The O&M
 7       costs information is derived from the imputed adopted costs in
 8       PG&E’s 2023 GRC. (See WBCA WP, Attach. B, WP006.)
 9   •   Benefits Data: Includes the wildfire benefit (the wildfire risk
10       reduction associated with each Circuit Segment for a particular
11       mitigation); public safety benefit (the non-wildfire risk a Circuit
12       Segment poses to the public); baseline reliability benefit (the
13       monetary value of avoided CMI due to implementing a particular
14       wildfire mitigation); EPSS benefit (the reduction in EPSS exposure
15       associated with each Circuit Segment when a particular mitigation is
16       implemented); and PSPS benefit (the reduction in PSPS exposure
17       associated with each Circuit Segment when a particular mitigation is
18       implemented).
19   •   Mitigation Effectiveness: Estimated blended average
20       effectiveness expressed as a percentage for each Alternative
21       Mitigation. PG&E calculates effectiveness by assessing how well
22       individual mitigations and mitigation combinations reduce ignition
23       risk from unplanned outage events and equipment attributes
24       (“outage combinations”). PG&E assessed the effectiveness of more
25       than 2,700 outage combinations that have occurred in PG&E’s
26       HFTD areas during wildfire season. PG&E Subject Matter Experts
27       (SME) reviewed each combination, defined by a basic event and
28       three attributes (supplemental ignition cause, involved equipment,
29       and equipment condition), and assigned effectiveness ratings
30       reflecting each mitigation’s ability to prevent that combination.
31   •   Climate Impacts: Wildfire and reliability risk benefits consider
32       anticipated climate change impacts from 2028-2082 using two key
33       factors: (1) Fire Weather Index (FWI) Analysis; and (2) Heat Day
34       Analysis. (See also WBCA Section G.4 (Core Capability 4).)

                                  -294-
 1        •   Financing Data: Includes financing elements used to calculate
 2            annual cash flows and compare costs and benefits by Alternative
 3            Mitigation including Present Value of Revenue Requirement,
 4            nominal and real discount rates and inflation rates. (See also Ch. 5,
 5            Section C.3 a. and WBCA WP, Attach. B, WP006.)

 6   d. Model Solution
 7            The WBCA Model is not a predictive or optimization-based model
 8        that is calibrated or trained; rather, it ingests wildfire ignition risk, public
 9        safety risk, and reliability risk estimates from upstream risk models
10        (WDRM, OPRM), with standardized cost, financial, and effectiveness
11        assumptions. It evaluates the present value (PV) of lifetime benefits and
12        costs of each mitigation considered, applying consistent discounting,
13        asset life assumptions, and climate adjustment multipliers.
14            As the WBCA is an algebraic aggregation of fixed inputs rather than
15        a fitted model, there is no parameter estimation, validation accuracy, or
16        convergence criterion associated with its solution. It does not solve a
17        non‑convex optimization problem, train an over‑parameterized network,
18        or evolve a physical simulation over space and time.

19   e. Model Output
20            The WBCA outputs Circuit Segment BCR values for each
21        comparison: (1) 100 percent Underground; (2) 100 percent Overhead
22        Hardening; (3) 100 percent Remote Grid; and (4) Hybrid – 50 percent
23        Underground/50 percent Overhead Hardening.
24            PG&E uses WBCA outputs to inform mitigation selection for each
25        Eligible Circuit Segment. If the WBCA output indicates that a hybrid
26        solution is the preferred mitigation, PG&E further analyzes the hybrid
27        solution through the Feedback Loop in Screen 3. (See Ch. 3,
28        Section D.3. for details of the Feedback Loop and Screen 3 process.)

29   f.   Uncertainty
30            To account for uncertainty throughout the various factors in the
31        WBCA, PG&E, consistent with the IOUs’ proposal in Application
32        (A.) 26-02-005, includes an estimate uncertainty range when using the
33        WBCA outputs for mitigation decision-making. The BCR estimate


                                         -295-
 1               uncertainty range provides a transparent mechanism to account for
 2               known model limitations and to incorporate site-specific risk factors not
 3               fully represented in quantitative outputs, described in Chapter 3, Section
 4               D.3.a.6.
 5                    The BCR estimate uncertainty range is estimated to be 30 percent,
 6               consistent with Energy Safety’s decision on our 2026-2028 WMP.185
 7               To operationalize this uncertainty range for Project selection, we apply a
 8               comparison framework when evaluating Mitigation Alternatives with
 9               close BCRs. Specifically, when the BCR for undergrounding is at least
10               70 percent of the BCR of an alternative, undergrounding is considered
11               comparable. This 70-percent comparison standard reflects the
12               30-percent uncertainty range and does not represent a separate
13               eligibility threshold or a modification to the BCR methodology.

14           g. Toy Problems
15                    The Toy Problem with varying inputs and associated outputs of the
16               WBCA are included in Workpaper WBCA Toy Problem (Attach. B,
17               WP024). The values in the Toy Problem are representative of
18               real-world data as the costs and benefits of individual Projects will vary.

19           h. Shelf-Life
20                    PG&E expects to use this model for the life of the EUP. We expect
21               to update the model with updated inputs aligned with each WDRM risk
22               model version update, consistent with Section D.1.h below. PG&E plans
23               to update WBCA cost assumptions generally annually to align with the
24               prior year’s actual costs. These assumptions will be discounted back to
25               2028 dollars so that projects can be compared equally throughout the
26               EUP. As the WBCA model relies on the WDRM, OPRM and Enterprise
27               Bow Tie data and models, PG&E will update the WBCA model version
28               every four years beginning in 2028 to align with the anticipated timing of
29               the 2031-2034 WMP and GRC.

 1       7. Model Report Chapter 6 – Enterprise Risk Bow Tie

 2           a. Model Usage
 3                    PG&E’s Enterprise Risk Bow Tie model quantifies enterprise risks
 4                using a company-wide risk assessment methodology in compliance with
 5                the CPUC’s RDF. The Bow Tie models support quantitative
 6                assessments of risks and mitigations for major proceedings including
 7                RAMP and GRC and internal planning and decision-making.186
 8                    For the EUP, PG&E primarily uses the Wildfire Risk Bow Tie model
 9                (WLDFR) to quantify the annual expected Wildfire Risk associated with
10                PG&E’s electric infrastructure in risk-adjusted dollars. This annual
11                Wildfire Risk value is used to evaluate the potential risk reduction from
12                system hardening programs. PG&E also uses safety risk values from
13                other Enterprise Bow Tie models (e.g., PSPS, EPSS, PCEEE) to
14                capture additional safety consequences in the Overall Utility Risk
15                reduction. This approach aligns with the RDF by providing a consistent,
16                monetized metric for comparing and prioritizing risk mitigation strategies.

17           b. Model Type
18                    The Bow Tie models can be considered mathematical, probabilistic
19                models. In a Bow Tie model, a Risk Event is represented with a list of
20                drivers that potentially lead to the Risk Event occurring with estimated
21                likelihood and a list of outcomes describing consequence severity if the
22                Risk Event occurs. Outcomes are characterized by probability
23                distributions of the potential levels of impact from a risk event across
24                consequence attributes such as direct safety, indirect safety, electric
25                reliability, and financial attributes, then aggregated into a single CoRE
26                value after applying the CPUC Cost-Benefit Approach. Annual risk is
27                calculated as the sum, over all outcomes, of the product of each
28                outcome’s expected annual frequency and its corresponding CoRE.

29           c. Key Inputs
30                    Below are the key inputs for the Wildfire Risk Bow Tie Model:


     186 Further detail of the Enterprise Bow Tie Model is outlined in A. 24-05-008, PG&E’s 2024
         RAMP Report, Exhibit (PG&E-4), Chapter 1 available here: 2024-ramp-application-
         pge051524.pdf. See also PG&E’s GRC, A.25-05-015, Exhibit (PG&E-4), Ch. 3.

                                               -297-
 1      •   PG&E facility ignition data: Internal ignition investigation records
 2          used to estimate wildfire ignition frequency and consequence.
 3      •   PSPS damages and hazards data: Field observations of damaged
 4          equipment and hazard conditions identified during post-PSPS event
 5          patrols, enabling estimation of prevented potential ignition incidents.
 6      •   CAL FIRE large fire records: Public data on wildfires exceeding
 7          300 acres within PG&E’s service territory, including fire location,
 8          acres burned, fatalities, and structures destroyed. This data
 9          supports consequence distribution fitting and allocation of frequency
10          into large and destructive fire outcomes.
11      •   EPSS outage data: Actual sustained outage events on
12          EPSS-enabled circuits, recorded in PG&E’s Integrated Logging and
13          Information System (ILIS) outage database. This data provides the
14          count and details of outages (location, cause, CMI, etc.), used to
15          estimate the number of ignitions avoided due to EPSS enablement.
16      •   Value of Statistical Life (VSL): Standardized dollar valuation of
17          human life/safety per U.S. Department of Transportation guidance,
18          used to monetize fatalities and serious injuries.
19      •   Value of Service (VoS): Dollar-per-minute cost of interrupted
20          service per customer (expressed as $ per customer minutes
21          interrupted), from the LBNL ICE Calculator v1.0 (the version in effect
22          when the 2024 RAMP was prepared), used to monetize the electric
23          reliability impact (customers minutes interrupted).

24   d. Model Solution
25          The Bow Tie models calculate annual risk as the sum, across all
26      outcomes, of expected annual frequency multiplied by the CoRE. For
27      the Wildfire Risk Bow Tie model, frequencies are estimated as the sum
28      of annualized historical PG&E ignition counts, avoided ignitions from
29      PSPS and EPSS. PSPS avoided ignitions are estimated by multiplying
30      historical PSPS damages and hazards counts by the outage-to-ignition
31      rates during similar historical conditions, and EPSS avoided ignitions are
32      estimated based on historical EPSS outage counts multiplied by
33      outage-to-ignition rate estimated during similar historical conditions.
34      Total frequency is then broken down by outcomes, by applying the

                                    -298-
 1        conditional probability of ignition resulting in each outcome, estimated by
 2        PG&E ignition data and CAL FIRE large fire records.
 3            The outcomes are characterized using probability distributions over
 4        the applicable consequence attributes (safety, indirect safety, electric
 5        reliability, and financial) based on PG&E ignition and outage data and
 6        CAL FIRE large fire data. The CoRE for each outcome is computed as
 7        sum of the expected value of each of the Attribute Values’ probability
 8        distribution monetized using the monetization factors (VoS and VSL)
 9        and Risk Attitude function following the CPUC’s Cost-Benefit Approach.

10   e. Model Output
11            The Wildfire Risk Bow Tie model provides several key outputs for
12        the Baseline per year. These include: (1) the Event Frequency, the
13        expected number of wildfire ignition events per year; (2) the Expected
14        Consequences by Attribute, which are provided in natural units,
15        monetized levels and risk-adjusted levels; and (3) the Risk Value, which
16        is annual expected Wildfire Risk in risk-adjusted dollars, calculated by
17        multiplying frequency and CoRE.
18            The monetized annual risk values from the Bow Tie model feed into
19        the WBCA which uses the data to translate risk reductions for each
20        Alternative Mitigation and Additional Comparison into equivalent
21        monetized benefits. The WBCA model aggregates these annual
22        risk-adjusted benefit values and applies time-discounting. The WBCA
23        calculates BCRs that reflect risk reduction benefits in dollar terms
24        relative to mitigation costs using the Bow Tie model outputs to evaluate
25        Projects on a consistent basis.

26   f.   Uncertainty
27            The 2015-2024 data used to estimate ignition frequency and
28        consequence represents a single realization of a non-stationary process
29        and may not fully represent the current climate average conditions. This
30        contributes to statistical uncertainty in the estimated model parameters.
31        Applying the lower and upper bounds of the 50 percent Confidence
32        Intervals (CI) for key inputs yields a distribution overhead destructive fire
33        risk range of approximately 0.5x to 2x the point estimate. (See


                                       -299-
 1      Attach. B, WP027 for information for the key inputs and their confidence
 2      intervals.)
 3          The input data used for Wildfire Risk Bow Tie model does not suffer
 4      from missing data due to improvements in PG&E ignition data quality
 5      control. The Bow Tie model is a closed-form expected-value calculation
 6      in which risk equals ignition frequency multiplied by consequence per
 7      ignition. As a result, the relationship between input uncertainty and
 8      output uncertainty is approximately linear. Because the model does not
 9      rely on iterative solvers or stiff differential equations, we do not believe
10      that there is material uncertainty due to numerical instability.

11   g. Toy Problems
12          The Wildfire Bow Tie Toy Problem (Attach. B, WP027) provides the
13      toy-model inputs, outputs, and calculations. The low, medium, and high
14      cases are based on the lower bound of the 50 percent confidence
15      interval, the point estimate, and the upper bound of the 50 percent
16      confidence interval, respectively, for each key destructive fire risk input.
17      The resulting distribution overhead destructive fire risk estimates range
18      from approximately 0.5x to 2x the medium-case estimate.

19   h. Shelf-Life
20          This version of the Enterprise Bow Tie model is expected to be used
21      until the 2028 model update for the 2028 RAMP and 2031-2034 GRC.

1   E. Key Decision-Making Metrics and Enterprise Diagrams (EUP Guidelines
2      Section 2.7.3)

         The Key Decision-Making Metrics (KDMMs) are defined to be the collection of
    top-level metrics that the Large Electrical Corporation proposes to use to evaluate
    the efficacy of an Undergrounding Project. These KDMMs are not influenced by
    risk attitudes, risk tolerances, opportunity costs or any other decision-making
    parameters. They do not reflect financial considerations and must be used
    alongside financialized metrics reported in Screen 2 and Screen 4 to evaluate
    projects. The KDMMs measure key elements of risk and can be substantiated by
    real-world observations.
        The KDMMs will be used for approximating risk at the System-Level,
    Portfolio-Level, and individual Project-Level. A System-Level measurement
    accumulates information from the entire distribution system into a single number.
    A Portfolio-Level measurement accumulates information from every Circuit
    Segment on a Circuit which has one or more Confirmed Projects as well as their
    effects on the overall Circuit into a single number. A Project-Level measurement
    accumulates risk from all of the equipment on a single Circuit Segment.
       The Large Electrical Corporation must include the seven mandatory KDMMs
    described below and has the option to include five additional KDMMs of its
    choosing.
    a. The Large Electrical Corporation must include the following KDMMs:
        i.    Overall Utility Risk: A combined measure of Ignition Risk and Outage
              Program Risk that measures the total risk of wildfires and Outage Program
              Events related to wildfire risks. This is computed as the inner product of
              the likelihoods of adverse events and their consequences. This is an
              unweighted and unscaled calculation.
        ii.   Ignition Risk: The measure of impacts from wildfire at a given location.
              This metric is the product of two factors: (1) the likelihood a wildfire will
              occur, and (2) the potential consequences of a wildfire originating from
              this location. This is an unweighted and unscaled calculation.
        iii. Ignition Consequence: The total anticipated adverse effects from a
             wildfire on each community it reaches. This metric considers the wildfire
             hazard intensity, the wildfire exposure potential, and the inherent wildfire
             vulnerabilities of communities at risk.
        iv. Ignition Likelihood: The likelihood of an ignition at a given location given
            a probabilistic set of environmental conditions.
        v.    Outage Program Risk: The measure of reliability impacts from Outage
              Programs at a given location. This metric is the product of two factors:
              (1) the likelihood an Outage Program Event will be required due to
              environmental conditions exceeding design conditions, and (2) the
              potential consequences of the Outage Program for affected customers,
              considering exposure potential and vulnerability. This is an unweighted
              and unscaled calculation.


                                              -301-
         vi. Outage Program Consequence: The total anticipated adverse effects
             from an Outage Program for a community. This considers the Outage
             Program exposure potential and inherent Outage Program vulnerabilities
             of communities at risk.
         vii. Outage Program Likelihood: The likelihood of an Outage Program
              being deployed at any given time, given a probabilistic set of
              environmental conditions. This measure should capture both the
              probability of an Outage Program Event(s) being initiated at given time
              and the length of time of those Outage Program Event(s).
     b. Up to five additional KDMMs proposed by the Large Electrical Corporation
        may also be included. For each additional KDMM, the Large Electrical
        Corporation must include the following information in the Overview Section of
        the Risk Modeling Methodology:
         i.     Provide a definition, numerical calculation, and units.
         ii.    Explain each proposed KDMM, including how the KDMM contributes to
                measuring Ignition Risk and/or Outage Program Risk.
         iii. Report the proposed KDMMs at the same resolution and frequency as the
              required KDMMs.
 1
 2             The KDMMs are the top-level metrics used to evaluate the efficacy of an
 3     Undergrounding Project and to approximate risk at the System-Level,
 4     Portfolio-Level, and Project-Level. PG&E’s EUP uses the seven required
 5     KDMMs listed in Section 2.7.3 of the EUP Guidelines.
 6             Each of the 11,482 Circuit Segments that make up our system is unique in
 7     terms of its Wildfire Risk (likelihood and consequence) and Reliability Risk
 8     (likelihood and consequence). The system variation is reflected in the KDMMs.
 9             PG&E uses KDMMs in many aspects of our decision-making. The KDMMs
10     are used to establish Portfolio-Level Standards, Project-Level Thresholds and
11     Project-Level Standards, all of which support our Plan Mitigation Objective. The
12     six ignition and reliability risk KDMMs (numbers 2-7 described below) roll-up to
13     the Overall Utility Risk KDMM which we consider when selecting Alternative
14     Mitigations and prioritizing Projects for execution. PG&E’s definition for each
15     KDMM is provided below.
16     1. Overall Utility Risk: The combination of Ignition Risk and Outage Program
17             Risk, along with considerations for climate change and escalation. This is
18             represented as a dollar value and is an unscaled and unweighted value.
19             (See Section D.5 of this chapter.)



                                               -302-
 1   2. Ignition Risk: Ignition Risks are Circuit Segment relative risk values based
 2       on the outputs of the WDRM. Ignition Risk is the product of the Probability
 3       of Ignition for an asset or location and the Wildfire Consequence at that
 4       location. The relative WDRM risk values are then calibrated against the
 5       absolute value of PG&E’s Enterprise Risk Bow Tie for distribution Wildfire
 6       Risk. Ignition Risk is represented as a dollar value. (See Sections D.1 and
 7       D.2 of this chapter.)
 8   3. Ignition Consequence: Ignition Consequence represents the mean
 9       expected damages conditional on an ignition occurring on a given Circuit
10       Segment. It is calculated by dividing the monetized Ignition Risk by the
11       Ignition Likelihood (i.e., the annual expected number of ignitions). (See
12       Section D.2 of this chapter.)
13   4. Ignition Likelihood: Ignition Likelihood, also known as the Probability of
14       Ignition, is aggregated for a Circuit Segment from the suite of distribution
15       asset and contact from object event probability models. The event
16       probability models predict the likelihood of an ignition for an asset or location
17       over the length of one fire season. Ignition Likelihood is represented in
18       ignitions per year. (See Section D.1 of this chapter.)
19   5. Outage Program Risk: This is the summation of EPSS Risk and PSPS
20       Risk, representing the total monetized impact of outages caused by an
21       Outage Program and is used to calculate the Overall Utility Risk. (See
22       Sections D.3 and D.4 of this chapter.)
23   6. Outage Program Consequence: This quantifies the impact of an
24       outage caused by an Outage Program on a Circuit Segment in dollars per
25       outage minute and is used to estimate the customer impact in terms of
26       the VoS lost for the count and type of customers impacted. (See
27       Section C.1.b of this chapter.)
28   7. Outage Program Likelihood: This is defined as the expected number of
29       outage minutes per year caused by an Outage Program on a Circuit
30       Segment. It is calculated by summing the EPSS Likelihood and PSPS
31       Likelihood. (See Section C.1.b of this chapter.)

 1           The formulas for each KDMM for system aggregation and Portfolio-level
 2       aggregation are provided in the KDMM Formulas Workpaper.187 The KDMM

 4       1. Enterprise Diagrams (EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.3.1)
 5
           The Large Electrical Corporation must provide one or more entity relation
      diagram(s) of the system(s) used for quantifying Ignition Risk and one or more
      entity relation diagram(s) of the system(s) used for quantifying Outage Program
      Risks.
           Each diagram must show how input data feeds into independent sub-models
      and identify the KDMMs, and all precursor calculations used in generating each
      KDMM. A precursor calculation is an intermediate modeling value with
      explainable meaning that is computed from the input data and determined in the
      process of computing the KDMM. For example, an unscaled consequence score
      is considered a precursor calculation for a scaled risk score, but an intermediate
      activation value of a neural network is not considered a precursor. Similarly, if a
      risk score is normalized by distance (i.e. units of risk per mile), then the raw risk
      score is considered to be a precursor calculation.
 6
 7               The enterprise diagrams show how data feeds into the sub-models and
 8           models that compute the KDMMs. The diagrams show input data, model
 9           components, KDMMs and precursor metrics. The precursor calculation is
10           an intermediate modeling value that is computed from the input data and
11           determined in the process of computing the KDMM:

1   F. Model Risk Landscape (EUP Guidelines Section 2.7.4)

         The Model Risk Landscape is the collection of all inputs, outputs and
    intermediate calculations used in the Risk Modeling Methodology. This includes
    all KDMMs, their precursor calculations, and any additional numerical evidence
    that the Large Electrical Corporation uses to evaluate or report the risk reduction
    of an Undergrounding Project or Alternative Mitigation. The Large Electrical
    Corporation must incorporate the elements of the Model Risk Landscape in its
    narrative supporting the Risk Modeling Methodology.
        All claims involving the comparative risks of individual Undergrounding
    Projects must be substantiated by numerical comparisons between Model Risk
    Landscapes using the same version and calibration of the Risk Modeling
    Methodology.
        A Model Risk Landscape is determined by these four elements:
    1. The model version must indicate a unique configuration of the models as
       detailed in Section 2.7.5.2 of these Guidelines.
    2. The calibration settings must uniquely identify the collection of non-project
       related input data fed into the models or used in historical tables.
    3. The project list must refer to all projects that the model is considering in a
       specific evaluation for this measurement of Model Risk Landscape.
    4. The forecast time must indicate what instantaneous time or accumulative
       period the model is evaluating.


2          PG&E explains how the elements of the model risk landscape are
3      incorporated into our Risk Modeling Methodology in Section C.1, Overview of
4      Risk Modeling Methodology, above. Each element of the model risk landscape
5      is outlined below:
       (1) Model configuration: See Section I (Version and Calibration Changes)
           below for further details on PG&E’s response to Section 2.7.5.2 of the
           Guidelines.
       (2) Calibration settings: See the Model Report Chapters (Sections D.1–D.7)
           for comprehensive details regarding the input data incorporated into the
           models and the historical tables utilized.
       (3) Project list: See Section I (Version and Calibration Changes) and Core
           Capability 6 (Section G.6) below for details of PG&E’s Baseline approach.
       (4) Forecast time: See Core Capability 4 (Section G.4) below.
